translations.text: Ecclesiastical History, that is, the histories of the Church, by Mar Eusebius of Caesarea.
The first book of the histories of the Church.
Chapter One. The subject of its opening. Chapter Two. Summary sections concerning the preexistence of the divinity of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
Chapter Three. The names Jesus and Christ, which were known and honored among the holy prophets. Chapter Four.
The teaching of reverence for God that he proclaimed was neither a shadow nor something foreign. Chapter Five. The times when he appeared among human beings. Chapter Six.
In his time, as prophecy had declared, the rulers came to an end who, from ancient times, through the ancestral line of the Jews,
had been their leaders, drawn from their own people; and Herod became the first king over them from among the Gentiles.
Chapter Seven. The record of Christ’s genealogy, concerning which the evangelists appear to disagree with one another. Chapter Eight.
The murderous plot that Herod devised against the children of Bethlehem, and the terrible end that befell him. Chapter Nine. The time of Pilate.
Chapter Ten. The Jewish high priests in whose days our Lord taught. Chapter Eleven. The testimonies given concerning John the Baptist and Christ.
Chapter Twelve. The disciples of our Savior. Chapter Thirteen. An account of the king of Edessa.
Chapter One. The subject of its opening. I have wished to set down in writing the succession of the apostles from the days of our Savior down to our own time,
and how many events, and of what kind, are said to have occurred in the histories of the churches,
and who those people were who served with distinction as heads and leaders in the well-known congregations,
and who those people were who, in each generation, proclaimed the word of God, whether orally or in writing,
and who and how many the teachers of the error of falsely named knowledge were, and at what times they sprang up,
and mercilessly attacked Christ’s flock like destructive wolves. Along with these things, I will record what immediately befell the Jewish people because of what they dared to do against our Savior,
and how and at what times God’s good news was persecuted by the Gentiles, and which people in every age endured the struggle for the name of our Lord,
through tortures, torments, and bloodshed; and along with these things, also the martyrs of our own days,
and the help given through our Savior’s mercy in every age. Since I wish to write these things, I ought to begin my account
with the earliest dispensation of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. But I ask those with discernment to understand from my own words—
for I acknowledge it—that fully carrying out this promise is beyond my strength.
For we are the first to undertake this subject, like someone traveling an untrodden road, and we pray that God will be our guide,
and that our Lord’s power will come to our aid. For we have found no clear footprints of others who traveled this road before us,
but only small starting points for histories, which various people, in the times when they lived, left us in separate portions.
And, as though from a great mountain, with the radiance of their voices they cry out as though from a resting place on high.
They direct us along the road we should take and set the course of our account straight for us, without error.
Now all the things that we consider suitable for this subject, from those scattered throughout the records of the earlier writers,
we will gather like flowers from meadows of words—the flowers of their voices—and incorporate them into the narrative of our history. We will present the succession of our Savior’s apostles,
the memory of which is preserved in the well-known churches down to our own day, if not of them all, then at least of those who are known among them.
The labor of this subject that we have undertaken is very worthwhile, since, among the earlier writers who belonged to the church,
we have not found anyone who devoted himself to writing about this subject. But I hope there will be some benefit
for those who love learning in the telling of this history. Until now, some of this subject
has been outlined by us, section by section, in the chronological histories that we previously compiled. But now I have made every effort to complete this history that we have undertaken.
Chapter Two. Sections of the chapters concerning the preexistence of the divinity of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
I will therefore begin my account, as I said before, with the exalted and glorious divinity of Christ, which precedes this dispensation in the flesh.
For it is also fitting for someone who intends to set down in writing the history of the church’s affairs
to begin his account of our Lord from above. For it is from his divinity that his humanity received this title of Christ.
For his form has two distinct aspects and can be compared to a body: his divinity is the head,
and his humanity [?], which he put on for our salvation, is compared to the feet. Therefore, when we begin our account with the preexistence of his divinity,
the history will be complete in its proper order. Through this, the early origin and antiquity of the Christians will also become known,
which was glorious before God even in ancient times, and did not, as some suppose, appear only recently.
As for the birth and the glory of Christ’s being, no account is sufficient to describe them, as the Spirit of God said in prophecy:
“Who can recount his generation?” For just as no one knows the Father except the Son, so no one can know the Son as he truly is
except the Father alone, who begot him. For the light that existed before the world, the wisdom that exists in its own perfect being, and the living Word who is God,
who was with his Father from creation—who can conceive of him worthily except the Father? He alone is the offspring of the Godhead,
who existed before all created things, visible and invisible, the commander of the immortal heavenly hosts,
the one who is Wonder and Counselor, who carries out the Father’s hidden will, who is the creator of everything together with the Father,
who is the cause of everything that came into being, who is the true and only Son of God, who is Lord and God and King over all,

who possesses dominion and authority equally, together with power, divinity, and glory, from the nature of the Father’s being, according to the mystery that the Scriptures declare concerning his divinity.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Everything came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being. This same thing also Moses, the first and chief of the prophets,
when he wrote by the Spirit [?] of God about the coming into being and ordering of created things, wrote about him, about Christ, that he is the creator and maker of everything.
That is, about God the Word, who was begotten from the beginning. God made him his partner in the formation of humanity. For God said,
“Let us make a human being in our image, according to our likeness.” Another prophet confirmed this statement when he said about God in his songs of praise,
“He spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created.” That is, he associates the Son with the Father in what he wills.
To this [?], the chief Word, [?] all those who became renowned for righteousness and for the glorious conduct of reverence for God,
those of Moses’ company and those before him, Abraham and his sons, and those who afterward appeared as righteous people and prophets,
saw him with the clear eye of the mind, and [?] offered him the worship due to the Son of God. He was the teacher of them all concerning the knowledge of the Father.
For it says, “The Lord God appeared to Abraham as an ordinary man while he was sitting beside the oak of Mamre.” Abraham fell down and worshiped.
Although with his eyes he saw a human being, he worshiped him as God and pleaded with him as Lord, acknowledging that he was not mistaken about who he was,
when he spoke these words: “Lord, Judge of all the earth, let this judgment not be carried out.” Now God and the Lord who judges all the earth,
who appeared in human form—who else could he be called but God the Word, who existed from ancient times, about whom it is said in the psalm,
“He sent his word and healed them and rescued them from destruction”? About this one, who is truly Lord together with the Father, Moses plainly says,
“The Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord.” This one, who appeared to Jacob in human form,
Scripture calls God. For he said to Jacob, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but your name will be Israel, because you have prevailed with God.”
Jacob called that place “Vision of God,” for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been spared.”
For as for the appearances of God that have been recorded, to suppose that they were appearances of subordinate, ministering angels
is not permitted to us. For whenever one of them appeared to human beings, Scripture does not conceal his identity: it calls them neither Lord nor God,
but angels, as one can easily learn from many passages. This one, Joshua too, who succeeded Moses, as one ruling over the angels of heaven,
the archangels, and the glorious powers, calls “commander of the Lord’s armies,” when he saw him in human form.
For it is written that when Joshua was in the plain of Jericho, he raised his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, with his sword drawn and held in his hand.
Joshua approached him and said to him, “Are you one of us or one of our enemies?” He said to him, “I am the commander of the Lord’s armies, and now I have come.”
Joshua fell facedown on the ground and said to him, “My lord, what do you command your servant?” The commander of the Lord’s armies said to Joshua,
“Take your sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy.” From here it becomes known from these very words.
That this was not the one who appeared to Moses. For Scripture says that these same words were also spoken to him:
“When the Lord saw that Moses had approached to look, the Lord called to him from the bush and said, ‘Moses, Moses!’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’
And he said, ‘Do not come any closer. Take your sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is a holy place.’
And he said to him, ‘I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob.’” Thus it was already known
that before the world there existed a living being, complete in its own person, which shared with the Father and God of all in the formation of everything that was created.
This being was called the Word of God and Wisdom. Thus the Word existed as God from the beginning, and he appeared to certain individuals, though not to everyone.
We have said these things briefly. But humanity’s earliest way of life will clearly show why he was not proclaimed to all nations in ancient times as he is now.
It lacked the strength to receive the teaching of Christ’s glorious wisdom. For when the first human being despised God’s command,
he was deprived of that glorious life and immediately cast into this short-lived mortal life. He exchanged that delight in God for this accursed earth.
Those who came after him and filled the whole earth proved worse than he was, except for one or two. And, like animals,
they chose for themselves a life that was no life at all. They did not even give any thought to cities, civilized conduct, or wisdom.
As for laws, judgments, or the pursuit of wisdom, they would not accept even their names. Instead, they lived like wild, savage herds in the wilderness.
Through the great wickedness of their own will, they corrupted their rightful natural reasoning and the peaceful seed of knowledge within the soul.
They gave themselves over completely to every kind of defilement. Sometimes they destroyed one another, and sometimes they killed one another.
Sometimes they ate human beings. In those battles of the giants that are famous among everyone, they even planned to build a tower from earth to heaven.
In the madness of their minds, they prepared to wage war from their own dwelling place against the one who is God over all.
Because they behaved in this way, God brought punishment upon them through floods of water and fire, as though they were forest thickets spread over the whole earth.
With continual famines, plagues, wars, and fire striking down from above, he brought them to an end.
And through the bitter suffering of these punishments, he restrained the grievous sickness of their souls.
But when wickedness had spread over almost everyone and, like a powerful drunkenness, overshadowed and darkened human souls,
then the Wisdom of God, who is the eternal Word, the one who existed from the beginning, in his great compassion for humanity,
sometimes appeared through visions of angels, while at other times the Power of God himself, who is our Savior, appeared in human form to one or two of his friends of old.
For they could not see him in any other way. But when, through these people, the seeds of reverence for God had been sown among a multitude of human beings,
one entire people, the Hebrews, turned to reverence for God. Yet because they still followed many of the nations’ ancient customs,

he introduced to them, through the prophet Moses, the image and symbol of the Sabbath, circumcision, and other symbolic observances. He did not, however, impart the full reality of the mystery itself.
Now when the law laid down for these people became widely known, it spread among all human beings like a sweet fragrance.
Through these people, moreover, also a great many of the nations, through the lawgivers and philosophers who were in every region,
the minds of many were turned from that harshness and brutality toward peace and gentleness, so that there would be abundant peace,
and love and fellowship with one another. And henceforth, for all human beings, for all the nations in the world,
as people who had already received help and were now able to receive knowledge of the Father, he, that teacher of excellent and glorious things,
who shares with the Father in all good things, the Word of God and his Wisdom, put on a body and brought reconciliation to the human race.
He appeared at the beginning of Roman rule, and did and suffered the things that fulfilled the words of the prophecies.
For it had been foretold through the prophets that God [?] would come into the world as a human being, and would perform glorious deeds,
and teach all the nations to worship the Father. Moreover, concerning the excellence of his knowledge, his new teaching, and his marvelous deeds,
it had been foretold, and along with these things, also the manner of his death, his resurrection from the dead, and his ascent into heaven,
and that his humanity was perfected through his divinity. As for his kingdom at the end, Daniel saw a vision of God in the Spirit,
and depicted it for us in human terms. For he said, “I watched as thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down. His clothing was white as snow,
and the hair of his head was like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire. A river of fire flowed and came out from before him.
A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened.”
And afterward he said, “I watched as one like a son of man came on the clouds of heaven and [?] as far as the Ancient of Days.
He was brought before him, and authority, honor, and a kingdom were given to him, and all nations and languages would serve him.
His authority is an everlasting authority that does not pass away, and his kingdom will not be replaced.” These things were clearly fulfilled in our Savior himself,
who was in the beginning with God, the Word who is God, and who was called the Son of Man because he put on our humanity in the last days.
But since in another discourse we have collected and gathered from the prophets everything said about our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, these things are sufficient for the present account.
Now it is time to show how the name of Jesus Christ was honored among the prophets, the friends of God.
Chapter Three. On the name of Jesus and of Christ, which was known and honored among the holy prophets. Moses was the first to show that the name of Christ was revered and glorified.
Through heavenly patterns, and through [?] and earthly likenesses, according to the voice that said to him, “Make everything with such care,
according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain,” he revealed the high priest of God. And insofar as it was possible for him to be named among human beings,
he called this very person Christ. And for this exalted office, which stood above every rank among human beings,
he assigned the name of Christ, for honor and praise. In this way he made it known that the name of Christ is a divine name. Again, Moses himself,
He also foresaw the name Jesus through the Spirit of God and bestowed it on him as a distinguished title, a name that had never before been used among human beings,
until the name Jesus was made known to Moses. And this very name Jesus, for the first time, upon the man who, in figures and types, received leadership over the whole people
after his death, he bestowed as a name. But he had previously had another name, the one that had been [?] for him by his people.
That was Hoshea son of Nun. But Moses himself called him Joshua, as an honor greater than a royal crown. For this Joshua son of Nun
had put on the likeness of our Savior, who alone received leadership over the fulfillment of the true ministry,
which had been entrusted to Moses in mystery and in types. Now Moses, upon two men who were with him,
who surpassed all the people in their admirable conduct—one in his high priesthood, and the other who received leadership after him—
bestowed, as an honor, the name of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. The prophets who came afterward also proclaimed Christ explicitly by name.
They also testified beforehand to what he was to suffer at the hands of the Jews, and also to the calling of the nations that would take place through him.
At one time Jeremiah spoke as follows: “The breath of our nostrils, the Lord’s anointed, was caught in their pits, he of whom we said, ‘In his shadow
we shall live among the nations.’” Again, David, astonished at these things, said: “Why have the nations raged and the peoples plotted in vain?
The kings of the earth and its rulers rose up and took counsel together against the Lord and against his anointed.” After this, he spoke as though in the person of Christ:
“The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.’”
It was not only those honored with the high priesthood, who were symbolically anointed with fragrant ointment,
whom the name Christ adorned among the Hebrews, but also the kings whom the prophets anointed as in a mystery of God.
They made them anointed ones, as bearers of a shadow. For they too had put on the likeness of him who alone is the true Christ,
who reigns over all—in kingship, authority, and leadership. Again, some of the prophets who were anointed were also figuratively called anointed ones.
For the figure that these men bore pointed to him who is the true Christ, God the Word,
who alone is high priest over all, and alone is king over all created things,
and alone is the chief of the Father’s prophets. The proof of this is that not one of those earlier men who were symbolically anointed,
whether priests, kings, or chief prophets, possessed such glorious divine power
as our Savior, our Lord Jesus, displayed, he who alone is the true Christ. And not one of these men, even though they held honored ranks
and were praised among their people throughout all generations, ever called those under their authority Christians
after that borrowed figure which they possessed. Nor did any of them receive the honor of worship from their subjects.
Nor, even after their deaths, did people show such loving devotion toward them as to be ready to die for their sake.
Nor, among all the nations under heaven, had there ever been such [?] for any one of those who came before.
For neither did their symbolism possess such power as to accomplish anything like this, as truth itself demonstrated through our Savior.
He did not receive the insignia and symbols of the high priesthood from anyone, nor did he belong by bodily descent to a priestly family.
Nor did he establish his kingdom through armed men, nor was he called a prophet like those who had come before.
Nor did he have any rank or authority among the Jews. Yet, although not symbolically, he was truly adorned with all these things by the Father.
For, as I said before, he was not deemed worthy of all these things in the same way as they were, and called Christ for that reason.
Rather, because he alone is the true Christ, he named Christians after his holy and glorious name and filled the whole world with them.
There were no longer types or likenesses, but revealed truth and a heavenly way of life.
And he imparted the glory of his commandments to those who obeyed him. His anointing was not one prepared with fragrant substances.
Rather, he received it through the Spirit of God, as befits God, from the very being of the Father's divinity. Isaiah also teaches this very thing.
Speaking as though in the person of Christ, he proclaimed: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.
He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind.” And it was not Isaiah alone; David also proclaimed concerning him:
“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is an upright scepter. You have loved righteousness and hated injustice.
Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond those who were anointed.” In this statement, in the first clause, he calls him God.
In the second, he honors him with “the scepter of your kingdom.” Then, as he proceeds in the same statement, after the power of divinity and kingship,
in the third place he shows that he became the Anointed One, not with oil prepared from created things, but with that anointing [?] of gladness that is in God.
This showed the superiority of his anointing, which was distinct from that of those earlier men, who were anointed symbolically and figuratively with material substances.
And again, in another place, he spoke of him in this way: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool beneath your feet.’ And in the splendors of holiness, from the womb, from before time, I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not lie:
‘You are a priest forever in the likeness of Melchizedek.’” Now this Melchizedek, whom the Scriptures identify as a priest of God Most High,
is not shown to have been anointed with fragrant oil, nor did he belong to the hereditary lineage associated with the priesthood of the Hebrews.
For this reason our Savior is called an anointed one and a priest in his likeness, and not in the likeness of those who were anointed ones and priests through insignia and types,
but through the oaths he received. For this reason, the account [?] does not report that he was physically anointed by the Jews,
nor that he came from a priestly family, but that he was begotten of God himself before created things,
and holds a priesthood that neither dies nor grows old, forever and ever. He received a spiritual and divine anointing.
This is the great and clear proof of it: of all who have lived in every generation down to our own day, he alone is called Christ.
Among all the people throughout the world, everyone bears witness to him and acknowledges him by this name.
Greeks. And to this day, throughout all creation, he is honored as a king by all who acknowledge him.
He is spoken of with greater wonder than the prophets and is praised as truly the high priest of God.
And beyond all these things, he is God the Word, begotten before all ages. By nature he has from his Father the honor of worship, and he is worshiped as God.
For he truly comes from the one who is truly God. But what surpasses everything
is that those who love him honor him not merely with shouting or with spoken words, but with the soul’s perfect love.
And bearing witness to him is dearer to us even than our lives. We have rightly placed all these things before the account of the history,
so that no one should suppose that the teaching of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, is recent and new because of the events of the time of his humanity.
Fourth [?]. That the teaching about devotion to God proclaimed by our Savior was neither recent nor foreign.
Again, so that no one should suppose that his teaching is foreign and recent, as though it had only just been proclaimed, or that we have nothing in common with the rest of humanity,
let us also say a little about this. For although the coming of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, has only recently shone upon all humanity,
and we acknowledge that our people is new, nevertheless the people who have believed in him are not a small or weak people situated somewhere in a corner of the earth.
Rather, they are present among all nations and are numerous, fearing God and neither destroyed nor overcome.
God is always their helper. And so, suddenly, a people honored with the name of Christ appeared before everyone.
One of the prophets also marveled at this, foreseeing with the eye of the Holy Spirit what was going to happen, and spoke as follows:
“Who has heard of such things? And who has seen anything like this—that the earth should go into labor in one day, and a people be born in a single hour?”
This same prophet also made known the name, saying, “You who fear my name will be called by a new name, which will be blessed on earth.”
But although we are new, and the name of Christians has only recently become known among all nations,
the way of life itself, its power, and the established practice of its worship were not recently devised by us.
Rather, from the very beginning of humanity’s formation, it was practiced by the earliest people who loved God, through their natural understanding,
as we shall now show. The Hebrew people are not new; rather, their antiquity is honored among humanity.
For they are a well-known people, and they possess accounts, both oral and written, about people of ancient times, who were few and small in number,
but who excelled before the flood in righteousness, devotion to God, and other praiseworthy ways of life. After it, there were others, one after another, from among the sons
of Noah and his descendants, down to Abraham, in whom the Hebrews boast as the chief of their forefathers.
All those [?] whose righteousness was attested, from Abraham back to the first human being.
If someone were to say that they were Christians in their deeds, even if not in name, he would not depart from the truth.
For what this name [?] requires of a Christian is precisely this: knowledge of Christ and his teaching,
and self-control, righteousness, perseverance in good conduct, and the profession of reverence for God:
to acknowledge that there is only one God over all. In all these things, those people of ancient times were no less diligent than we are.
For they were not concerned about bodily circumcision, just as we are not, nor about observing Sabbaths, just as we are not,
nor about distinctions between foods or the other things that Moses was the first to introduce
and handed down through symbols for those after him to observe. Nor do Christians now observe such things.
Moreover, they clearly knew Christ himself, the Son of God. For it has been made known that he appeared to Abraham,
made promises to Isaac, and spoke with Israel, with Moses, and with the prophets who came after him. From this you can understand
that those very friends of God were considered worthy of the name [?] “anointed ones,” as the word says about them: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets.”
It is therefore clear that this very worship of God, now proclaimed to all nations through Christ’s teaching, should be considered the original and ancient worship
among all those men of Abraham’s household who were friends of God. And although it is said of Abraham that, after a long time, he received the commandment of circumcision,
before that, it is attested that he was justified by faith, as the word of God says about him: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”
While he was in this state, before circumcision, God appeared to him—that is, Christ, the Word of God—and spoke to him
about those who would later be justified as he was, in these words of promise to him: “In you all the families of the earth will be blessed,”
and that he would become a great and numerous nation, and that all the nations of the earth would be blessed in him. That this has been fulfilled in us is evident from the following.
For he was justified by faith in the one who appeared to him, who is the Word of God. He turned away from his fathers’ idols
and from his former misguided practices, and acknowledged the one God over all. He served him through noble deeds,
not through observance of the law given through Moses. And that all the families of the earth and all the nations are blessed in him
has now been made known through deeds that are far clearer and more evident than words. For that same noble way of life is found only among Christians.
What, then, prevents us from acknowledging that we have received from Christ the same way of life and pattern of worshiping God
as those ancient friends of God? His teaching should therefore not be considered new and foreign. Rather, we should truly say
that this alone is the original and true worship of God, which has been handed down to us through Christ’s teaching.

Chapter Five: On the times when he appeared among human beings.

After this introduction, which needed to be placed before the histories of the church,
Let us now speak of our Savior’s appearance in the flesh, and advance into the narrative as though proceeding along a road.
Let us call upon God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior, the Word of God, that he may help us establish the truth of these accounts.
It was the forty-second year of the reign of Augustus, twenty-eight years after Egypt had been subjugated,
and Antony and Cleopatra had died, and the so-called mighty dynasty of the Ptolemies had finally come to an end,
when our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in accordance with the prophecy concerning him,
during the first census, which took place then under Quirinius’s governorship of Syria. This census, which took place in the time of Quirinius,
is also mentioned by Flavius Josephus, a well-known man among the historians of the Hebrews.
He also follows it with another account concerning the sect of the Galileans that arose at that time.
Luke also mentions this for us in Acts, saying, “After him Judas the Galilean arose in those days of the census,
and some of the people followed him. He too perished, and those who had been persuaded by him were scattered.”
The man we mentioned earlier also agrees with these things, setting them down in his own words as follows:
“Quirinius, a member of the senate, who had held other offices and passed through them all, becoming consul, and who was also highly distinguished in other respects,
came to Syria with a few companions, having been sent by Caesar to be an impartial judge of the people and an assessor of their property.” A little later he says:
“But Judas, a Gaulanite from a city called Gamala, joined forces with Zadok the Pharisee and worked eagerly to stir up a revolt among the people.
For they said that this census would bring slavery, and they encouraged the people and filled them with confidence in the hope of freedom.”
And in the second book of the history of the Jewish War, he wrote these things about this same man:
“In his time a Galilean man named Judas arose. He drew the people into rebellion and reproached the people of the country,
if they agreed to pay a poll tax to the Romans and, after God, to have mortal masters over them.” These are the words of Josephus.
At that time Herod had received the kingship over the Jews, becoming the first king from among the Gentiles to rule over them.
In him the prophecy given through Moses was fulfilled, which said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor an interpreter from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs.
And he shall be the expectation of the nations.” This prediction had remained unfulfilled,
as long as they were allowed to have rulers over them from their own people, beginning with Moses and continuing until the reign of Augustus,
in whose days Herod, the first ruler from among the Gentiles, received authorization from the Romans to rule over the Jewish people.
As Josephus explains, he was Idumean by descent on his father’s side and Arabian on his mother’s side. Africanus also gives an account,
and he too was no ordinary man among the historians.
As those who know his history well say about him, Herod had a father named Antipater, the son of Heros of Ashkelon.
He was one of those who served in the temple of Apollo.
This Antipater was taken captive by bands of Edomites when he was a boy, and he remained with them.
For his father, who was poor, did not have enough to pay his ransom. And when he had been brought up in their customs,
he eventually became a friend of Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews. The son of this Antipater was Herod, who lived in the days of our Savior.
When the kingship of the Jews came to this man of such origins, the one awaited by the nations was now at the door, as the prophecy had said.
From his days, those from whom chiefs and rulers had arisen disappeared—the succession that had begun with Moses.
Before their captivity and deportation to Babylon, they had first begun to appoint Saul and David as kings over them. But before the kings and chiefs,
they were governed by those who were called judges, who in turn had begun after Moses and Joshua, who succeeded him.
After their return from Babylon, government among them did not come to an end, for the high priests were in charge of their affairs,
until Pompey, the Roman general, rose against them, captured Jerusalem, plundered it, and defiled their sanctuary.
He even entered the Holy of Holies. And the man named Aristobulus, who held the kingship by succession from the days of their ancestors,
he sent in chains to Rome with his sons. He handed over the high priesthood to this man's brother, Hyrcanus.
From then on, he required the entire Jewish people to pay tribute to the Romans.
Then Hyrcanus too, with whom the succession of high priests came to an end, was taken captive by the Parthians.
Then, as I mentioned earlier, he received kingship over the Jewish people from [?] the Roman Senate and from Emperor Augustus.
In his days Christ came, the hope of salvation arrived, and the calling of the nations was fulfilled, as had been declared in prophecy.
Sixth: That in his time, as the prophecy had said, the chiefs came to an end—those who from ancient times, through the succession of their ancestors, had provided rulers over them.
And Herod became the first king over them from among the Gentiles. After the time when chiefs and rulers had ceased among the Jewish people, the high priesthood too,
which from the days of their ancestors had been maintained among those who received it by succession in every generation, was suddenly thrown into disorder in the time of our Lord.
You have Josephus as a trustworthy witness to these things. He explains that when Herod received the kingship from the Romans,
he no longer appointed high priests from that original family, but gave this honor to ordinary men.
Like Herod, his son Archelaus also caused disorder in the high priesthood, as did, after him, the Romans who assumed authority over the Jews.
This same Josephus explains that Herod was also the first to lock away the sacred robe of the high priests and bring it under his own control.
He did not allow it to remain in the custody of the high priests. Archelaus did the same, and after him the Romans.
We have said these things to demonstrate the final prophecy, which was fulfilled when our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, appeared.
Moreover, this is stated plainly in Daniel, in the specified number of weeks that he set as the limit until the Messiah, the ruler.
We have discussed these elsewhere. He prophesied that, after they were completed, the anointed succession that had existed among the Jews would be destroyed.
This very thing is plainly shown to have been fulfilled at the time of the birth of our Savior, our Lord Jesus. Let these things be preserved [?] to establish the accuracy of the chronology.
Chapter Seven. On the genealogy of Christ, in which the evangelists appear not to agree with one another.
Now because the evangelists Matthew and Luke have handed down Christ’s genealogy to us differently, and seem to many to contradict one another,
and each of the believers who is not acquainted with the truth of this designation is ready to devise explanations, let us present the account we have received concerning this.
It is the account that Africanus, whom we mentioned a little earlier, wrote in a letter to Aristides.
He also wrote about the agreement of the genealogies recorded by the evangelists, and criticized the conjectures that many had made about this,
saying that they were false and did violence to the truth. He set out the account he himself had received in these words: “Since the names of the generations in Israel were reckoned
either according to nature or according to the law—according to the law, that is, when someone was born to be reckoned as the son of a brother who had died childless, to preserve his name.
For the hope of the resurrection of the dead had not yet been clearly given.
Mortals substituted this for the promise that was to be fulfilled in the resurrection, so that the name of the dead man would not disappear.
Now, among those whom we have recorded in this genealogy, some sons descended from their natural fathers, while others were born to one man and became the sons of another.
Thus the names of both were recorded: those who fathered the children and those for whom the children were born.
For this reason, neither evangelist spoke falsely in reckoning the generations according to nature and according to the law. For the family lines of Solomon and Nathan became intermingled,
through those who raised up children for their brothers who had died, and through those who married two wives.
These same children were rightly regarded as the sons of those who had died, according to the law,
and as the sons of those who had fathered them, according to nature. Thus both these genealogical accounts truly come down to Joseph,
differently, indeed, but accurately. To make what I have said clear, I will recount the difference between the family lines.
When the generations are counted from David through Solomon, Matthan is found to be third from the end. He fathered Jacob, Joseph’s father.
But from Nathan, David’s son, as Luke shows, Melchi is found to be third from the end. For Joseph was the son of Heli, the son of Melchi.
Our purpose, then, is to show concerning Joseph how the account presents both men as his fathers, through whom the family lines descend:
Jacob from Solomon and Heli from Nathan; and how Jacob and Heli were both brothers.
Before them, their fathers, Matthan and Melchi, both married the same woman, whose name was Estha, and fathered two brothers by one mother.
For the law did not forbid a woman who had been widowed or divorced by her husband to marry another man.
First, Matthan, whose lineage is traced from Solomon, fathered Jacob. When Matthan died and she was widowed, Melchi married her.
His lineage is traced from Nathan. He belonged to the same tribe, but to another family, as we said earlier.
When he married her, he fathered Eli. Thus, although these two family lines are distinct,
we find that Jacob and Eli were brothers by the same mother. When his brother Eli died childless, Jacob married his wife
and fathered Joseph by her, the third in the line. He was his son by nature, and for this reason it is written, “Jacob fathered Joseph.”
Legally, however, he was Eli’s son. For Jacob raised up offspring for him because he was his brother.
For this reason the record of his genealogy was not broken off. When Matthew lists him, he says, “Jacob fathered Joseph.”
Luke, however, reckoning upward from below, says, “As was supposed, he was the son of Joseph, the son of Eli, the son of Melchi.”
For in the case of a lineage based on law rather than nature, he could not say, “He fathered.”
Instead, because this relationship was one of adoption, he omitted “he fathered” until he traced the line up to Adam.
He said, “The son of Adam, the son of God,” and ended there. We have not said these things without evidence, nor are they some mere conjecture.
Rather, those who belonged to our Savior’s family according to the flesh, or who knew him, taught them plainly and handed them down truthfully, together with the following account.
The Edomites [?] attacked Ashkelon, a city in Palestine, and took captive from the temple of Apollo, which stood beside the city wall,
Antipater, the son of Herod, who was a servant in that temple, along with the other captives, and led him away.
Since this priest did not have the means to pay for his son’s release, Antipater was brought up according to the customs of the Edomites.
Later he became friends with Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews. He served as his envoy to Pompey and secured for him his kingdom,
which was being torn apart and devastated by his brother Aristobulus. After succeeding in these affairs, he became an administrator—that is, the governor of Palestine.
His son Herod succeeded Antipater after he was treacherously murdered out of envy for his great success.
He in turn [?] became king over the Jews by order of Antoninus, Emperor Augustus, and the Senate.
His sons were Herod the tetrarch and the other tetrarchs. These accounts also agree with the history of the Greeks.
Until that time, the genealogies of the Hebrews had been recorded in the archives, including even those of converts,
such as Ahiud from the Ammonites and Ruth from the Moabites, and the mixed multitude that came up with them from Egypt.
But Herod, because he had no place in the lineage of the house of Israel, and his conscience tormented him over his shameful ancestry,
burned the entire written record of the genealogies of the Jews, thinking that he would appear to come from a distinguished family.
Since there was no one else who could trace his family line from the public records and take it back as far as the patriarchs, or to the proselytes,
or to those of mixed ancestry among them, a few of the diligent people among them made a simple record of their family lines,
either because they remembered the names, or because they happened to possess those records we mentioned earlier.
The Lord’s relatives boasted of their connection with our Savior’s family. They were from Nazareth and Cochaba, villages in Judea.
When they went out to other lands, they recounted what they could from the book of days, that is, from the book of genealogies.
Whether this is how it happened or otherwise, I do not think anyone else can find a clearer account.
Everyone with discernment should join us in this endeavor, even if the account has no supporting testimony, since no one can offer an account better and more reliable than this.
The Gospel, however, is certainly reliable. At the end of this letter he added the following:
“Matthan, who descended from Solomon, fathered Jacob. When Matthan died, Melchi, who descended from Nathan, also fathered Heli by the same woman.
Heli and Jacob were therefore brothers, sons of the same mother. Heli died without children,
and Jacob raised up offspring for him by fathering Joseph: by natural descent, for himself, but according to the law, for Heli.
Thus Joseph was the son of both.” Africanus said all these things. Now, because Joseph was recorded in the genealogies,
Mary too was necessarily shown along with him to belong to the same tribe, because according to the law of Moses,
they were not permitted to mix one tribe with another. For he commanded that a woman should be joined in marriage to a man from the same people and the same tribe,
so that the family’s allotted inheritance would not be transferred from tribe to tribe. Let this much suffice on these matters.
Chapter Eight. The murderous plot Herod devised against the children of Bethlehem,
and the terrible end that befell him. Now when Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea, according to the testimony of prophecy, at the time we indicated earlier,
Magi came from the east and asked, “Where is the king who has been born to the Jews?
For we have seen his star.” This was the reason for the entire journey they had undertaken with such great eagerness: to come and worship the newborn child as God.
Herod was deeply disturbed by this matter, for he thought that his rule was being taken away from him.
He asked the people’s teachers of the law where they expected the Christ to be born. When he learned that Micah’s prophecy said Bethlehem,
with a single command he ordered all the children in Bethlehem and throughout its surrounding territory, aged two years and under,
to be killed, in accordance with the time the Magi had told him. He thought that Jesus too would perish along with those children.
But a vision of an angel forestalled his plot, informing Jesus’ family of what was about to happen. They took him and fled to Egypt.
These things the sacred text of the Gospel teaches. Now we should see what befell Herod because of his outrageous actions against Christ and against those children of Bethlehem.
For immediately, at that very moment, the righteous judgment of God overtook him, while he was still alive in the world.
Already here, he showed him beforehand what he would suffer after departing from the world. And the royal prosperity that he had expected would be his—
many sorrows overtook it because of the murders he committed in his household, of his wife and his sons, and of the rest of those who were beloved and [?] in his family.
But we cannot enumerate these things now, for the account of their history is related at length by Josephus in the histories he wrote.
At the very time of the murderous plot he carried out against our Savior and those children, the blow of God overtook him and pursued him to his death.
It would not be amiss to hear the historian’s own words, which he wrote as follows about the terrible end of his life.
He says that Herod’s illness grew much worse, for God was exacting punishment from him for his wrongdoing.
For the fire of a low fever burned within him. Outwardly it did not reveal its burning to the same extent that its torment intensified within.
He had no desire at all to take any food, because it would not pass through.
There was an ulcer and severe pain in his intestines, and a watery swelling in his feet. His genitals, he says, had rotted and swarmed with worms.
The shortness of breath that afflicted him also tormented and distressed him, with a foul smell and frequent, labored gasping.
Severe pains struck him from every side, and he had no strength to endure them. It was said by those who spoke as though from God,
and by those who wisely foretold such things, that because of the many wicked murders he had committed,
God was exacting punishment from him, the king. Again, in another historical account similar to this,
this same historian said of him that when the illness seized him, it subjected his body to various pains.
For he had a lingering fever and incessant itching throughout his body, and severe pain in his intestines.
His feet were swollen like those of someone suffering from a buildup of fluid, and his genitals had a putrefaction that bred worms. There was also shortness of breath,
called in Greek orthopnea and dyspnea, and severe distress in all his limbs. Those who spoke as though from God said
that this illness was punishment. But while he was being tormented by all these pains, he struggled to live and looked for deliverance.
He sought ways to obtain treatment for himself. He crossed the Jordan and used the hot spring at Callirrhoe,
whose waters flow into the Asphalt Lake and are sweet and pleasant to drink. The physicians thought it best to bathe his whole body there in oil.
When he was completely immersed in a vessel full of oil, he collapsed and his eyes rolled back. Great alarm arose among his servants.
But he endured the pain. [?] his soldiers fifty shekels, and much gold to the governors and his friends.
He returned to Jericho, raging, embittered, and threatening death itself. He became all the more determined in plotting an evil deed.
For he gathered prominent men from all the towns of Judea into the place called the horse-racing arena, and ordered that they be counted.
He called his sister Salome and her husband Alexas and said to them, “I know that my death will be a festival for the Jews.
But I can have others mourn for me and make the mourning over me splendid, if you are willing to carry out my command.
As soon as I die, set soldiers over these men who are imprisoned and kill them,
so that all Judea and all my household will weep for me, even against their will.” A little later he spoke again.
For he was in distress because he could not take food, and he was racked by the severe pain of a cough.
As he suffered from his pains, he wanted to bring forward the day of his death. He took an apple and asked for a knife.
For he was accustomed to cut it up and eat it that way. Then he stood up to see whether anyone was there to stop him.
He raised his right hand to kill himself. . . . Along with all these things, this same historian relates
that, a short time before he died, one of his sons, in addition to the two others whom he had already killed—
he killed this third one too, and then died in bitter pain. Such was the end of Herod’s death, when just judgment was exacted from him
for killing those children in Bethlehem through the plot he devised against our Savior. Afterward an angel appeared to Joseph in Egypt and told him
to take the child and his mother and go to the land of Judea. He told him that those who sought the child’s life had died.
After this, the evangelist says that he heard that Archelaus had become king in place of his father Herod, and he was afraid to go there.
He saw in a dream that he should go to the region of Galilee. Concerning the reign of Archelaus after Herod, the historian whom we mentioned earlier agrees,
telling how, through the will of his father Herod and the commands of Augustus Caesar, he received the kingship over the Jews,
and how, after completing ten years, he lost his kingship, while his brothers governed tetrarchies,
that is, one of the four divisions of the land of Israel: Philip, Herod the younger, and Lysanias.
Chapter Nine: The Times of Pilate. This same Josephus also says in his history
that in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar—for he received the supreme authority and the whole empire after the fifty-seven years of Augustus’s administration and rule—
Pontius Pilate, he says, received authority over the land of Judea and remained there for ten years, until Tiberius died.
Thus the falsehood fabricated by those who fraudulently composed memoirs about our Savior is easily exposed.
They circulated them some time ago. First, the very date recorded by those who fabricated this falsehood exposes their lie.
For in what they dared to write, they recorded that our Savior’s suffering took place in the fourth consulship of Tiberius, which fell in the seventh year of his reign.
At that time Pilate had not even set foot in Judea, if we should accept the testimony of Josephus, who wrote, as we have already related,
that in the twelfth year of Tiberius’s reign Pilate became governor of Judea by Tiberius’s command.
And in these years, as the evangelist said, in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate governed one of the four divisions of Israel,
and the tetrarchs Herod, Lysanias, and Philip were governing the rest of Judea,
our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Messiah of God, was beginning to be about thirty years old. He came to receive John's baptism, and from that time he began proclaiming the good news.
Chapter Ten: On the high priests of the Jews in whose days our Lord taught. Now the Holy Scripture says concerning our Savior
that the entire period of his teaching was completed during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas.
That is, during the years from the high priesthood of Annas to the beginning of the high priesthood of Caiaphas.
The intervening period was not even four years. For the ordinances of the Law had been overthrown among them.
From that time, the practice by which the high priest was entitled, according to ancestral tradition, to hold office throughout his life had been abolished.
They received appointment to the high priesthood from the Roman governors from time to time.
And they did not retain, from time to time, the authority of the high priesthood. And they did not remain in it for more than one year.
Josephus himself relates that after Annas there were four high priests up to Caiaphas. In his book of history he says as follows:
"Valerius Gratus removed Annas from the high priesthood and appointed Ishmael son of Phabi as high priest after him.
After a short time he removed this man too and appointed Eleazar, the son of Annas the high priest.
When this man too had completed a year, he removed him and appointed Simon son of Camithus. When this man too had completed his year,
Joseph, who was Caiaphas, succeeded him." Thus the entire period of our Savior's teaching does not amount to even four years.
For four high priests completed four years from Annas until Caiaphas took office, each of them serving his year.
As for Caiaphas the high priest, the Gospel makes it clear that he was high priest in the year in which our Savior suffered.
From this we learn that the period of our Savior's teaching was as we have already said.
Now our Savior and Lord, a short time after the beginning of his proclamation, called the twelve apostles.
These alone, above all his other disciples, he named apostles as a special honor.
And afterward he appointed seventy others, whom he also sent ahead of him two by two to every place and town where he was going to go. ...
Chapter Eleven: On the testimonies given concerning John the Baptist and Christ. After a short time, Herod the tetrarch beheaded John the Baptist.
The holy Gospel mentions this. Josephus also relates it and mentions Herodias by name,
saying that she was his brother's wife and that Herod took her as his wife, wronging his first wife, whom he had lawfully married.
She was the daughter of Aretas, king of the people of Petra. He separated Herodias from her husband while her husband was still alive.
For her sake he also killed John. He went to war with Aretas because his daughter had been cast aside.
In this war, when battle took place, Herod’s entire army was destroyed. These things happened to him because of the evil plot he carried out against John.
Josephus himself, in his testimony about John, also acknowledges that he was an exceptionally virtuous and righteous man and a baptizer,
just as it is written about him in the holy Gospel. He also relates that Herod lost his kingdom because of Herodias,
with whom he was driven out and banished beyond the borders into exile, to live in Vienne, a city of Gaul.
Josephus wrote these very things about John as follows: “Some of the Jews thought that Herod’s army had been destroyed by God,
and that vengeance for John, who was called the Baptist, was justly being exacted from him. For Herod killed this John, who was a good man.
He instructed the Jews to practice virtue and justice toward one another, and, while practicing reverence for God, to give thought to his baptism.
For in this way baptism seemed acceptable to him: not as a means of asking forgiveness for particular sins, but for the purification of the body,
after the soul had first been purified by righteousness and by the other qualities that grow along with it. They were also deeply stirred by hearing his words.
But Herod, seeing how persuasive he was with the people, feared that the matter might lead to rebellion.
For they appeared to do everything on his advice. So he reasoned within himself
that it was much better to have him killed beforehand, before he could bring about a change, rather than fall into regret after an upheaval had taken place.
Because of this suspicion of Herod’s, John was sent in chains to the prison called Machaerus, and there he was killed.”
These things he said about John. In this same book of his history he also mentions our Savior as follows:
“At this time there was a wise man named Jesus, if indeed it is right for us to call him a man.
For he performed wonderful deeds and was a teacher of people who eagerly receive the truth.
He made disciples of many Jews and also of many Gentiles. He was the Christ.
On the testimony of the leading men of our people, Pilate handed him over to the punishment of crucifixion. Yet those who loved him did not cease loving him.
For after three days he appeared to them alive again. God’s prophets had spoken these things about him, along with ten thousand other wonders like them.
And to this day the people called Christians, who take their name from him, have not died out.” These things the historian, who was himself one of the Hebrews,
set down long ago in his writings about John the Baptist and our Savior. What refuge, then, is left to those who have now been exposed and confounded,
who fabricated and compiled records against their own interests? But what has been said thus far is enough.
Chapter Twelve: On the Disciples of Our Lord. The names of our Savior’s apostles are known to everyone from the Gospel.
But no account listing the names of those seventy disciples is known anywhere. Barnabas, however, is said to have been one of them.
The Acts of the Apostles mentions him explicitly in many places, as does Paul when writing to the Galatians.
It is also said that Sosthenes, whose name is written alongside Paul's in the letter to the Corinthians, was one of them.
As Clement said in his history, Cephas too—the one whom Clement said in his history [?].
Cephas too, about whom Paul said, “When Cephas came to Antioch, I rebuked him face to face,” was one of those seventy.
He bore the same name as Peter the apostle. And Talmai, who was numbered among the apostles in place of Judas, and also Justus, who [?] with him in the drawing of lots,
are said to have been among the seventy. Thaddeus too is said to have been one of them. I will now set down the account about him that has come down to us.
You can also find more than these seventy who were known to have been disciples of our Savior,
as is clear from the testimony of Paul, who said that after our Savior's resurrection from the dead, he appeared first to Cephas,
and after him to the Twelve, and afterward he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once. Some of these, he said, had fallen asleep,
but many of them were still alive at the time when he wrote these things. Afterward, he said, he appeared to James,
who was one of those said to be our Savior's brothers.
And again, from these [?] the Twelve, there were many who became apostles, as Paul himself did.
For he adds, “Afterward he appeared to all the apostles.” These things have been stated briefly.
Chapter thirteen: The account of the king of Edessa. The account concerning Thaddeus was as follows.
When the divinity of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was being proclaimed to all people because of the wonderful miracles he was performing,
multitudes, even from regions far from the land of Judea, who were suffering from illnesses and pains of every kind,
were coming to him in the hope of healing. King Abgar too, who was renowned for his valor among the nations east of the Euphrates,
had his body ravaged by a severe disease for which there was no human cure.
When he heard and learned of Jesus' reputation and of the miracles he was performing, about which everyone testified with one voice,
he sent a letter of petition through a man of his own, begging him to come and heal him of his illness.
But our Savior did not agree to go to him at the time when he invited him. He did, however, honor him with a letter.
For he promised him that he would send one of his disciples to heal his illnesses and give life to him and all his relatives.
Nor was there any delay in fulfilling his promise. After he rose from the dead and was taken up to heaven, Thomas the apostle, one of the Twelve,
sent Thaddeus, who was himself numbered among Christ's seventy disciples, to Edessa through God's working,
to be a herald and proclaimer of the good news of Christ's teaching. Through him Christ's promise was fulfilled.
You have written testimony to these things [?], taken from the book of records that was in Edessa, whose kingdom was still in existence at that time.
Now, among the documents that were there, which contained accounts of what had happened from the earliest times down to Abgar,
these too are still found preserved there to this day. There is nothing to prevent us from hearing the letters themselves, which we have taken from the archives.
Their text, translated from Aramaic into Greek, reads as follows. Copy of the letter written by King Abgar to Jesus.
It was sent to him in Jerusalem through Ananias the courier. Abgar the Black, ruler of the country, to Jesus, the good Savior who has appeared in the region of Jerusalem: greetings.
I have heard about you and about the healing performed by your hands without medicines or roots. For it is said
that you make the blind see and the lame walk, cleanse lepers, and drive out unclean spirits and demons.
You heal those tormented by chronic illnesses and raise the dead. When I heard all these things about you,
I concluded that one of two things must be true: either you are God, who has come down from heaven and does these things,
or you are the Son of God and do these things. For this reason I have written to ask you to take the trouble to come to me
and heal this illness that I have. For I have also heard that the Jews are grumbling against you and want to harm you. I have a small and beautiful city that is large enough for us both.
Copy of what Jesus wrote through Ananias the courier to Abgar, ruler of the country. Blessed is the one who has believed in me without seeing me.
For it is written about me that those who see me will not believe in me, and those who have not seen me will believe and live.
As for your request that I come to you, I must complete here everything for which I was sent.
After I have completed it, I will be taken up to the one who sent me. When I have been taken up, I will send you one of my disciples to heal your illness
and also to give life to you and those with you. The following account is also attached to these letters in the Aramaic language.
After Jesus had ascended, Judas Thomas sent him Thaddaeus the apostle, one of the seventy. When he arrived, he stayed with Tobias son of Tobias.
When word about him spread, they informed Abgar: “An apostle of Jesus has come here, just as he wrote to you.”
Thaddaeus began to heal every illness and disease by the power of God, so that everyone was amazed. When Abgar heard of the great and wonderful things he was doing and the healings he performed,
he thought that this was the man about whom Jesus had written to him, saying, “When I have been taken up, I will send you one of my disciples, who will heal your illness.”
He sent for Tobias, with whom Thaddaeus was staying, and said to him, “I have heard that a powerful man has come and is staying in your house.
Bring him up to me.” When Tobias came to Thaddaeus, he said to him, “King Abgar sent for me and told me to bring you up to him
so that you may heal him.” Thaddaeus said, “I will go up, for it was to him that I was sent with power.”
So Tobias rose early the next day, took Thaddaeus, and came to Abgar. When they went up, his nobles happened to be standing there.
Immediately as he entered, Abgar saw a great vision in the face of Thaddaeus the apostle.
When Abgar saw Thaddaeus, he bowed down before him. Amazement seized everyone standing there.
For they had not seen the vision that appeared to Abgar alone. He began asking Thaddaeus,
“Are you truly a disciple of Jesus, the Son of God, who told me, ‘I will send you one of my disciples,
who will heal you and give you life’?” Thaddaeus answered, “Because you have believed so strongly in the one who sent me,
I have been sent to you. And if you continue to believe in him, the requests of your heart will be granted to you.” Abgar said to him, “To such an extent I [?] in him,
that I wanted to lead an army and destroy those Jews who crucified him, had I not been restrained on account of the Roman Empire.”
Thaddaeus said, “Our Lord fulfilled his Father’s will, and when he had fulfilled it, he was taken up to his Father.” Abgar said to him,
“I too have believed in him and in his Father.” Thaddaeus said, “For this reason, I am laying my hand on you in his name.”
When he did this, Abgar was immediately healed of his illness and the pain he had. Abgar was amazed,
because, just as he had heard about Jesus, so he now saw it in deeds through his disciple Thaddaeus, who healed him without medicines or herbs.
He healed not only him but also Abdu son of Abdu, who had gout. He too had come in and fallen at his feet.
When Thaddaeus prayed over him, he was healed. He also healed many other inhabitants of their city. He performed great deeds and proclaimed the word of God.
After this, Abgar said to him, “You, Thaddaeus, are doing these things by the power of God. We too are amazed at them.
But besides all these things, I ask you to tell me about the coming of Christ: how it happened, and about his power,
and by what power he performed these things I have heard about.” Thaddaeus said, “For now I will be silent. But because I have been sent to proclaim the word of God,
gather all the inhabitants of your city for me tomorrow. I will preach before them and sow the word of life among them.
I will speak about the coming of Jesus and how it happened, and about his mission and why he was sent by his Father,
and about his power and his deeds, and about the mysteries he spoke of in the world, and by what power he performed these things, and about his new proclamation, his lowliness, and his humility,

and how he humbled himself, emptied himself, and made himself lowly, and was crucified and descended to Sheol, and broke through the barrier that had never before been broken through, and raised the dead,
and descended alone but ascended to his Father with a great multitude.” So Abgar commanded all the inhabitants of his city to gather in the morning
and hear the preaching of Thaddaeus. Afterward, he ordered that gold and silver be given to him, but Thaddaeus would not accept it.
He said, “If we have left behind what was ours, how can we take what belongs to others?” These things happened in the year three hundred and forty.
These things, translated word for word from Aramaic into Greek, have been placed here at their proper point in time, not without purpose.
The first book is complete.
The Second Book of the History of the Church.
Chapter One: On the acts of the apostles

Chapter Two: How Tiberius was stirred when he learned about Christ.
