Chapter One: On the acts of the apostles after Christ ascended. Everything that needed to be explained briefly beforehand, before the histories of the church:
concerning the divinity of our Savior, the antiquity of the foundations of our teaching, and the antiquity of the practices of the Christian gospel;
and not only concerning [?], but also concerning the appearing of our Lord in recent times, his suffering, and the choosing of his apostles—
we briefly set out the evidence for these things in the preceding book. Now let us also relate what happened after his ascension.
Some of these things we will record from the Holy Scriptures, and others from histories in secular literature, mentioning them in their proper times.
First, then, Tolmai, who was one of our Lord's disciples, as we have already said, was chosen for the apostleship in place of Judas the betrayer.
Through prayer and the laying on of the apostles' hands, seven approved men were appointed to serve the community: Stephen and his companions.
He was the first after our Lord to be stoned to death at the hands of those who killed their Lord; and together with the laying on of hands that he received,
As though he had been chosen for this very purpose, he was the first to receive the crown of victory belonging to Christ’s martyrs—a crown that matched his name.
Now James, who was called our Lord’s brother because he too was Joseph’s son—Joseph was the man who was thought to be Christ’s father,
to whom Mary the virgin was betrothed; before they came together, she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit,
as the holy text of the Gospel teaches—this James was called “the Just” by the people of old because of his excellent conduct.
It is related that he was the first to receive the bishop’s throne in the church of Jerusalem. Clement writes about him as follows:
“Peter, James, and John, after our Savior’s ascension, being men who had been honored by the Savior himself, had no need of glory.
Instead, they chose James the Just to be bishop of Jerusalem.” In this same account, he also said these things about him:
“After our Lord rose from the dead, he entrusted his knowledge to James the Just, John, and Peter.
They passed it on to the rest [?] of the apostles, and those apostles to the seventy, one of whom was Barnabas.
There were two men named James. One was the Just, who was thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple and was struck with a wooden club by a fuller and died.
The other was the one who was beheaded.” Paul also mentions this James the Just, writing as follows:
“I saw none of the other apostles except James, our Lord’s brother.” Along with these things, our Savior’s promise to the king of Mesopotamia was also being fulfilled.
For Thomas, through God’s working, had sent Thaddaeus to Edessa to be a herald and preacher of Christ’s teaching,
as we explained a little earlier from the document found there. When he arrived in that region, he healed Abgar by Christ’s word.
He astonished all the inhabitants of the region with the wonderful miracles he performed. Through his messengers, he sent them fully to his deeds [?],
and brought them to worship Christ’s power and made them disciples of the teaching of life.
Because of him, the whole city of Edessa remains devoted to Christ’s name to this day, and great evidence of our Savior’s help is plainly visible among them.
These things have been related on the basis of the accounts of earlier generations. Let us now return to the holy Scriptures.
When the first fierce persecution of the church in Jerusalem arose from the Jews at Stephen’s martyrdom,
all the disciples except the twelve were scattered throughout Judea and Samaria, as holy Scripture says.
Some of them traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. They did not, however, dare to proclaim God’s word to the Gentiles,
but preached the good news only to Jews. Paul, meanwhile, was still full of murderous threats against the church.
He entered the homes of believers, seized men and women, and handed them over to prison.
Philip too, one of those chosen for service along with Stephen, was among those who had been scattered.
He went down to Samaria, filled with God’s power, and was the first to proclaim God’s word to the people there. God’s grace was so vigorously at work in him.
How Simon the magician, along with many others, was exposed by his words. Now Simon was renowned at that time among those who were being led astray by his sorcery,
for they regarded him as the great power of God. Then he too, amazed at the wonderful miracles of God that were taking place through Philip,
made a pretense of embracing faith in Christ, even to the point of receiving baptism.
And we should marvel at this very thing: to this day it is practiced by those who belong to his filthy heresy,
who employ the deceit of their father, which is passed down among them like the disease of a malignant ulcer.
They harm and destroy those into whom they can mix the evil gall hidden within themselves.
But many of them, once exposed for what they are, have been rejected and cast out, just as Simon himself, when exposed by Peter the apostle,
received the punishment he deserved. Meanwhile, as the good news of life grew and gained strength every day, by God's providence,
the eunuch of the queen of Ethiopia had come to Jerusalem. According to the custom of that country, a woman rules over them to this day.
He was the first of the Gentiles to receive the good news of God from Philip, through a revelation from God. He became the firstfruits of the believers from all the nations.
When he returned to his country, he proclaimed there the knowledge of the God of all and the life-giving coming of our Savior to humanity.
Through him the prophecy was fulfilled in deed which says, “Ethiopia will be first to stretch out its hand to God.” Along with these, Paul too, the chosen instrument,
not of a human being, nor from human beings, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ and God his Father, who raised him from the dead,
through that vision and the revelation of the voice that came to him from heaven, was found worthy of the calling and became an apostle.
Chapter Two. How Tiberius was moved when he learned about Christ from Pilate.
Now, while our Savior's glorious resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven were becoming known and being proclaimed to many,
in accordance with the ancient custom of the governors of the nations, who reported every new occurrence to the one who held imperial authority,
so that nothing that happened would escape his notice—our Savior's resurrection from the dead was becoming known throughout Palestine—
Pilate therefore informed Emperor Tiberius about the miraculous signs of our Lord
and that, after he rose from the dead, many believed him to be God. Tiberius himself submitted this matter to the Senate.
But the Senate rejected the matter because it had not first been examined by them, according to the ancient custom
that among the Romans no one could be a god except by the Senate's decision and decree. It appeared that this was the reason,
but in truth it was because it was not fitting that the living teaching of God should be established by human judgment and decision.
Although the Roman council rejected the proposal submitted to it concerning our Savior,
Tiberius himself remained of his original opinion and contemplated nothing hostile toward the teaching of Christ.
These things were said by Tertullian, a man thoroughly versed in the laws of the Romans.
He was distinguished in other respects as well, and was one of the well-known and celebrated men in Rome.
In the defense he composed on behalf of the Christians in Latin, which was translated into Greek, he included the following words:
“Let us also examine these laws on the basis of their nature. You have an ancient law that a god may not be established by the emperor
until he has been approved by the Senate. Marcus Aemilius acted in this way concerning a certain idol, Alburnus. This has worked in our favor.
For among you, divinity is granted by human judgment. Consequently, unless a god pleases a human being, he cannot be a god.
According to this, it is the human being who must show favor to the god. Now Tiberius, in whose days the name of the Christians entered the world,
when he was informed from the land of Palestine how this teaching had first taken hold,
also informed the Senate. He himself knew that this teaching pleased him.
But the Senate rejected the matter because it had not itself examined it. He, however, stood by his decree and threatened death
to those who accused the Christians.” This came into his mind as though prompted by providence from heaven,
because the good news [?] was still at its beginning, so that the teaching of the Word might spread unhindered throughout the whole earth.
Chapter Three: How the Good News of Christ Spread Throughout the Whole World in a Short Time. Thus, by power [?] and encouragement from heaven,
the good news of life suddenly dawned upon the whole world like the rising sun. Then, according to the testimony of the divine Scripture,
the voice of the evangelists and apostles went out into all the earth, and their words were heard to the ends of the world.
The good news increased in every city and village, and suddenly many churches were established, like threshing floors filled with tens of thousands of people.
Those whose souls had been bound by the tradition of their ancestors and their former error in the ancient sickness of idol worship,
through the power of Christ, by means of his disciples, through teaching and marvelous deeds,
were freed as though from evil masters and released from harsh bonds. They despised the multitude of their gods
and confessed that there is only one God, the Creator of all. They honored him with upright and truthful conduct and with chaste and holy practices,
which our Savior had sown among human beings. As the grace of God was also being poured out upon the rest of the nations,
first, in Caesarea in Palestine, Cornelius and his entire household accepted faith in Christ
through a vision from God and the ministry of Peter. There were also many others from the nations in Antioch,
to whom those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen had proclaimed the good news. The church in Antioch was growing and increasing.
And while many were gathered there, including the prophets who had come from Jerusalem, and with them Barnabas and Paul and a large gathering of the brothers,
The name “Christians” was then first spreading as though flowing from an abundant spring. And Adda, one of the prophets who were with them,
prophesied about the famine that was going to occur. Paul and Barnabas, when they had completed their ministry there, were sent to serve the brothers.
Chapter Four: How, after Tiberius, Gaius appointed Agrippa over the Jews, removing Herod from his kingship.
Tiberius reigned for twenty-two years and died. After him, Gaius took over the government.
At that time he placed a crown on Agrippa and appointed him king over the Jews, over the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias.
A short time later, he also handed over Herod’s tetrarchy to him along with these, and deposed Herod together with his wife Herodias,
on many charges of wrongdoing. This Herod was the one who lived at the time of our Savior’s suffering. Josephus is a witness to these things.
Chapter Five: How Philo went on an embassy to Gaius on behalf of the Jews. In his days, Philo was renowned in many respects.
He was a man known not only for our learning but also for that of the Hebrews. He was Hebrew by descent,
and was second to none of the renowned men in Alexandria. How much effort he devoted to the divine teaching of his ancestors
is clear and evident from his work. We need not describe his proficiency in the discipline of secular learning,
for he was a rival of Plato and Pythagoras. It is said of him that he surpassed all his contemporaries.
He wrote in five books an account of what happened to the Jewish people in the days of Gaius and handed it down to us.
He also spoke of the madness of Gaius, who called himself a god and disgraced his rule in countless ways,
and of the evils the Jews suffered in his days, and of his own journey to Rome as an envoy on behalf of his fellow Jews living in Alexandria,
and how he stood before Gaius in defense of the ancestral laws. Gaius laughed at him and mocked him, and he nearly met his death at his hands.
Josephus also mentions these things in the histories he wrote, in these words: “During the unrest that arose in Alexandria between the Jews living there and the Gentiles,
three envoys were chosen from each side and went to Gaius. One of these Alexandrian envoys, whose name was Apion,
was making many slanderous accusations against the Jewish people. Among other things, he said that they even treated Caesar’s honor with contempt.
For all those subject to Roman rule erected altars and temples for him,
and in every other respect received him as a god. Only among these Jews was he held in no honor.
They did not honor him with statues or swear by his name. Apion made many malicious accusations by which he thought Gaius would be enraged,
as indeed seemed likely. But Philo, who had undertaken the embassy on behalf of the Jews, was a man distinguished in every respect.
He was the brother of Alexander son of Alabarchus, and was trained in philosophy.
But although he was capable of forcefully rebutting these slanderers, Gaius stopped him and drove him from his presence.”
It was clear, however, that in his anger against them he would do them some harm. Philo left his presence after being insulted.
He said to the Jews who were with him, “We should take courage, for while Gaius is angry with us, God is in fact becoming favorable to us.” This is what Josephus said.
Chapter Six: How many calamities overtook the Jews after their outrage against Christ. Philo himself, in what he wrote about his embassy,
clearly described, one after another, everything that had happened to them. But I will leave out many things and present those that plainly show readers
what befell the Jews immediately because of their outrage against Christ. He relates, then, that first, in the days of Tiberius, in the city of Rome,
Sejanus the prefect, who had been given freedom by the emperor to undertake great affairs,
was intent on destroying the entire Jewish people. In Judea itself, Pilate, in whose days they committed their outrage against our Savior,
wanted to do something in the temple in Jerusalem that was unlawful among the Jews, and he caused them great distress.
After Tiberius died and Gaius succeeded him in power, he insulted many people in many ways, but especially harassed the whole Jewish people in many ways.
We can learn a little about these things from the words of the writer, who writes about them as follows:
“Such was Gaius’s mental sickness toward everyone, but especially toward the Jewish race, whom he hated bitterly.
He took possession of the houses of prayer in the other cities for himself, beginning with those in Alexandria.
Everywhere he filled them with images and statues bearing his own likeness. For by eagerly accepting what others erected for him,
he was, in effect, erecting it for himself. As for the temple in the holy city, which had remained inviolate,
the emperor himself altered it and made it a temple of his own, so that it would be called the [?] temple of Gaius.” But countless calamities, difficult to recount,
befell the Jewish people in Alexandria in his days. This same writer recounts them, and Josephus also agrees with him,
showing that from the days of Pilate, when they committed their outrage against our Savior, terrible afflictions began to overtake the whole people.
Listen, then, to what he makes known in the second book of The Jewish War, in these words:
“When Pilate was sent by Tiberius as governor over Judea, he secretly brought images of Caesar into Jerusalem by night.
When day came, this caused a great uproar among the Jews. Those who were nearby were appalled at the sight,
because their laws had now been trampled underfoot. For they would not allow an image of anything to be placed in their city.”
When you compare these things with the Gospel text, you understand that the cry they shouted before Pilate caught up with them without delay:
“We have no king but Caesar.” This same writer also recounts another calamity that befell them, in these words:
“After these things he stirred up another disturbance. The temple treasury, which was called Corban,
he spent on the construction of an aqueduct. It brought water down from three hundred stadia away. Because of this, the assembled people were in an uproar.
When Pilate came to Jerusalem, they rose against him, behaving insolently and shouting. But because he already knew about their unrest,
he mingled the Roman troops with the crowd, armed but covered on the outside with ordinary clothes.
He forbade them to use swords and ordered them to strike those who were shouting with clubs.
He gave them a signal from his judgment seat. As the Jews were being beaten, many of them died from the blows.
Many others, while fleeing, were trampled by one another and perished. At the calamity that befell those who were killed,
the crowd was astonished and fell silent. Along with these things, he shows that countless calamities occurred in Jerusalem itself,
and that from then on disturbances, wars, and calamities of every kind did not cease in the cities and throughout Judea,
until the final destruction overtook them in the years of Vespasian. Thus the righteous judgment of God overtook the Jews for what they had dared to do against Christ.
Chapter 7. How Pilate killed himself. It is fitting that we should know
that Pilate, who lived in the days of our Savior—the one whose times we have discussed—in the years of Gaius,
is said to have fallen into severe distress, so that under overwhelming pressure he became his own killer.
By his own hands he received the punishment he deserved, and the righteous judgment of God swiftly overtook him, as the Greek historians relate about him.
Chapter 8. The famine that occurred in the years of Claudius. After Gaius had held imperial power for not even four years,
Claudius succeeded him as emperor. In his days a famine occurred throughout the earth.
Even those outside our teaching handed down an account of this in their writings, just as Luke related in Acts, speaking about the prophet Adda,
who had prophesied about the famine that was going to occur, and how, through Paul and Barnabas,
the brothers in Antioch sent aid to those in Judea, each according to what he could afford.
Chapter 9. The martyrdom of James the apostle. “At that time”—clearly meaning in the years of Claudius—
“King Herod laid hands on some from the church to mistreat them, and he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.”
Concerning this James, Clement also related an account worthy of remembrance,
drawing on the tradition of those who preceded him: the man who had brought James into court, he says, was moved when he saw him bear witness.
He too declared [?] that he himself was a Christian. Both of them were led away, and as they were going along the road,
he asked James to forgive him. James thought for a little while and said to him, “Peace be with you,” and kissed him.
Thus both of them were then beheaded together. As it says in the divine Scripture,
when Herod saw that the killing of James pleased the Jews, he seized Peter and put him in prison.
He would have killed him too, had he not, through a vision from God, when an angel stood over him miraculously at night,
been freed from those chains and sent out to serve in proclaiming the message. Such was the providential care shown to Peter.
Chapter Ten: How divine judgment immediately overtook Agrippa, also called Herod, when he persecuted the apostles...
There was therefore no delay in punishing the king for his insolence toward the apostles.
For immediately after his insolence toward the apostles, the heavenly wrath of God's judgment struck him down.
As Acts shows, he came to Caesarea, and on an appointed festival day he put on splendid royal clothing,
sat on a raised platform, and addressed the people. All the people praised him for his words and said,
“These are the words of a god, not of a human being!” Immediately the angel of the Lord struck him, and he became infested with worms and died.
We should marvel at how Josephus's account agrees with the divine Scripture even in this miraculous event, bearing witness to the truth.
He gives the following account: When he had completed three years of his reign over all Judea, he came to the city of Caesarea,
which had formerly been called Strato's Tower. There he held a festival of spectacles in honor of Caesar, for the preservation of Caesar's life.
Distinguished men of very high standing had gathered there from the province. On the second day of the spectacles,
he put on a splendid robe woven entirely of silver and came to the theater at the beginning of the day. When the first rays of the sun fell on that silver,
it shone and flashed astonishingly. Fear and trembling seized those who were looking at its gleaming rays.
Immediately the flatterers began shouting from every side, saying things that were not for his good.
For they called him a god and begged him to be gracious to them. They said, “Although until now we have feared you as a human being,
from now on we acknowledge that you are above mortal nature.” But the king did not rebuke them for these things
or reject their wicked flattery. A little later he looked up and saw the angel standing above his head.
Immediately he understood that this was the cause of his misfortune, though previously it had been the cause of his good fortune.
Distress seized his heart, and immediately pain arose in his belly and set in violently. Looking at his friends,
he said, “I, whom you were calling your god, am now commanded to leave this world.
The fate appointed for me has exposed the falsehood of the cries you shouted to me. I, whom you called immortal, am now being led away to die.
But I accept the fate that God wills. For I have not lived badly, since I lived in the hope of lasting happiness.”
As he said these things, he was tormented by the severity of the pain. They therefore hurriedly carried the king to his palace.
Word spread to everyone that he would soon die. The crowd of people, together with women and children, sat on sackcloth.
And according to the law of their ancestors, they pleaded with God on behalf of the king. They wept and lamented.
The king was reclining on a high terrace and looking down at them as they lay on their faces. He too was weeping.
But when the pain in his belly overwhelmed him, he departed from this world miserably within five days. He had lived fifty-four years.
He had reigned for seven years: four during the reign of Gaius Caesar and three under the rule of Claudius Caesar.
He governed Philip’s tetrarchy for three years. In the fourth year, Herod’s territory was also added to his.
I marvel at how Josephus agrees with the Holy Scriptures in these matters as well as in others.
And if anyone has doubts because of the king’s name, the time and the event nevertheless show that it is the same man.
For either his name was changed through a copyist’s error, or he had two names, as many people did.

11. On Theudas the Deceiver.

Now, since Luke again introduces in Acts the account of what Gamaliel said when they were deliberating about the apostles:
“At that time Theudas arose and claimed to be someone great, speaking about himself. He was overthrown, and all those who had followed him were scattered.”
Let us set down what Josephus also wrote about this man. For he relates it as follows: “When Fadus was governor of Judea,
a certain deceiver named Theudas persuaded a large number of people to take their possessions and follow him to the Jordan River.
For he claimed to be a prophet and said that at his command he would divide the river and make an easy passage for them.
By saying these things, he led many astray. But Fadus did not leave them undisturbed in their folly.
For he sent troops and cavalry against them. They fell upon them unexpectedly and killed many of them.
They also captured many alive. They seized Theudas himself, cut off his head, and took it to Jerusalem.”
After these things, he also mentioned the famine that occurred during the reign of Claudius.

12. On Helena, Queen of Mesopotamia.

“At the same time, a great famine also happened to occur in Judea.
During it, Queen Helena bought wheat from Egypt at great expense in gold and distributed it to those in need.”
You can see that these things agree with Acts, which [?] as follows: “The disciples who were in Antioch,
each according to his means, decided to send relief to the poor who lived in Jerusalem.
And they did so, sending it to the elders through Barnabas and Paul.” As for this Helena whom this historian mentioned,
her notable monuments still stand before the gates of Jerusalem to this day. This woman is said to have ruled Mesopotamia.

13. On Simon the Magician.

While faith in our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ was being spread among all people,
the enemy of human life was scheming to seize the imperial city first. He brought there Simon, about whom we informed you a little earlier.
And through the [?] of his magical craft, he drew many of those living in Rome into his error.
Justin, who lived a short time after the apostles, reports this.
He was renowned for his teaching about devotion to God. I will set out what should be said about him at the appropriate times.
In his first defense of our teaching, which he addressed to Antoninus, he wrote as follows:
“After our Lord was taken up to heaven, the demons raised up men who claimed to be gods.
Not only did you not persecute them, but you even considered them worthy of honor.
There was Simon, a Samaritan man from the village called Gitta. In the years of Claudius Caesar, through the craft of the demons working within him,
he performed magical signs in Rome, the city of your empire, and was thought to be a god.
You honored him as a god with a statue that you made for him in the river called the Tiber, between the two bridges.
On it is written in Latin: ‘To Simon, the holy god.’ Most of the Samaritans, and a few among other peoples,
acknowledge him as the supreme god and worship him. There was also a woman named Helena, who traveled around with him at that time and had previously practiced prostitution in Tyre in Phoenicia.
It is said that she had previously received this thought from him.” This is what Justin said about him.
Irenaeus also agrees with him in the first book he composed against heresies, where he wrote both about the man himself and about his filthy, defiled teaching.
It would therefore be unnecessary for me to recount it in this account. Those who wish to learn about him and about the leaders of heresies who came after him,
their beginnings and the whole course of their crafty practices, can learn from the writings of Irenaeus. First, then, as we have received the account,
Simon was the originator of all the heresies. From his time until now, those who follow his heresy
outwardly vie with the chaste way of life of Christians, which is renowned among everyone for its purity.
Yet they have fallen back into the very error of idol worship from which they thought they had been delivered.
For the images and likenesses of Simon himself and of Helena, whom we mentioned as having been with him—
these they worship with incense, sacrifices, and libations. Their more secret practices are too repulsive to speak of.
As people say, anyone who first hears these things from the books they possess is astonished and amazed.
For they truly amount to mental derangement and folly [?]. They are such that not only can they not be committed to writing,
but they should not even be recounted by the lips of decent people, because of their extreme repulsiveness and impurity.
For the defilement of this heresy surpasses anything a person could imagine as repulsive and polluted. They amuse themselves with wretched women filled with every kind of evil.
At that time, the power of evil raised up this Simon, the father and author of all these evils.
and the hater of good things and the adversary of human life, like a great enemy against the great and holy apostles of our Savior.
Chapter Fourteen: On the Preaching of Peter the Apostle in Rome. But the heavenly grace of God, working vigorously through its servants,
wherever they arrived and appeared, quickly extinguished the enemy’s burning flame.
Through their hands it tore down and humbled every lofty thing raised against the knowledge of God. For this reason, neither Simon’s company nor that of any others who sprang up after him
could stand in the days of the apostles. For the light of truth and God the Word were victorious and stronger than everything—
he who then shone upon humanity from God. His power was mighty on earth, and he dwelt in his apostles.
Then that magician whom we have described was struck in the eyes of his mind, as though by the glorious rays of God,
when Peter the apostle had previously rebuked him in the land of Judea for the evil things he was doing. He fled far away from there,
and traveled from east to west, thinking to himself that, if he were there, he could live as he pleased.
When he entered the city of Rome, the power that accompanied him was working vigorously within him. Here, in a short time, his efforts were so successful
that they even erected a statue there in his honor, as though he were a god. But his purpose did not prosper for long [?].
For immediately afterward, in that same reign of Claudius, the providential care of God’s grace and mercy
led that mighty and great apostle, who because of his glorious conduct was the head of all his companions—
Peter—and brought him to Rome to confront this destroyer of the world. Like a victorious commander of God, he was equipped by that grace with the armor of God.
He brought a precious cargo of spiritual light from the east to those in the west.
He proclaimed to them the good news of the kingdom of heaven, saying, “This is the light and the Word that gives life to human souls.”
When the word of God reached them, Simon was immediately extinguished, and his power was dissolved.
Chapter Fifteen: On the Gospel of Mark. The light of reverence for God shone so brightly in the minds of Peter’s hearers
that his proclamation of the teaching through hearing the spoken word alone did not satisfy them.
Instead, with many entreaties they persuaded Mark, who wrote the Gospel and who was Peter’s follower, to leave them a written record of the teaching
that they had received orally, since he had not done this before. They were the occasion for this writing of the Gospel of Mark.
When Peter learned of this, which the Holy Spirit had revealed to him, and recognized the eagerness of these people,
he sent out this writing for the building up of the churches. Clement relates this in his history,
and the bishop of Hierapolis, whose name was Papias, also bears witness with him. Peter mentions this same Mark in his first letter, which he wrote from Rome,
where he refers to the city figuratively, calling it Babylon, and says, “The chosen church in Babylon, chosen like you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark.”
Chapter Sixteen: How Mark first preached the knowledge of Christ to those in Egypt. It is said of this Mark
that he was the first to go to Egypt and preach there the Gospel that he also committed to writing. He was also the first to establish a church in Alexandria.
Chapter Seventeen: What Philo recounts about the ascetics in Egypt.
Thus, from the very beginning, a congregation of believing men and women had been established there, devoted to the perfect practice of wisdom,
so that Philo even wrote a book about them: about their dwellings, their gatherings, their communal life, and the rest of their way of life.
It is said of this Philo that during the reign of Claudius, when Peter was preaching in Rome, he spoke with him there.
This seems likely, because he worked on and composed this book that we have mentioned a long time afterward,
and it plainly describes the order of worship preserved in the church to this day.
Moreover, he recounts the way of life of the solitaries among us accurately, just as it is. He not only knew them,
but also approved of them and admired them. He praises those people, disciples of the apostles, who lived in his own time.
They were of Hebrew origin and still observed many of the ancient customs in the Jewish manner.
First, he affirms that he has added nothing beyond the truth out of his own inclination in what he recounts in the treatise he wrote about the way of life of the solitaries.
He says that they were called Comforters, and that the women who were with them were called Comforters as well.

He gives the reason for this name by which they were called: either, he says, because, like physicians, they comforted and healed the souls of those who approached them from the suffering caused by evil,
or because they pleased God through their pure and holy service. For either he himself gave them this name, which suited their purpose,
or they really had been called this from the beginning, because the name Christian had not yet become known everywhere.
First, however, he testifies that they divested themselves of their possessions, saying: “When they begin the solitary life,
they free themselves from their possessions and from every worldly concern. Then they go outside the city wall
and live in fields and gardens. They regard association with those who do not follow their way of life as harmful and disturbing.”
They did these things out of their fervent love for the faith, and they strove to emulate the way of life of the prophets.
The Acts of the Apostles also shows that all who became disciples of the apostles sold everything they owned
and distributed to each person whatever they needed, so that there would be no one among them who lacked anything.
For those who owned lands and houses, as the account says, sold them and brought the proceeds
and laid them at the apostles’ feet, so that each person could be given whatever they needed. Philo testifies to similar things about these people,
saying in his own words: “This way of life exists everywhere throughout the world. For it was fitting that, from the perfect good…
so that Greeks and barbarians also accept them. They are numerous in every city in Egypt, and especially in Alexandria.
The outstanding men from every region go to one place suited to them, as though to a city where solitaries reside.
It is above the lake called Mareotis and is situated on high ground for safety and because of the temperate air.
After this he described what their way of life was like—that is, how it resembled that of the churches everywhere.
“For this reason,” he says, “they have a holy house there, called a house of chastity and solitude, in which they live alone.
They perform there the mysteries of a chaste way of life. They bring nothing in there: neither food nor drink,
nor anything required for the body's needs, but only laws, sayings set down by the prophets, hymns,
and everything through which wisdom and the fear of God are increased and perfected.” A little later he says:
“From morning until evening they spend the whole day in their work. As they read the holy Scriptures,
they grow wise in the wisdom of their ancestors and interpret the wonders recorded in them. For the words expressed in writing,
they consider to have mysteries of wondrous things inscribed in them. They also possess writings of ancient men who were the founders of their instruction,
who left them a record of their approach to interpretation. They study these as though looking into a mirror and emulate their manner of thought.”
It seems that this man heard these things that he relates from them while they were discussing the holy Scriptures.
As for his statement that they possess writings of the ancients, it seems that he was speaking of the Gospels and the writings of the apostles.
And the accounts of ancient interpretations of the prophets that he mentioned were perhaps the Epistle to the Hebrews and Paul's other letters.
Again, concerning the hymns and songs of praise that they compose themselves, he writes as follows: “They do not merely occupy themselves with understanding the Scriptures,
but also compose their own songs and hymns of praise to God in every meter, with dignified melodies.” He also said many other things about them.
But I thought it appropriate to select and set down those useful things that resemble the way of life of the churches.
If anyone thinks that the things described are not practices belonging to the teaching of the Gospel, but could also apply to others,
let him be persuaded by the words he says afterward. From these he will receive indisputable testimony, if he has discernment.
For he writes as follows: “They lay self-restraint in their souls like a foundation,
and upon it they build the rest of their admirable practices. None of them tastes food or drink before sunset.
For they judge that the pursuit of wisdom belongs to the light, while the body's needs belong to darkness. For this reason they set aside the daytime for wisdom,
and give a small portion of the night to the body's needs. Some of them remember food only after three days—
those in whom love for the pursuit of wisdom is firmly established. Others take such pleasure and delight in being abundantly nourished by wisdom,
so that they scarcely taste anything for six days, because they have become accustomed to a more excellent food. These words of Philo plainly agree with our way of life, beyond dispute.
But if, after this, anyone still argues and is not persuaded, let him too put aside his doubt when he receives clear proofs,
which are found only among Christians in the practice of the gospel’s teaching. For he said of these people that there were also women among them,
many of whom had grown old in virginity. They had preserved their chastity not under compulsion, like others among the pagans, but entirely of their own free will,
out of zeal and love for the wisdom of reverence for God, in which they strive to share. For this reason they have rejected bodily desires.
They long not for mortal offspring but for immortal offspring, which only a soul that loves God can bring forth. A little later, as he proceeds with his account,
he states clearly: “For they regard the interpretation of the sacred writings as something expressed through allegories.
For these people consider the whole Law to resemble a human being.
They compare the words expressed in written form to the body, and the hidden meaning concealed within them to the soul.
This community has devoted itself especially to understanding that meaning, seeing in these outward expressions, as in a mirror, the wonderful beauties of understanding.”
Why need we add anything further about what he also relates concerning their assemblies: that they keep the men apart by themselves, and likewise the women?
Thus this writer spoke about this practice, which continues among us to this day:
that on the day of the feast of our Savior’s Passion, it is our custom to spend the time in fasting, keeping vigil, and reading the sacred writings.
This very pattern was described in his book by the man we mentioned earlier, when he recounts the vigil of the great feast that we celebrate,
its service, the hymns sung during it, and how one person sings in an orderly manner while the others listen silently and respond at the end of the verse.
He also describes how, on these particular days, they sleep humbly on the ground and taste no wine at all, as he wrote in his own words:
“Nor do they eat anything from which blood flows. Their drink is water, and their food is bread and salt with hyssop.”
Along with these things, he wrote about the orders of those who preside and are entrusted with the work of the church, the ministry of the deacons, and the exalted rank of the episcopate.
Anyone who wishes to learn the precise details of these things should learn them from this man’s own account.
Chapter Eighteen: How Many Writings of Philo We Know. That Philo encountered the first preachers of the gospel’s teaching
and the customs handed down by the apostles, and wrote these things, is clear to anyone who wishes to examine them. He was rich in expression and excellent in thought,
and lofty and exalted in his understanding of the divine writings. In particular, he produced explanations of the words of Scripture in every kind of form.
He composed an interpretation of the book of Genesis, proceeding through it in order, and wrote on it an exposition of the allegories of the sacred laws.
He also treated separately, section by section, the subjects investigated in the sacred writings and resolved the questions concerning them.
He also wrote about the questions found in the book of Exodus and their solutions, just as he had written about the book of Genesis.
Among his discourses are two on farming and two on drunkenness.
He also has other works that he wrote separately, with titles concerning their subjects, such as the discourse he wrote on how the mind, when awakened, [?] and curses.
And on the confusion of languages; on flight and discovery; on gathering for the sake of learning; and on who becomes the heir of the things that belong to God.
And on the explanation of things that are alike and things that are opposites; and also on three virtues about which Moses wrote along with others.
And also on the changes of names found in the Scriptures and why they were changed; and, in the same work, also on the two covenants.
He also has a work on sojourning, and on the lives of wise men perfected in righteousness, or unwritten laws.
And also on giants, and on the fact that God does not change; and another five on Moses’ statement that dreams were seen as coming from God.
These are all the works we know he composed on the book of Genesis. On Exodus, we know that he composed five books of questions and their solutions.
And one on the tabernacle, and one on the Ten Commandments, and four on the things stated in the Law that belong under those Ten Commandments;
and on the animals from which offerings were made, and which ones are offered as sacrifices, and on the things laid down in the Law:
blessings for the good, and punishment and curses for the wicked. Along with all these are the books he composed individually,
such as the one he wrote on providence, and those on the Jews, on ways of life, and on Alexander,
and on whether dumb animals possess reason. Along with these is also the work on how every wicked person is a slave,

and, in this same work, on how every earnest man is free. Along with these is the work he composed on the way of life of solitaries, from which we recounted the way of life of the apostles’ disciples.
An explanation of the Hebrew names found among the nations in the Law and the Prophets is also said to be his. Now this man went to Rome during the reign of Gaius and wrote about Gaius’s wickedness.
He wrote about him mockingly, supposedly on the praises of Gaius.
It is said that this book was read before the entire Roman Senate during the reign of Claudius, was praised, and was placed in the library there.
Chapter nineteen: What disaster befell the Jewish people on the day of Passover in Jerusalem at this time.
Paul the apostle completed the proclamation of the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome.
Aquila and Prisca escaped from Rome with other Jews and reached Asia.
There they associated with Paul, while he was still laying the foundations of the church there
and strengthening them. The book of Acts tells of these things. While Claudius was still ruling the empire,
on the day of the Passover festival, a riot and disturbance broke out in Jerusalem. As the people crowded together at the exits of the temple,
thirty thousand Jews were trampled by one another and died. The festival turned into mourning for the whole people, and there was lamentation in every house.
Josephus reported these things. Claudius appointed Agrippa, the son of Agrippa, king over the Jews.
He sent Felix as governor over the whole territory of Samaria and Galilee, and the territory called Perea.
After ruling the kingdom for thirteen years and eight months, he left Nero to succeed him in power and died.
Chapter Twenty: What happened in Jerusalem in the days of Nero. In the days of Nero, while Felix was governor of Judea,
Josephus also tells of the disputes and disturbances that arose among the priests against one another. He wrote as follows in his histories:
“A dispute flared up between the chief priests and the priests and leaders of the people of Jerusalem.
Each of them formed a band of bold and disorderly men and became their leader. As they quarreled with one another,
they spoke maliciously against one another and threw stones. There was no one to restrain them, but, as in a city without a ruler,
these things happened there unchecked. The chief priests had reached such a degree of shamelessness and insolence
that they even sent their servants to the threshing floors and took the tithes that were due to the priests.
Consequently, one could see priests dying of poverty. So completely had the violence of those troublemakers overpowered the whole community.”
The same historian also relates that at that very time a kind of bandit appeared in Jerusalem.
In broad daylight, in the middle of the city, they killed those they encountered. Especially during the festivals, they mingled with the crowd,
hiding swords beneath their clothes and using them to stab prominent men.
When their victims fell, they themselves joined those protesting against the murderers. Because of their behavior, they were not recognized.
The first to be killed was Jonathan the high priest. After him, many were killed every day.
The fear was worse than the suffering itself, for everyone was constantly expecting death, as though at war.
Chapter Twenty-One: Concerning the Egyptian who is also mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. After these things, Josephus also said the following, among other things:
“An Egyptian man, a false prophet, inflicted on the Jews a calamity greater than these.
This deceiver came into the country and assumed the title of prophet. He gathered about thirty thousand people around him, and they were led astray into following him.
After leading them around, he brought them from the wilderness to the mountain called the Mount of Olives. From there he intended to force his way into Jerusalem.
Once he had seized the Roman garrison, he would rule the people as a tyrant, with the armed men who were with him. But Felix forestalled his threat,
confronting him with Roman troops. The whole populace also joined them in the attack. When battle began, that Egyptian fled with a few men.
Many of those who were with him were captured or perished.” Josephus said these things in the second book of his history.
We should compare what is said here about this Egyptian with what is said in the Acts of the Apostles,
where that military commander spoke to Paul when the crowd of Jews in Jerusalem was rioting against him in the time of Felix.
“Are you not,” he said, “that Egyptian who some days ago stirred up a revolt and led out into the wilderness
four thousand men who were evildoers?” These things happened in the time of Felix.
Chapter Twenty-Two. How Paul was sent in chains from Judea to Rome, and how, after presenting his defense, he was cleared of every charge.
Festus was sent by Nero to replace Felix. When Paul appealed for judgment, he was sent to Rome in chains.
Aristarchus was there with Paul, and for this reason Paul calls him somewhere “my fellow prisoner.”
Luke, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, also ends his account at this point, saying of Paul that he spent two years in Rome, released from his chains,
and that he preached the word of God there without hindrance. It is said of the apostle that, after he had presented his defense on his own behalf
at that time, he went out again to the ministry of preaching. But when he came to that city a second time, he was then brought to his end through martyrdom.
While imprisoned there, he wrote the second letter to Timothy. In it he described both his first defense and his subsequent death.
Accept, then, his own testimony about these things. He said, “At my first defense, none of the brothers came to stand beside me,
but they all abandoned me. May this not be counted against them. But my Lord alone stood beside me and gave me strength, so that through me the preaching might gain courage
and all the nations might hear. I was rescued from the lion’s mouth.” By these words he clearly shows
that at that first defense he was rescued from the lion’s mouth so that his preaching might be completed—that is, from Nero,
whom he calls a lion because of the fierceness of his anger. And because he had seen in the Spirit that the time of his death had not yet arrived,
he followed “I was rescued from the lion’s mouth” with “My Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and save me in his kingdom in heaven.”
This points to his subsequent martyrdom, about which he speaks plainly in this same letter:
“My time to be offered as a sacrifice is near, and the time of my rest has come upon me.” Now, in this second letter to Timothy,
he indicates, as he writes it, that Luke alone was with him. But at his first defense, not even Luke was there.
It is therefore clear that Luke brought his account in the Acts of the Apostles to an end at the time when he was with Paul.
We have said these things to show that Paul’s death by martyrdom did not occur at the time when, as Luke wrote, he went to Rome.
It seems that at first Nero was not harsh toward this teaching, and for this reason he readily accepted Paul’s first defense.
But when he grew more brazen, he attacked the apostles as well as committing his other offenses.
Chapter Twenty-Three. How James, who is called the brother of our Lord, suffered martyrdom.
Now, when Paul appealed to Caesar’s tribunal and was sent to Rome by Festus, the Jews, having failed in that plan, [?] the brother of our Lord,
who had received from the apostles the episcopal throne in Jerusalem. Their brazen attack against him happened in this way: they brought him into their midst.
They wanted him to renounce faith in Christ before all the people. But he, contrary to everyone's wishes and expectations,
openly confessed in a loud voice before all the people that our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, is the Son of God.
When they could not bear his testimony—for everyone believed that he was righteous because of the perfection of his conduct in wisdom and the fear of God in which he lived—
for they had found an opportunity to exercise power, since they had no governor, because at that time Festus had died in Judea,
and the administration there was without leaders or governors. As for the manner of James's death,
we have already made it known above from the accounts in Clement's writings: they threw him from the pinnacle of the temple, and he was beaten to death with a wooden club.
But in his fifth book of history he speaks precisely about him, saying that he was the first to receive authority from the apostles.
He tells his story as follows: “James, our Lord's brother, received charge of the church from the apostles, and down to our own time.
For many were called James, but this man was holy from his mother's womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink.
He ate nothing that had life in it. No razor touched his head. He did not anoint himself with oil or use a bathhouse.
He alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. For he wore no wool, but linen.
He would enter the temple alone, and they would find him on his knees, asking forgiveness for the people,
until his knees became hard like a camel's, because he constantly knelt and worshiped God and asked forgiveness for the people.
Because of his outstanding righteousness, he was called ‘the Righteous One,’ and ‘the people's bulwark and their righteousness,’ as the prophets say about him.
Now some people from those seven sects that existed among the people, which I mentioned earlier in these accounts,
would ask him, ‘What is the gate of Jesus?’ He told them that he is the Savior. And some of them believed that Jesus is the Messiah.
But these sects mentioned above did not even believe that he had risen from the dead,
or that he would come to repay everyone according to their deeds. Those who believed did so because of James.
When many, even among the people's leaders, were coming to believe, there was an uproar among the Jews, the scribes, and the Pharisees, who said,
‘All the people are being driven to look for Jesus as the Messiah.’ So they gathered and said to James, ‘We ask you to restrain the people,
because they have gone astray over Jesus, thinking that he is the Messiah. We ask you to persuade everyone who has come for the day [?] of Passover concerning Jesus.
For we all trust you. We and all the people testify that you are righteous
and show no favoritism toward anyone. So persuade this crowd not to go astray over Jesus.
For all the people, and all of us, trust you. So stand on the pinnacle of the temple, so that you may be visible from above
and your words may be heard by all the people.’ For all the tribes, together with the Gentiles, had come for Passover.
So the scribes and Pharisees whom we mentioned earlier set him on the pinnacle of the temple.
They shouted to him, “Righteous one, whom we should all obey, the people have gone astray after Jesus, who was crucified.
Tell us what the gate of Jesus is.” He answered in a loud voice, “Why do you ask me about the Son of Man?
He is seated in heaven at the right hand of the great Power, and he will come on the clouds of heaven.”
Many were strengthened in their faith and were praising God because of James’s testimony, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
Then those same scribes and Pharisees again said to one another, “We have done badly
by giving Jesus such testimony. But let us go up and throw him down, so that they will be afraid and will not believe him.”
They shouted, “Oh! Oh! Even the righteous one has gone astray!” And they were fulfilling what is written in Isaiah:
“Let us do away with the righteous man, because he is of no use to us. Therefore they will eat the fruit of their deeds.” So they went up and threw the righteous man down.
They said to one another, “Let us stone James the Righteous.” They began stoning him, because he had not died when he fell.
But he turned and knelt down, saying, “I beg you, Lord God, Father of all, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
While they were stoning him like this, one of the priests, a descendant of Rechab son of Rechabim, one of those about whom the prophet Jeremiah testified, shouted:
“Stop! What are you doing? The righteous man is praying for you!” One of them, a fuller, took the wooden club with which he used to press clothes
and struck the righteous man on the head. In this way he was martyred. They buried him where he was, beside the temple.
To this day his monument stands beside the temple. He was therefore a true witness [?] to Jews and Gentiles that Jesus is the Messiah.
Immediately afterward Vespasian took them captive. Clement related these things at length. Hegesippus also gave an account agreeing with them.
He said that James was so admired by everyone and so renowned for righteousness
that even those Jews who had understanding held that this was the reason Jerusalem was taken captive immediately after his martyrdom.
This happened to them for no other reason than their outrageous action against him. Indeed, Josephus too
did not hesitate to testify to this in writing, in these words: “These things happened to the Jews as vengeance for James the Righteous,
who was the brother of Jesus who is called the Messiah, because, although he was a righteous man, the Jews killed him.”
He himself also describes his death in these words: “When Caesar heard of the death of Festus, he sent Albinus as governor over Judea.
But Ahus [?], the young man whom we mentioned as having received the high priesthood, was harsh and extremely reckless. He belonged to the sect of the Sadducees,
who are harsher in judgment than all the other Jews, as we said earlier. Since Ananus was of this character,
he thought he had found a suitable opportunity, because Festus had died and Albinus was still on the road.”
He convened a council of judges and brought before it the brother [?] of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, along with some other men.
He brought charges against them as men who had committed wrongdoing and handed them over to be put to death.
But all the gentle people in the city who strictly observed the laws were displeased by this act.
They secretly sent word to the king, asking him to write to Ananus, telling him not to do such things anymore.
For even before this he had not acted rightly. Some of them, when Albinus was coming from Alexandria,
met him and informed him about Ananus, saying, “He had no authority to convene a council of judges without your command.”
He was persuaded by them and wrote angrily to Ananus, threatening to call him to account.
King Agrippa also removed him from the high priesthood for this reason, after he had held it for three months, and appointed Jesus son of Dammaeus in his place.
These things are related about James, to whom the first of the catholic letters is attributed. We should know, however, that it is not accepted.
For not many of the early writers mentioned it, nor the letter called Jude, which is also one of these seven catholic letters.
Nevertheless, we know that these too, along with the others, are read in many churches.
Chapter 24. Annianus was the first to succeed Mark in the church of Alexandria. In the eighth year of the reign of Emperor Nero,
Annianus took over the ministry of the church of Alexandria after Mark the evangelist.
Chapter 25. On the persecution that took place during Nero’s reign, in which Paul and Peter received the crown of martyrdom for their devotion to God
in Rome. As Nero grew stronger in his rule, he plunged into evil schemes and armed himself against devotion to God.
This is not the time for us to describe the nature of his wickedness. Many have given detailed accounts of him,
from whom anyone who wishes can learn about this man’s madness: how he recklessly destroyed tens of thousands of people
and reached such a depth of murderous depravity that he did not even refrain from killing members of his own household and his loved ones.
For he killed his mother, his brothers, his wives, and many of his relatives by every kind of death, as though they were enemies and foes.
It was fitting, then, that in addition to all these things, this too should be recorded about him: he proved to be the first emperor to persecute devotion to God.
Tertullian the Roman also mentions him to us [?] in this way, saying, “Read the book of your records,
and there you will find that Nero was the first to persecute this teaching in Rome. He was cruel to everyone,
after he had subjugated the whole East. And we take pride in having such a man as the first of our killers.
For anyone who knows that time can understand that it was a great favor for us to be condemned by Nero.”
Thus this man, beyond all who had been enemies, was proclaimed to be the first enemy of God, having risen up to kill the apostles.
Paul, then, was beheaded in Rome itself, and Peter too was crucified upside down, as is related in the histories.
The names of Peter and Paul, which have remained attached to the burial places there down to the present day, confirm this account.
Not only this, but also a churchman named Gaius, who lived in the days of Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome,
while debating with Proclus, who championed the teaching of the Phrygians,
said these very things about the places where the holy bodies of the apostles we mentioned earlier are laid:
“For my part,” he says, “I can show you the apostles’ monuments of victory. For if you wish to go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way,
you can find the monuments of victory of those who established this church.” As for their both having suffered martyrdom together at the same time,
Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, made this clear in writing to the Romans, saying: “You too
have united through your teaching the planting made by Peter and Paul in Rome and Corinth.
For both of them planted and taught together in Corinth. Likewise, they also taught together in Italy and suffered martyrdom at the same time.”
Chapter Twenty-Six. On the many calamities that the Jews suffered, and on their final war with the Romans.
To make the account of these events still more credible, Josephus also relates the many calamities that overtook the Jewish people.
Among many other things, he makes clear in his account that many of those held in honor among the Jews were tormented with scourging in Jerusalem
and crucified upside down at the hands of Florus, who was governor of Judea,
when the beginning of the war was stirred up in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign. Throughout Syria, during the revolt that the Jews undertook,
bitter turmoil overtook the members of the Jewish people everywhere at the hands of the inhabitants of the cities. They were slaughtered without mercy, as in war.
One could see cities filled with unburied corpses. Children, old people, and women lay thrown together,
without even their nakedness being covered. The whole region was filled with indescribable suffering. Yet the threat of tortures was worse
even than the things being recklessly done every day. Josephus said these things in his account. These, then, were the things that befell the Jews.
The second book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished.

Chapter 1. In which lands the apostles proclaimed Christ. The holy apostles and disciples of our Savior had gone out into the whole world.
As tradition indicates, Parthia was allotted to Thomas as the region in which to preach, Scythia to Andrew, and Asia to John, who lived among its people.
His death took place in Ephesus. Peter, meanwhile, was in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia.
He finally went to Rome and was crucified upside down, for he himself had requested to suffer in this way. But what shall we say about Paul,
who [?] and finally suffered martyrdom in Rome during the reign of Nero? These things are stated by Origen, one after another.
Chapter 2. Who was the first to take leadership in the church of Rome. After the martyrdom of Paul and Peter,
Linus was chosen as the first bishop over the church of Rome. Paul mentions him at the end of the letter he wrote to Timothy from Rome.
Chapter 3. On the letters of the apostles. There is one accepted letter of Peter, the one called the first.
The early elders also used this letter in their writings without hesitation. But the second letter,
We have not received it as accepted among the holy Scriptures. Nevertheless, many have found it useful and have taken an interest in it as in the other books.
But the Acts and the Gospel, and what is called the Preaching, together with the elders [?], the Revelation, which are attributed to him—
we do not know that these were handed down to us by the elders of the church. For none of the ancients, nor even any of the writers in the church down to our own days,
has used them as testimony to the message. As we proceed with this history, we also explain, in the course of its narrative,
which church writers in their own times used which disputed books, and how they used them,
and what they have said about the holy Scriptures that the church acknowledges without dispute,
and about those that are not so acknowledged. Of the letters attributed to Peter, we know only one to be genuine,
which our ancient forefathers also acknowledged. But Paul's fourteen letters are plainly well known.
We should know, however, that some in the church of Rome rejected the Letter to the Hebrews and said that it was not Paul's.
We will also set down, in their proper periods, what our predecessors said about this letter.
As for the Acts attributed to Paul, according to the tradition we have received, they are regarded as doubtful.
Since Paul himself, in the final greeting of the Letter to the Romans, mentioned Hermas along with others—
the man said to be the author of the book called The Shepherd—we should know that some of the ancients did not accept it.
As far as they are concerned, it is not placed among the books acknowledged by the church. Others, however, judge it very useful,

because it is especially instructive for those [?]. Yet they judge it very useful, because it is especially instructive for those beginning instruction. For this reason it is also read in many churches.
Some of the earliest writers also used it previously. These, then, are the things I said I would explain about the books of God: which are accepted without dispute,
and which are those that not everyone acknowledges.
Fourth [?]. On the first succession [?] of the apostles. Paul preached to the Gentiles and laid the foundations of churches from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum.
This is known from his own words and from what Luke related in Acts.
As for Peter, it is plainly known from his words in the letter that we have said is accepted in the church
in how many places he preached Christ to those of the circumcision and handed on to them the message of the new covenant—
that is, to those Hebrews who were scattered in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.
But who became their genuine imitators and were chosen to shepherd the churches that had been established
is not easy for us to say now, unless perhaps someone can gather this from Paul's words. For he had countless helpers,
and, as he calls them, they were his fellow workers in the gospel. He deemed many of them worthy of an unforgettable remembrance.
He regularly listed them in his letters, bearing witness about them. Nor was he alone in doing this; Luke also did so in Acts.
He mentions by name those among them whom he knew. As for Timothy, it is reported that he was the first bishop of Ephesus.
Likewise, Titus was bishop of the churches in Crete. Luke, however, was originally from Antioch.
He had previously been a physician. He spent most of his time with Paul, and he also associated closely with the other apostles.
He demonstrated the ability to heal souls that he had acquired from them in the two books he wrote through the Spirit of God:
in the Gospel, where he testified in writing that it was according to what had been handed down to him by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word,
whom he said he had followed [?]; and in the book of the Acts of the Apostles.
What he wrote was not what he had heard, but what he had seen with his own eyes, and not from hearsay. They therefore say
that Paul regularly referred to Luke’s Gospel as his own whenever he said, “As it is written in my Gospel.”
As for the rest of those who accompanied Paul, Paul himself testifies that Crispus went to Galatia.
As for Linus, whom he mentions in the second letter to Timothy as having been with him in Rome,
we have already stated that he was the first after Peter to receive the bishopric of the church of Rome.
And concerning Clement, who became the third bishop in Rome, Paul himself testifies that he was his helper and fellow worker.
There was also Dionysius, who is mentioned in Acts as belonging to the Areopagus. He was the first to believe when Paul taught there.
Another Dionysius, who was bishop of the church of Corinth, reports about him that he became the first bishop in Athens.
As we proceed with this history, we will speak about those who received the succession from the apostles, each in their own time. But now let us return to the historical account.

Chapter Five. Concerning the final captivity of the Jews after Christ.

After Nero had reigned for thirteen years, and after him Galba and Otho for a year and a half,
while Vespasian was winning the war against the Jews in Judea itself, the Roman army stationed there proclaimed him emperor.
He immediately entrusted the war against the Jews to his son Titus, and he himself went to Rome.
After our Savior’s ascension, the Jews, in addition to their insolence toward him, devised many plots against the apostles as well.
First they killed Stephen by stoning him. Then, after him, they beheaded James the son of Zebedee, John’s brother. Besides these,
they also killed James, who after our Savior’s ascension had received the episcopal throne there, as we have already said.
They also devised many schemes to put the remaining apostles to death and drove them out of the land of Judea.
But they were sent by our Lord among the nations to proclaim the good news in his name. The people of the church in Jerusalem also, through a revelation given to the distinguished men among them,
had been instructed before the war to leave the city and go and settle in [?], in a city called Pella.
All those in Jerusalem who believed in Christ, so that all the holy people would be gone from it.
Then a judgment of vengeance from God would come upon it, upon the royal city of the Jews and upon the whole land of Judea,
because of what they had dared to do against Christ and his apostles, so that he might wipe out that generation of wicked people from that land.
What calamities befell the whole people everywhere, and how the inhabitants of Judea in particular were tormented with terrible sufferings;
how many tens of thousands fell together by the sword and famine, dying in many different ways, and how many cities of Judea were taken captive;
also what terrible calamities were experienced in Jerusalem itself by those who had fled there to take refuge in it as a fortified city;
the course of the entire war and everything that happened during each part of it, and how at last the sign of the abomination of desolation stood, as spoken of by the prophet,
over that famous temple, which from ancient times had belonged to God, and how it was utterly destroyed by fire—
anyone who wishes to learn these things accurately can learn them from the history Josephus wrote.
We should make known how, as this same Josephus explains, people had gathered from all Judea during the days of the Passover festival
and entered Jerusalem, where about three million people were confined as though in a prison.
For it was fitting that on those very days when they had assembled and dared to act against our Savior and the benefactor of all, Christ the Son of God,
they should be confined as though in a prison, and destruction should overtake them through God's righteous judgment.

Six. On the famine that had gripped the Jews.

I will leave aside the individual things that befell the Jews through the sword and in other ways,
and speak only of the bitter sufferings that overtook them through famine, so that those who read this book may know, even if only briefly,
that punishment for their audacity against Christ quickly overtook them from God. Take, then, the fifth book of Josephus's history and read what happened at that time.
He says this: “For those who had possessions, it made no difference whether they remained or perished.
For they would fabricate a charge against someone that he wanted to surrender to the Romans, and he would perish because of his possessions.
Along with the famine, the audacity of the rebels also grew stronger, and every day both these evils blazed more fiercely.
No wheat was openly visible anywhere. For they would burst in, enter houses, and search them.
If they found anything, they would beat the people for denying it [?]. And if they found nothing,
they would torture them as people who had hidden it out of distress. The evidence of whether anyone had anything or not
was the appearance of these wretched people's bodies. Those among them whose bodies were holding up were thought
to have an abundant supply of food. But to kill those who were close to dying of hunger—
this required no deliberation. Many secretly exchanged their possessions for a single measure of wheat.
If they were rich; and those who were poorer than they were, on barley. They hid themselves in their inner rooms.
Some of them, because of their extreme need, ate the wheat just as it was, without grinding it.
Others baked it, as necessity dictated. Nowhere was a table set at all.
They snatched the food straight from the fire and ate it before it was cooked. That meal was a source of suffering.
The very sight of it deserved tears. Those who were stronger snatched it from their companions.
Those who were weak wailed. The distress of hunger surpassed every other suffering, and nothing destroys shame as it does.
Things that in other circumstances would provoke indignation are treated as nothing under its power. Women snatched from their husbands, and children from their fathers.
Most degrading of all, mothers snatched food from their babies’ mouths. And although they saw their beloved children in their arms,
they did not hesitate to take the drops [?]. They saw them in their arms; they did not hesitate to take the drops of their lives.
Even when they ate in this way, they could not hide. Those troublemakers reached everywhere.
They caught hold of whatever the others were snatching up. For whenever they saw a shut door anywhere,
this was a sign that those inside were eating some food. Immediately they broke down the doors and rushed inside.
They squeezed their throats and forced the food out. Old men who clung to their food were beaten.
The hair of women who hid any food was torn out. There was no mercy for elderly women or babies.
They picked up the babies, lifted them by the food they were holding, and dashed them to the ground.
But when people had already eaten the food before they entered, because they had not caught them in time,
they grew bitter, like people who had been grievously wronged. They devised cruel forms of torture to search out food.
They forced wedges into the private parts of those being tortured and drove sharp rods into their anuses.
What a person suffered to make him admit to a single small loaf or a handful of barley flour was horrifying even to hear about.
Their torturers were not even hungry. They considered it a small act of cruelty to snatch things out of necessity.
Rather, they practiced cruelty and prepared provisions for themselves in advance for the days to come.
They intercepted those who crept out at night toward the Roman guard posts to gather wild greens and grass.
Just when these people thought they had escaped their enemies, they snatched from them whatever they had brought.
Often they begged them and implored them by the fearsome name of God
to give them a small share of what they had brought back through such toil and hardship. But they gave them none of it.
Yet this was welcome to them: that they should not perish outright along with their [?]. After this, he adds other things and says:
“For the Jews, he says, hope of survival had been cut off along with their means of escape. Famine was growing severe in every house and every family, consuming the people.
The rooftops were full of women and infants lying wasted and prostrate, and the streets were full of dead old men.
Boys and young women wandered about, moving through the streets like shadows. They would fall wherever suffering overtook any one of them.
Those who were suffering could not bury their loved ones. Anyone who still had the strength grew weary because of the great number of the dead.
He did not know what would happen to him himself. For many of them fell down upon those they were burying and died.
Many died before they reached the grave. Yet amid these bitter afflictions there was no lamentation or weeping.
For famine overpowered every feeling. With dry eyes, those suffering the agony of death watched those who died before them.
A deep silence and a night full of death surrounded the city. Yet worse than all these things were the robbers.
They plundered the dead in their houses and stripped the ornaments from their bodies. Then they went out laughing.
They tested the sharpness of their swords on the corpses and thrust them through those who lay there still alive.
But those who begged them to lend them their right hand and their sword, to deliver them from starvation, they arrogantly ignored.
Each of the dying fixed his gaze on the temple, leaving the rebels behind alive. At first, however, they
ordered that the dead should be buried at the expense of the public treasury, because they could not bear the stench. But when they could no longer manage the burials,
they threw them from the wall into the ravines.” When Titus passed by those ravines and saw that they were full of dead bodies, with fluid flowing from the corpses,
he groaned, raised his hands toward heaven, and called God as his witness, saying, “This deed is not mine.” After Josephus had said a little more,
he added these words: “I will not hold back from saying what grief commands me to say. I believe
that if the Romans had delayed coming against these insolent men, that city would either have been swallowed up by a chasm or destroyed by a flood,
or the fire of Sodom would have been sent upon it. For God had endured this godless generation more than those who suffered those things.
For through these men’s insolence the entire people also perished with them.” Again, in the sixth book, he wrote as follows:
“Countless people fell among those who were being destroyed by famine in the city.
Their sufferings cannot be recounted. For in every house where even a shadow of food appeared, there was a battle.
Loved ones attacked one another and snatched away the miserable provisions that sustained their lives. Yet they were not believed to be destitute, even when they were dying.
Instead, those robbers searched even the dying,
in case death had overtaken any of them while he still had something hidden in his clothing. Others, in their destitution, with their mouths gaping like dogs,
Children wandered about, straying from door to door. They staggered like drunkards because of the distress that surrounded them.
They would rush into the very same houses two or three times in a single hour.
Necessity turned everything into food—even things that filthy animals would not eat.
They gathered these things and ate them. In the end they did not even refrain from eating the straps fastened around their waists and their footwear.
They stripped the hides covering the shields and chewed them. People even used individual stalks of hay as food,
and sold a small weight for four assarions. But why need we speak of the lifeless things they used as food during the famine?
For I have an act to relate, the like of which is not reported to have happened among either Greeks or barbarians. It is horrifying even to tell,
and difficult for anyone hearing it to believe. But let no one suppose that I am inventing some new marvel for humanity.
For I would gladly have left this crime unmentioned and passed over it, had it not had countless witnesses.
Indeed, I would have done my people little kindness by leaving unmentioned in words what had actually been done.
