There was a woman among those who lived beyond the Jordan named Mary, the daughter of Eleazar, from a village named Beth-hazor,
which means “house of hyssop.” She was a woman distinguished by her family and wealth. She fled with many others to take refuge in Jerusalem and was trapped there.
The tyrants had seized the possessions she had brought with her into the city from beyond the river.
As for what remained of her household belongings, and any food she happened to find,
the armed men would rush in and seize it from her. She complained bitterly,
and often insulted and cursed those robbers, trying to provoke them into killing her.
But none of them killed her, either out of anger or out of pity. And if she managed to find any food, she was only laboring for others.
Every possibility of finding anything was being cut off, while hunger was inflaming her anger. This woman,
taking counsel from her rage and desperation, assaulted nature itself. She seized her son, who was still nursing, and said:
“Poor child! For whom should I preserve you amid war, famine, and rebellion? Even if we survive, slavery to the Romans awaits us.
But famine will come before slavery, and these rebels are worse than both.
Come, then, be food for me, madness for these rebels, and a tale for the whole world—
the one tale still missing from the sufferings of the Jews.” Having said this, she killed her son, roasted him, and ate half of him.
She covered the rest and kept it. Immediately the rebels caught the smell of this abominable deed.
They drew their swords and threatened to kill her unless she showed them what she had prepared.
But she immediately said to them, “I have also kept a good portion for you from what I had left over from my son.” Then she uncovered it and showed it to them.
Immediately trembling seized them, and they were stunned and paralyzed by the sight. Then she said, “This is my son, you wretches,
and the deed is mine. Take and eat, for I too have eaten. Do not now be weaker than a woman or more compassionate than a mother.
But if you are righteous and shrink from my sacrifice, I have already eaten,
and I have kept what remains for myself.” After this they left that place in fear and trembling, scarcely bringing themselves to leave even this food for the woman.
Immediately the whole city was filled with this dreadful report. Everyone pictured this suffering before his eyes,
and shuddered at it as though he himself had done it. Those tormented by hunger had only this desire: to die.
Those who had already died were considered fortunate, because they had not [?] heard or seen such evils.
Chapter Seven: On What Christ Foretold. Such, then, was the punishment that came upon the Jews for the injustice and wickedness they committed against the Christ of God.
It is fitting to compare these events with the unfailing prophecy of our Savior, who said, “Woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days!
Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath. For there will be great distress,
such as has not occurred from the day the world came into being until now, and never will occur again.” Now this same historian
added up the number of those who perished by famine and the sword, and said that it amounted to one million two hundred thousand.
The remaining rebels and robbers were killed after the city's destruction, as they identified one another.
Those who were young, tall in stature, and distinguished in bodily appearance were kept for the public spectacles.
The rest of the people, aged seventeen and above, were bound and sent to Egypt to labor. Many were distributed among the provinces
to perish in public spectacles by swords and wild beasts. Those aged seventeen and below were taken captive and sold.
Their number was ninety thousand. These things took place in this way in the second year of Vespasian's reign,
in accordance with the foreknowledge of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, through the power of his divinity, foresaw and foretold the things that were to happen, just as they happened.
He wept over the city, as it is written in the Holy Gospel, and spoke to Jerusalem in this way:
“If only you knew the things that make for your peace, even on this day of yours! But they are hidden from your eyes.
Days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you and press you on every side.
They will raze you to the ground, and your children within you.” Again, he said concerning the people, “There will be great distress in the land and fierce wrath against this people.
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive among all nations. Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles
until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.” Again he said, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army,
“Then you will know that its destruction is at hand.” So when someone compares the words of our Savior with the accounts of this historian, who described the whole war,
how can he fail to marvel that our Savior’s foreknowledge is so wonderfully glorious,
and acknowledge that it truly belongs to God? As for what happened to the whole Hebrew people after our Savior’s suffering, and those cries that the whole assembly of the Jews were shouting,
asking that the robber and murderer should live and be given to them, while begging that the Author of life should be taken away from them,
we have no need to add anything to these accounts. But it is right that we append the following things to them,
which demonstrate his mercy and his gracious care: for forty whole years after their outrage against Christ, he held back from destroying them.
During those years, many of the apostles and disciples, and James, who was called our Lord’s brother and was the first bishop,
were still alive and going about in Jerusalem itself, and remained there in that place like a strong wall.
For God’s providence was still showing them patience, so that perhaps at some point they might repent and turn back from what they had done, and receive forgiveness and life.
Chapter Eight: On the Signs That Occurred Before the War. Along with all this patience, remarkable signs were also given to them,
of what was going to happen to them unless they repented. This same historian whom we mentioned earlier also considered these signs worthy of recording in his histories.
There is nothing to prevent us from setting these down as well as we proceed with the book. Take, then, and read what he says in the sixth book of his history, where he speaks as follows:
“At that time, those deceivers who bore false witness about God were persuading the wretched people
not to look at or believe the clear signs that were giving advance warning of the destruction that was to come.
Instead, like people deprived of their understanding, with neither eyes nor soul, they disregarded God’s proclamation.
First, a star resembling a spear stood above the city and remained upright for one hour.
Again, before they rebelled and war arose against them, when the people were gathering for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on the eighth of Nisan, at the ninth hour of the night,
a light shone so brightly over the altar and the temple that one would have thought it was bright daylight. It remained there for half an hour.
To ordinary people this seemed to be a good thing, but those who knew the Holy Scriptures explained beforehand
that these things were going to happen. At this same feast, someone brought a cow for sacrifice,
and it gave birth to a lamb in the middle of the temple. Again, the eastern gate of the inner court, which was made of bronze and was heavy,
could scarcely be closed in the evening by twenty men. It was secured with iron bars and had bolts extending deep down below.
At the sixth hour of the night, it was found to have opened by itself. A few days after the feast, on the twenty-first of Iyar, a certain apparition was seen.
It would seem difficult to believe, were it not that those who saw it tell of it, and the consequences of the signs also make it worthy of belief.
For before sunset, chariots were seen overhead throughout the whole region, and an armed army high up in the clouds, rushing about and encircling the city.
Again, at night during the feast called Pentecost, the priests entered the temple to perform their service, as was their custom.
They said that first they heard the sound of a shaking and pounding, and afterward a voice suddenly saying, “We are leaving this place.”
And things more terrifying than these. Now there was a certain countryman, an ordinary man named Jesus son of Ananias:
Four years before the war, when the city was at peace and had an abundance of everything,
he came to the feast at which they customarily made shelters for God. Suddenly he began shouting in the temple:
“A voice from the east! A voice from the west! A voice from the four winds! A voice against Jerusalem and against the temple!
A voice against bridegrooms and brides! A voice against all the people!” He went around through all the streets, shouting this all day and all night.
Some prominent men among the people were angered by this evil report. They seized the man and beat him severely.
But he neither answered those standing there with a word in his own defense nor said anything on his own behalf.
Instead, he kept shouting those same cries as before, as was his custom. The rulers thought that this man's agitation came from a demon.
They brought him before the Roman governor, and there they scourged him down to his bones. But he neither pleaded with them nor wept.
Instead, with every blow they struck him, he made this cry still more mournful with groans, saying, “Woe, woe to Jerusalem!”
This historian also recounts other astonishing things. He says that a prophetic utterance was found in Jerusalem, in which the following was written:
“At that very time, someone from among them would arise from [?] and rule over the whole world.” They thought that it had been fulfilled in Vespasian.
But he did not rule over the whole world, only over the Romans. Therefore this should be understood as referring to Christ,
to whom the Father said, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possessions.”
For at that very time the good news of the holy apostles went out throughout the whole earth, and their word was heard at the ends of the world.
Chapter Nine. Josephus and the Writings He Left Behind. Along with all these things,
concerning Josephus himself, who supplied us with the material for all these accounts in these books,
we should also explain where he came from and what his ancestry was. He himself gives this information too, saying:
“Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, who at first [?] with the Romans and finally, under compulsion, fell into their hands.”
At that time he was known not only among the Jews, his own people, but was also renowned among the Romans.
In his honor a statue of him was erected in the city of Rome, and the books he had worked diligently to write were considered worthy of being deposited in their repository of [?].
He set down the entire earlier history of the Jews in twenty books, and the history of the war with the Romans that took place in his own days in seven.
He wrote it not only in Greek but also in the language of his ancestors, as he himself testifies. And on account of his other writings, he deserves to be believed.
He also has two other works, carefully composed, on the antiquity of the Jews. In them he also argued against Apion the grammarian,
who had written against the Jews at that time, and against others who wanted to slander the Jewish people.
Chapter Ten: How Josephus mentions the sacred books. In his first discourse he gives this enumeration of the books of the covenant called the Old,
identifying those that are undisputed among the Hebrews, according to the ancient tradition. In his own words he teaches as follows.
The books of the covenant called the Old, identifying those that are undisputed among the Hebrews, according to the [?] tradition.
In these words of his he teaches as follows: “We have tens of thousands of books that disagree with one another and contradict one another.
But there are twenty-two books that are rightly believed to belong to God, containing the record of all time.
Of these, five belong to Moses. They contain the laws and the account of the origin of humanity down to his own death.
This period is a little less than three thousand years. From the death of Moses until Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,
the prophets who came after Moses recorded what happened in their own times in thirteen books. The other four,
hymns. And everything that happened down to this present time in which we live has been written down. These writings, however, are not worthy of the same trust as those before them,
because there is no certain succession of prophets. Our conduct makes it clear how we approach the books of the prophets.
For throughout all this time that has passed, no one has dared to add [?], subtract from them, or change them.
For this has been implanted in the whole Jewish people from their very birth: to believe that these are God's commandments, to abide by them,
and, if necessary, to die gladly for them.” These statements by this historian deserved to be included here.
He also composed another account about reason's mastery, concerning the struggle of those described in the book called the Book of Maccabees,
Hebrews who triumphed because of their reverence for God. Again, at the end of the twenty books of history that he wrote, he mentions
that he intended to write four books explaining the beliefs of the ancestors of the Jews concerning God, his being, and the laws,
and why some things are permitted to be done and others are not [?]. He also has another work, as he himself mentions in his own words.
Along with these things, we should also repeat the words he placed at the end of his history, to establish the reliability of the testimonies we have taken from him.
He was arguing against Justus of Tiberias, who wanted, like him, to recount what happened in those times, because he had not written the truth.
He brought other accusations against this man in these words, saying: “Unlike you, I did not conceal my writings.
Instead, I presented my books to the emperors themselves, while the events were still there to bear witness. For I was personally confident that I had preserved the truth of the history,
and because I expected to receive testimony that I had altered nothing in it. I also presented this history to many others,
many of whom had taken part in the war itself, including King Agrippa and some of the sons of [?]. For this was what the emperor Titus wished.”
so that through them alone he might convey to people knowledge of his deeds, and send them as though written with his own hands.
And he ordered them to be read publicly before everyone. King Agrippa, for his part, wrote sixty-two letters,
testifying to the truth of this account. He included two of them in this narrative of his. We have now said enough about him.
Chapter Eleven. Simeon succeeded James in the church of Jerusalem.
Let us then turn to what followed the martyrdom of James and the destruction of Jerusalem that took place at that time.
The account says that the apostles and disciples of our Lord who were still alive at that time
gathered together from every direction, along with our Lord’s relatives according to the flesh, for many of them too were still alive at that time.
They discussed who ought to take James’s place, and they all unanimously decided
that Simeon son of Clopas, who is mentioned in the Gospel, was worthy of the episcopal throne of the church there.
He was, as they say, a cousin of our Savior. For Hegesippus relates that Clopas was Joseph’s brother.
Chapter Twelve. How Vespasian ordered a search for those descended from David.
Along with these events, after the destruction of Jerusalem, Vespasian ordered a search for all those of David’s lineage,
so that no one of royal lineage would remain among the Jews. For this reason, a severe persecution befell the Jewish people.
After Vespasian had reigned for ten years, his son, the emperor Titus, succeeded him. In the second year of his reign,
Linus, bishop of Rome, after holding office for twelve years, handed it over to Anencletus.
After Titus had reigned for two years and two months, his brother Domitian succeeded him.
Chapter Thirteen. Abilius became the second bishop in the church of Alexandria. In the fourth year of Emperor Domitian,
Annianus, who had been the first bishop of the church of Alexandria, departed this world after completing twenty-two years. Abilius succeeded him as the second bishop.
Chapter Fourteen. Anencletus became the second bishop in Rome.
In the twelfth year of his rule, after Anencletus had presided over the church of Rome for twelve years, Clement succeeded him.
Chapter Fifteen. About Clement, who came after three [?]. Concerning Clement, the apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, made known that he was his fellow worker in the gospel,
saying this: “With Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are written in the book of life.”
Chapter Sixteen. About Paul’s letter. This man has one great and remarkable letter, acknowledged by the church,
which he wrote on behalf of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth because of the unrest that arose there in Corinth at that time.
We know that this letter has been read publicly before all the people in many churches from ancient times down to the present.
That a disturbance arose in Corinth in his days is attested by a trustworthy witness, Hegesippus.
Chapter 17. The persecution that took place during the reign of Domitian. The emperor Domitian showed great cruelty toward many people.
For he killed not a few people of noble birth in Rome itself, and a great many prominent people, without a just trial.
He also drove countless distinguished people into exile beyond the borders, and their possessions were confiscated, though they were blameless.
Finally, he took over from Nero the role of being an enemy of God after him. For after Nero he stirred up a second persecution against us.
His father Vespasian, however, had not even considered doing anything harmful to us...
Chapter 18. John the apostle and the Revelation. It is said that John, the apostle and evangelist,
was still alive in the world at this time. Because of his testimony concerning the word of God, he was banished to live on an island called Patmos.
Now Irenaeus, when writing about the numerical value of the deceiver’s name, which is written in the Revelation called John’s,
said these things about John in the fifth book that he wrote Against Heresies. He spoke as follows:
“If his name needed to be proclaimed openly at this time, it would have been stated by the one who saw the revelation.
For it was seen not long ago, but more or less in our own generation, at the end of Domitian’s reign.”
At that time the teaching of our faith shone so brightly
that even writers outside our teaching did not hesitate to record in their histories the persecution and the martyrs who suffered in it.
They also specified the time precisely, saying that it was in the fifteenth year of Domitian.
Along with many others, they also gave an account of Flavia Domitilla, who was the daughter of the sister of Flavius Clemens,
one of the consuls in Rome at that time. Because of her testimony concerning Christ, she was banished as a punishment to an island called Pontia.
Chapter 19. How Domitian ordered those descended from David to be killed.
Domitian himself had ordered those descended from David to be killed.
An account handed down from earlier times says that some heretics accused the sons of Jude,
who was our Lord’s brother according to the flesh, on the grounds that they were descendants of David and relatives of Christ. Hegesippus relates these things as follows.
Chapter 20. Those related to our Savior. Hegesippus says:
“There were still relatives of our Lord alive in the world: the sons of Jude, who was called his brother according to the flesh.
They were denounced as descendants of David. A recalled veteran brought them before Domitian Caesar.
For, like Herod, he was afraid of the coming of Christ. He asked them, ‘Are you descendants of David?’
And they acknowledged it. Then he asked them again how much property they had and how much gold they possessed. They said:
The two of them together had only about nine thousand denarii, half of which belonged to each of them.
They did not have this in actual coins, but it was the value of the thirty-nine plethra of land that were their only possession.
From this they also paid taxes. And on their hands, as evidence that they worked with their own hands, was the hardness of their skin,
and their hands had become hardened from constant labor. When they were asked about Christ and his kingdom—what it was like, where it was, and when it would appear—
they answered that it was not of this world and did not exist on earth, but was above heaven, over the angels.
It would be revealed at the end of the world, when he came in glory to judge the dead and the living and repay everyone according to their deeds.
Domitian did not find fault with them over these things, but despised them as insignificant people and let them go free.
He issued an order that the persecution of the churches should cease. After these men were released, they visited the churches as witnesses
and as relatives of our Lord. There was peace, and they remained alive until the reign of Emperor Trajan.
Hegesippus said these things. But he was not the only one: Tertullian also mentions Domitian in this way:
“At one time Domitian too wanted to act as that man had, since he shared in Nero’s cruelty.
But, as I think, because he had a little understanding, he soon stopped and even brought back those whom he had persecuted.”
After Domitian, who had held power for fifteen years, Nerva succeeded him, and all the honors of Domitian were abolished.
All those who had been unjustly persecuted returned to their homes, and their property was also restored to them,
in accordance with the advice of the Roman Senate. These things are related by those who handed down in writing what happened in those times.
Then John the apostle also returned from the island to which he had been banished and came to Ephesus. He lived there, as the account of the earlier generations has handed down to us.

Chapter twenty-one. Cerdon became the third bishop of the church of Alexandria.

After Nerva had reigned for about one year,
Trajan succeeded him. In his first year, after Abilius had led the church in Alexandria for thirteen years,
Cerdon succeeded him. He was the third to hold office there, following Anianus, the first. At this time Clement was still leading the church of Rome.
He too held the third place among the bishops who had been there after Paul and Peter: Linus was first, and after him Anencletus.
Chapter twenty-two. Ignatius became the second bishop in Antioch.
In Antioch too, after Evodius, who had been the first bishop there, Ignatius was known at this time as the second bishop.
Likewise Simeon, the second bishop of the church of Jerusalem after James, the brother of our Savior, held the ministry at this time.

Chapter twenty-three. An account of John the apostle.

At this time John, the apostle and evangelist whom Jesus loved, was still alive in Asia.
He was governing the church there after returning from the island to which he had been banished, following Domitian’s death. That he was still alive at this time
can be established sufficiently from two trustworthy witnesses. These were teachers of the church’s true faith,
namely Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria. In the second book of the work he composed against heresies, Irenaeus wrote these words:
“All the elders in Asia who associated with John, our Lord’s disciple, testify that he handed this down to them.
For he remained with them until the time of Trajan.” In the third book of this same work, he makes the same point:
“Furthermore, the church of Ephesus was founded by Paul, and John remained among them until the time of Trajan.
It too is a true witness [?] to the tradition of the apostles.” Clement also indicates the time and adds an account that is very useful for those who love to hear
things that are good and beneficial. He includes it in the discourse he composed and wrote on the subject, “Which Rich Man Is Saved?” Take up his book and read it;
it contains the following: “Listen to a story—not a mere story, but an account handed down and preserved in memory concerning John the apostle.
For when that tyrant had died, John returned from the island of Patmos and came to Ephesus.
At their request, he would travel to the regions of the Gentiles: in some places to appoint bishops, and in others to establish churches,
and elsewhere to ordain to one of the church’s orders those whom the Holy Spirit pointed out to him.
He also came to a city a short distance away—some people even give its name—and attended to all the brothers’ needs.
In the course of all this, he saw a young man who was physically strong, handsome in appearance, and ardent in spirit.
He looked at the bishop who was standing there and said to him, ‘I entrust this young man to you with all earnestness, before the church and with Christ as witness.’
The bishop accepted him and made many promises. John repeated these same words to him and solemnly charged him again. Afterward, he went to Ephesus.
The elder took the young man entrusted to him home, fed him, persevered with him, and watched over him tenderly.
Afterward, he baptized him. After this, he relaxed his close attention and supervision, as though he had appointed the Lord’s seal as a perfect guardian for him.
But when the young man gained this freedom, idle and dissolute companions of his own age, steeped in evil habits, came and attached themselves to him.
At first they took him to lavish feasts. Afterward, they would also go out at night and rob people, taking him along with them.
Then they persuaded him to join them in doing things even worse than these. Little by little, he became accustomed to it.
Driven by the force of his nature, he bolted like a horse whose mouth is not restrained and which bites its bit on a smooth road.
He hurled himself violently into deep pits. When he had completely abandoned hope of his life in God [?],
he no longer contemplated doing anything small, but rather the greatest crime of all, since he was already lost once and for all.
He was determined to be like his companions. So he took these men and formed a band of robbers.
He readily became a chief of robbers and led them by force—a wicked and defiled murderer. Meanwhile, some time passed.
They summoned John to that city. When he had settled the matter for which he had come, he said to the bishop:
“Return to us the deposit that Christ and I entrusted to you, before the witness of this church over which you preside.”
At first he was astonished, thinking that he was being falsely accused concerning money he had not received. He could not believe this about something he did not possess,
yet he could not doubt John. But when John said to him, “I am asking for that young man and the soul of that [?],”
the old man sighed bitterly and wept. He said, “He is dead.” John said:
“How, and by what kind of death?” He replied, “He is dead to God. He turned out wicked and defiled, and finally became a robber.
Now, instead of being in the church, he is in the mountains, living as a rebel with others like himself.” John tore his clothes and struck his face with loud cries.
He said, “What a fine guardian I left for that young man’s soul! Quickly, bring me a horse and a man to show me the way.”
So he took them from the church and went. When he reached that place, he was seized by the robbers’ guards.
He neither tried to escape nor pleaded with them. Instead, he cried out, “This is precisely why I have come!
Take me to your leader.” At that moment the young man was waiting, fully armed. But when John approached and the young man recognized him,
he was ashamed and began to run away. John pursued him with all his strength, forgetting even his old age, and cried out:
“Why are you running away, my son, from your old, unarmed father? Have pity on me, my son! Do not be afraid. You still have hope of life.
I will answer to Christ for you. If I must die in your place, I will gladly endure it, just as our Lord did for us.
I give my own life for you. Stop, be still, and believe me. Christ sent me.” When the young man heard this,
he first stood still and looked down. Then he threw down his weapons and, trembling, wept bitterly. When the apostle approached and embraced him,
the young man poured out his spirit as best he could in abundant weeping. He baptized himself a second time with tears. But his right hand
was the only thing he kept hidden. The apostle gave him his assurance on this point and swore to him, “I will ask our Savior for forgiveness for you, and you will be pardoned.”
He brought that right hand to his face [?] and kissed it, as though it had been cleansed through repentance. He took him and brought him to the church.
With the earnest prayers he offered on his behalf, the continual fasts in which he labored alongside him, and fitting words of every kind, he comforted his mind.
He did not leave until he had restored him to the church. He provided an example of true repentance, a powerful demonstration of rebirth,
and a visible victory of resurrection. These are Clement’s accounts, set down for the benefit of those who hear them. ...
Chapter Twenty-Four. How the Gospels Were Composed. Let us now set out the writings of this apostle about which there is no dispute.
First, let us acknowledge his Gospel, which was known in all the churches under heaven.
But among the earlier ones, [?] is counted in fourth place, with those three before it.
Now let us describe Christ’s holy apostles, who were truly worthy of God and whose conduct was entirely pure.
Their souls were adorned with every excellent and praiseworthy quality.
They were untrained in speech, but they relied on the wonderful, divine power given to them by [?].
They did not even know how to proclaim their Master’s teaching with persuasive and artful words, nor did they devote themselves to this.
Instead, they relied solely on the demonstration of God’s Spirit, which was active in them, and on the power of Christ’s miracles, which were accomplished through their hands.
They proclaimed the knowledge of the kingdom of heaven throughout the world, but gave little attention to setting their words down in writing.
They did this because the ministry they performed was beyond human capacity.
For Paul, who was stronger than all of them in preparing his message and was also outstanding in understanding,
left nothing more in writing than these short letters, although he had countless unspoken things to say, as a man who had reached the vision of the third heaven.
He was also caught up into that glorious paradise and was considered worthy to hear words there that no human being is permitted to speak.
Nor did the rest of our Savior’s [?] disciples lack these things. There were twelve apostles,
and seventy other disciples, and many others besides these. Yet out of all our Lord’s apostles,
only Matthew and John left us written accounts. Even they, as the account indicates,
were compelled by necessity to write. For Matthew, who had previously been preaching to the Hebrews and was about to go to other countries,
handed down his Gospel to them in the Hebrew language, so that in his place the written account would supply them with the good news he had been preaching.
We have already spoken about Mark and Luke and the handing down of their Gospels. As for John, according to what is said about him,
he had been preaching the good news all along without writing, and finally came to write for this reason:
when the three Gospels that had been written were circulated among everyone and also reached him, as the account indicates, he accepted them.
He testified that they had written the truth, but said that they lacked this one thing: accounts of what had happened at the beginning of Christ’s teaching.
This statement is indeed true. We can therefore learn that all three of these evangelists
wrote only about what our Lord did in the single year after John the Baptist was committed to prison.
They made this very point clear at the beginning of their accounts: after the forty days during which our Lord fasted and was tempted,
they began their accounts at that time. For Matthew explains it this way: “When he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew from Judea to Galilee.”
Mark likewise says: “After John was handed over, Jesus came to Galilee.”
Luke, however, before beginning his accounts of our Lord’s deeds, observed this and said that Herod, in addition to all the evil things he was doing,
also added this: he shut John up in prison. So they asked John the apostle about these things,
that he should fill out in his own writing this [?] omitted by the earlier evangelists, and what our Savior did during it.
That is, what happened before John the Baptist was handed over to prison. He made this very point clear,
sometimes saying, “This was the first sign that Jesus performed, and he revealed his glory,” and sometimes mentioning John the Baptist amid the deeds of Jesus,
saying that he was still baptizing at Aenon near Salim. He made this clear explicitly when he said:
“John had not yet been put in prison.” Thus John wrote in his Gospel these things
that our Lord did before John the Baptist was handed over to prison. But the other three evangelists
recount what happened after John was handed over. When we are assured of these things, then, we recognize that the Gospels do not contradict one another,
because John’s Gospel contains accounts of Christ’s earlier deeds, while the others contain accounts of what he did in the later period.
It seems that this was why John said nothing about the record of our Savior’s ancestry according to the flesh: Matthew and Luke had already written it.
He himself began to write about his divinity, since this had been reserved for him by the Spirit of God, as for an outstanding apostle.
We have said these things about the writing of John’s Gospel. We have also previously explained the circumstances that gave rise to Mark’s Gospel.
Luke too, when beginning his book, first stated his reason for writing: many others, he said, had wanted to write rashly accounts of matters
about which he himself was fully convinced. And to spare us from the doubts that others instilled,
he handed down to us the truth of the matters he had received and verified through his close and constant companionship with Paul and his association with the rest of the apostles.
He wrote these things in his Gospel. These are the things we have said; we will also make known, at the appropriate points, the tradition of the early writers concerning them.
As for John’s writings, along with the Gospel he wrote, his first letter was also accepted without dispute by both earlier and later generations.
But there is dispute about the other two letters said to be his.
As for his Revelation, even to this day the opinions of many about it swing from one side to the other.
Concerning this too, we will present the opinions about it at the appropriate points, drawing on the testimony of the early writers.
Chapter twenty-five. On the writings: which are accepted and which are not. Now that we have reached this point,
it is fitting to list again the writings of the New Testament that we have already discussed. Let us place the holy Gospels first,
and after them the book of the Acts of the Apostles. After these let us arrange Paul’s letters, and after them John’s first letter.
Alongside it let us also count Peter’s first letter. After these, the Revelation of John as well, if it is judged appropriate.
And we set down, in their proper periods, the opinions that many held about it. Let these writings be placed among those acknowledged by the church.
Among those that are disputed, but are nevertheless accepted by many, is the second letter of Peter.
There are also the second and third letters called John's, whether they belong to the evangelist or to someone else of the same name.
Let these be placed among the disputed writings, along with the books of the Acts of Paul.
Also the work called the Shepherd and the Revelation of Peter, and with these the letter of Barnabas and the work called the Teaching of the Apostles.
And again, the Revelation of John, as I said earlier, if it seems right to place it in this category too. For some reject it,
while others place it among the genuine writings acknowledged by the church. There are also others who place the Gospel of the Hebrews among these,
in which the Hebrews who have accepted Christ take particular delight. Let all these be counted among the disputed writings.
It was therefore appropriate to arrange these writings in order, to distinguish which are the genuine writings, without any admixture of anything [?], of the church,
and which are subject to disagreement and dispute and are not included in the church's canon.
Nevertheless, many members of the church make use of them. But we should know that they are distinct from those writings that heretics put forward under the apostles' names,
namely, gospels attributed to Peter, Thomas, Bartholomew, or others, or Acts of Andrew, John, and the other apostles.
Not one of the church's writers in the succession has ever considered any of these worthy of mention in his writings.
The character of their language is very far removed from, and different from, that of the apostles. And the intention and outlook expressed in them
are utterly foreign to the true faith. They plainly show that certain heretics fabricated them out of their own minds.
For this reason, they should not even be placed among the disputed writings. Rather, we should turn away from them as foreign and rejected.
Chapter twenty-six: On Menander the sorcerer. Let us now proceed to the history of what followed. Menander succeeded Simon the sorcerer.
He showed himself to be a second instrument of Satan's activity, worse than the first. He too was a Samaritan.
When he had become fully skilled in sorcery, like his teacher, he made extravagant promises and said of himself
that he was the savior sent from above, from the invisible worlds, for the salvation of humanity.
He taught that no one could overcome the angels who made this world in any other way
unless he first came to the instruction in sorcery that he imparted and to the baptism administered by his hands.
Those who were considered worthy of it, he said, received eternal life in this world and remained in it without growing old or dying.
These things can easily be learned from the words of Irenaeus. Justin too, in the passage where he mentioned Simon,
also wrote an account of this man and said as follows: “Menander, who was himself also a Samaritan, from the village called Capparetaea, became a disciple of Simon.
He too went mad through the activity of demons and came to Antioch, where he led many astray through his skill in sorcery.
He persuaded those who followed him to believe that they would not die. Even now there are people belonging to his school who profess this.
But this was the activity of Satan, who, through these sorcerers who had taken on the name of Christ,
strove through sorcery to overcome the great mystery of reverence for God, so that through them the immortal life of the soul and the resurrection from the dead would be mocked.
These are the foundations of the church. But those who designated their teachers as their saviors fell away from the hope of truth.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: On the Heresy of the Ebionites. But the evil demon, unable to shake those who loved God's Christ,
found people who were caught by these things and led them astray after him. The early Christians rightly called them Ebionites,
because they held a poor and low view of Christ. For they considered him an ordinary human being like everyone else,
who became righteous through the cultivation of habitual conduct, and who was born from the union of a man and Mary. They said that observance of the Law was necessary for them,
not believing that they could be saved through faith in Christ alone and through the way of life he taught.
There were also others called by this same name who avoided the great audacity of those we have mentioned.
For they did not deny that our Lord was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit. Yet they did not acknowledge, as we do,
that he had existed from the beginning as the Word, God, and Wisdom. They also subscribed to the impiety of those first mentioned,
especially in their eagerness, like them, to maintain the bodily observances of the Law. These people
completely rejected all Paul's letters and called him an apostate from the Law. They used only the Gospel called the Gospel of the Hebrews,
and held the others in little regard. They observed the Sabbath and the other practices of Judaism just as the others did.
But they celebrated Sundays as we do, in remembrance of our Savior's resurrection. Because of this view they held, they received the name Ebion,
which indicates their impoverished understanding. For this is what a poor person is called in the Hebrew language.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Cerinthus, the Leader of a Heresy. We have received the tradition that in those same times Cerinthus became the leader of another heresy.
Gaius, whose words we quoted earlier, wrote about him as follows in his discussion:
"But Cerinthus too, who introduced a written account of absurd statements through revelations, as though he were a great apostle, falsely claimed, 'We learned these things from angels.'
He said that after the resurrection Christ's kingdom would be on earth, and that we would again serve bodily desires in Jerusalem.
Because he was an enemy of God's Scriptures, he wished to lead people astray by saying that there would be a wedding celebration lasting a thousand years."
Dionysius too, who was bishop of the church of Alexandria,
in the second discourse of On the Beginning, made certain remarks about John's Revelation, drawing on the tradition of earlier times.
And he mentions this man in these words: “Cerinthus, who founded this heresy called that of the Cerinthians,
wanted to attach a name to the error he had devised so that it would seem worthy of belief. For this was the teaching he proclaimed:
that Christ’s kingdom would be on earth. And the things he himself craved, since he was very fleshly and loved sensual pleasures,
were the things he dreamed would happen: satisfying the belly—that is, eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse—
and also things he thought he could describe in more distinguished terms than these: festivals, sacrifices, and the slaughter of animals.” These things Dionysius said about him.
Irenaeus also included a reminder of this man’s secret teachings in his first book Against Heresies.
He also recorded in his book an account worth remembering, drawn from the tradition of Polycarp, who said:
“John the apostle once entered a bathhouse to bathe. But when he learned that Cerinthus was inside, he sprang from his place and fled to the door,
because he could not bear to be under the same roof as him. He urged those who were with him to do the same, saying, ‘Let us flee,
lest the bathhouse itself collapse, since Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is inside it.’”
Chapter Twenty-Nine: On Nicolaus and Those Called by His Name.
Alongside these, the heresy called that of the Nicolaitans also arose and lasted a short time. The Revelation of John also mentions it.
These people boasted of Nicolaus, who was one of those chosen with Stephen to serve the needy.
Clement of Alexandria, in the third book of his account, said these things about him: “This man had a wife who was beautiful in appearance.
After our Lord’s ascension, the apostles reproached him for being jealous over her. He then brought his wife into their midst
and permitted her to become the wife of whomever she wished. Those misguided people said that this action agreed with the saying they teach:
that one must allow the body to indulge its pleasure. They took what happened and what was said in a crude, literal way.
For this reason, those who take their name from his heresy commit sexual immorality without restraint. But I have learned about Nicolaus that he had intercourse with no other woman
except the one he married. And concerning his children, I have also learned that his daughters grew old as virgins, and his son remained undefiled.
Since these things are so, it is clear that the permission he gave before the apostles concerning jealousy over his wife
was a renunciation of passion and resistance to the impulse of desire. But for others it became a pretext for indulging the body’s pleasures.
For I think that, in accordance with our Savior’s command, he did not wish to serve two masters: desire and our Lord.
They say that Tholmai also taught this: that we should fight against the body and subdue it,
and yield nothing to it for its pleasure, but nourish the soul with faith and knowledge.”
We have therefore said these things about those who at that time devised ways to distort the truth, and who quickly died out, as the saying goes.
Chapter Thirty. On the apostles who married in this world... Now Clement, whose words we have just mentioned,
after discussing these matters of which we have already spoken, turns again to people who reject marriage.
He lists for them the apostles who married in this world and says this: “Or do they perhaps reject the apostles too? For Peter and Philip also had children.
Philip even gave his daughters in marriage, and Paul, too, did not hesitate to greet his wife in one of his letters.
But he did not take her around with him, because of the restraint of his ministry.” But since we have mentioned these people, the wish is not [?]
to include this account also, which deserves to be told, from this same writer. In the seventh book of the work he composed, he wrote as follows:
“They say, then, that the blessed Peter saw his wife being led away to die and was moved by her gracious calling
and by her being escorted on her way to her true home. He spoke to her with encouragement and comfort, calling her by name and saying, ‘Remember our Lord.’
Such was the marriage of the blessed, and the perfect love of those dear to one another.” These things were appropriate to the subject before us,
and have been set down in this way in their proper chronological places. As for the departure of Peter and Paul from this world, and when it happened,
and how and where their bodies were laid after their departure, we have already spoken.
Chapter Thirty-One. On the departure of John and Philip. We have already spoken about the time of John.
The place where he was laid is known from the letter that Polycarp, bishop of Ephesus, wrote to Victor, bishop of Rome.
He mentions him together with Philip the apostle and his daughters, writing as follows: “In Asia, too, great lights have fallen asleep.
They will rise on the last day, at the coming of our Lord, when he comes in glory from heaven and seeks out all his saints:
Philip, who was one of the twelve apostles, has fallen asleep in Hierapolis,
along with two of his daughters who grew old as virgins. Another daughter of his, who lived under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, came to rest in Ephesus.
There is also John, who reclined against our Lord’s breast, who was a priest and wore the holy crown, and was a witness and teacher.
He fell asleep in Ephesus.” We have said these things about their departure also. Furthermore, in the debate of Gaius, which we mentioned a little earlier,
Proclus, who was debating with him, also spoke about the departure of Philip and his daughters in agreement with what we have already said.
“After this,” he says, “there were four prophetesses in Hierapolis in Asia, the daughters of Philip.
Their tomb is there, as is their father’s.” This is what he said. Luke, however, in the Acts of the Apostles,
mentions the daughters of another Philip, who were with their father in Caesarea in Judea at that time and had the gift of prophecy.
He speaks of them in these words: “We came to Caesarea, entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four virgin daughters who prophesied.” These, then, are the things we have received and learned about the apostles and their times,
And concerning the sacred writings they left us, and those that are disputed but accepted by many,
and those that are entirely rejected and foreign to the true faith of the apostles—we have spoken about these things. Let us now proceed to the subsequent history.
Chapter thirty-two: How Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, was martyred.
After Nero and Domitian, in the days of Trajan, whose times we are now recounting,
here and there in the cities, it is reported that persecution arose against us, apparently at the instigation of the people.
During this persecution, Simeon son of Clopas, whom we mentioned as having become the second bishop of the church in Jerusalem,
departed this world through martyrdom, according to the account we have received. Hegesippus, whose words we have used in many places, bears witness to these events.
While speaking about people belonging to heresy, he explains that some of these very people denounced Simeon at this time as a Christian.
For many days he was subjected to every kind of torture, so that he astonished the judge himself and those around him by his endurance.
Finally, in a manner resembling our Lord’s suffering, his departure ended on a cross. But there is nothing to prevent us
from hearing these things from the writer himself, who recounts them as follows: “Some of those very heretics denounced Simeon son of Clopas
as being of the house of David and as a Christian. He was martyred in the years of Trajan Caesar and Anticus, the consular governor.
He was a hundred and twenty years old.” This same Hegesippus says that the very people who denounced him,
when those belonging to the royal lineage of the Jews were being sought out at that same time,
were themselves also destroyed as people belonging to that lineage. On reflection, one can also conclude that this Simeon
was among those who had seen our Lord and heard him, taking the length of his life as evidence,
and because the Gospel mentions Mary the daughter of [?]. The account has already explained that he too was his son. This same writer
also indicates that other descendants of Judas, who was called our Lord’s brother, were alive during this reign.
After the account of their earlier testimony on behalf of faith in Christ, in the days of Emperor Domitian, he wrote as follows:
“They came and visited all the churches as witnesses and as relatives of our Lord. And when there was great peace [?] in all the churches,
they lived on until Trajan Caesar, until the time when Simeon son of Clopas was denounced by heretics like those already mentioned.
In the years of Anticus, the consular governor, he was tortured for many days and suffered martyrdom. Everyone, including the consular governor himself, marveled
at how he endured all this when he was a hundred and twenty years old. And he ordered him to be crucified.” Along with these things, this same man, while recounting these events,
added: “Until that time the church had remained a pure and uncorrupted virgin.
Even if there were people who wished to corrupt the sound rule of the life-giving teaching, they had remained hidden, as though in darkness, until that time.”
Now when the entire company of the holy apostles had departed from the world, and that whole generation which had been privileged to hear the wisdom of God with their own ears had passed away,
then godless error began to establish itself through the deception of those who were altering the teaching of the truth.
Since none of the apostles remained at that time, they sought openly and boldly to proclaim falsely named knowledge in opposition to the proclamation of the truth.
At that time, the persecution against us had spread throughout many regions,
so that even Pliny Secundus, the well-known governor, was troubled when he saw the great number of martyrs.
He informed the emperor about the many people who were being killed because of their faith. Along with this, he also informed him
that they had done nothing shameful or unlawful, except that when they rose in the morning they praised Christ as God.
They themselves rejected adultery, murder, and other evil offenses like these, and everything they did was in accordance with the law.
In response to this, Trajan issued the following order: the Christian people were not to be sought out,
but if they were accused, they were to be tried. By this very measure, much of the fierce persecution that had been raging was quenched.
Yet those who wished to devise ways to harm us did not lack pretexts. Sometimes it was people from the populace,
and sometimes it was the local judges who devised schemes against us,
so that persecution flared up in various places without an order from the emperor, and many of the faithful suffered martyrdom in struggles of every kind.
Chapter Thirty-Three. How Trajan forbade Christians to be sought out. We have taken this account
from that defense by Tertullian which we mentioned above as having been written in Latin. Its translation is as follows:
“Indeed, we find that the search for us was forbidden. For Pliny Secundus, the provincial governor, condemned some Christians and removed them from their ranks.
He was troubled by the great number of those who became martyrs. Since he did not know what to do, he informed Emperor Trajan, saying,
‘Apart from their unwillingness to worship [?], I found nothing shameful among them.’ He had also informed him
that the Christians rose early in the morning and praised Christ as God, and that in their teaching they gave these commands:
that a person should refrain from murder, adultery, oppression, robbery, and things like these.
In response, Trajan wrote that the Christian people were not to be sought out, but if they were accused, they were to be tried.” Such, then, were these events.
Chapter Thirty-Four. Evaristus became the fourth bishop in the church of Rome. In the third year of Trajan,
Clement, bishop of Rome, departed from the world after completing nine years in his ministry and in teaching the word of God. He handed over his ministry to Evaristus.
Chapter Thirty-Five. Justus became the third bishop in the church of Jerusalem. After Simeon too had completed his course, as we said above,
Justus succeeded him to the episcopal throne of the church of Jerusalem. He was one of the Jews who had believed in Christ.
For at that time there were tens of thousands of believers among the circumcised. In those days Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was renowned in Asia.
He was a man who had associated with the apostles and had received his office as bishop from those who had seen and served our Lord.
In his days the bishop of the church of Hierapolis was well known. His proper name was Papias.
Chapter Thirty-six: About Ignatius and His Letters. And Ignatius, who to this day is renowned among many,
was the second bishop after Peter in the church of Antioch. This account is told about him:
He was sent from Syria to the city of Rome and was devoured by wild beasts because of his testimony for Christ.
As he passed through Asia, under the strict watch of the guards who held him, he strengthened the cities he entered
with words of comfort and encouragement. Above all, he urged them to be on their guard against heresy,
because it was still spreading widely at that time. He asked them not to depart from the tradition of the apostles.
To give them ample warning, he resolved to testify to them in writing as well. When he entered Smyrna, where Polycarp was,
he wrote a letter to the church in Ephesus, mentioning that Onesimus was their shepherd.
He wrote another to Magnesia, the city beside the River Maeander. In it he also mentions that there was a bishop there named Damas.
He wrote yet another to the city of Tralles, stating that there was a leader there named Polybius.
Along with these, he also wrote to the church of Rome. In that letter he appealed to them not to plead for him to be spared martyrdom and so deprive him of the hope he cherished.
It is fitting to quote a little from these letters as evidence of what has been said. He writes in these words:
"From Syria as far as Rome," he says, "I am fighting wild beasts, at sea and on land, by night and by day,
bound to ten leopards—that is, a troop of soldiers. The more kindly we treat them,
the worse they behave. Through their mistreatment I am becoming more fully a disciple. Yet this does not mean that I have been justified.
I greet the wild beasts prepared for me, and I pray that they may soon be brought to me. I will urge them to devour me quickly,
not as with others whom they feared and would not approach. Even if they hold back and are unwilling to approach me,
I will force myself upon them. Bear with me. I know what benefits me. Only now am I beginning to be a disciple.
Let nothing visible or invisible begrudge me this, so that I may be found worthy of Jesus Christ.
Fire and cross, a pack of wild beasts, the scattering of bones, the severing of limbs, the destruction of the whole body, and the torment of Satan—
let them all come upon me, if only I may be found worthy of Jesus Christ."
He wrote these letters from the city we have mentioned to the churches we have listed. But when they passed from Troas to Smyrna,
He also wrote to those in Philadelphia and to the church in Smyrna, and particularly to Polycarp, the bishop there.
He knew that Polycarp had been a close associate of the apostles, and he entrusted his flock in Antioch to him as a good and faithful shepherd.
He urged him to care diligently for his flock. And he, while he—while writing to those in Smyrna, used these words, though I do not know where he got them.
He spoke this way about Christ: “Even after his resurrection, I know him in the flesh, and I testify and believe that he is so.
And when he came to Peter and his companions, he said to them, ‘Come, touch me and see that I am not a bodiless spirit.’
And immediately they approached him and believed.” Irenaeus also knew of his martyrdom, and he mentions his letters and speaks as follows:
“As one of our own people said, when he was condemned to be thrown to wild beasts because of his testimony concerning God:
‘I am God’s wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found to be pure bread.’”
Polycarp also mentions these things in the letter he wrote to the Philippians, in these words:
“I ask all of you to be persuaded and to persevere in all the endurance that you saw with your own eyes,
not only in those blessed men, Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, but also in others who were from among you,
and in Paul himself and the rest of the apostles, being assured that all these did not run in vain,
but in faith and righteousness. And now they are in the place that was their due, with our Lord, with whom they suffered.
For they did not love this, but Jesus, who died for us and rose from the dead for our sake.” And afterward he said:
“You and Ignatius wrote to me that if anyone goes to Syria, he should also take your letters.
I will do this if I have a suitable opportunity, either myself or through someone whom I send to serve as a messenger on your behalf as well.
The letters sent to us by Ignatius, and the other letters that we have here with us, we have sent to you, as you instructed us.
They are appended below to this letter, and you can benefit greatly from them.
For they contain faith, endurance, and every kind of instruction needed for reverence toward our Lord.”
Such were the events concerning Ignatius. After him, Heros assumed the bishopric of Antioch.
Chapter Thirty-Seven. On the evangelists who were distinguished up to that time. Among those who were distinguished in their days
was also Quadratus, along with Philip’s daughters, concerning whom [?] was also Quadratus, along with Philip’s daughters,
of whom it is said that they possessed the gift of prophecy. There were also many others who were well known in their days,
who held the first rank in the succession from the apostles. These disciples, worthy of God, were such
that they built upon the foundations laid everywhere by the apostles, and further strengthened the proclamation.
And they were sowing the life-giving seed of the kingdom of heaven abundantly throughout the whole world. For many of the disciples at that time
were lifting their souls through the word of God, in the abundance of their fervent love for Christ.
First they fulfilled our Savior’s command and distributed their possessions to those in need.
Afterward they traveled through the regions and carried out the work of evangelists, proclaiming the word of faith.
They handed on to them the holy writings of the Gospel. These men laid the foundation of the faith in distant regions,
and appointed others as shepherds, entrusting them with the care of those who had first become disciples.
They themselves then turned to other regions and peoples, with God’s grace and help.
For even at that time the Spirit of God was performing marvelous miracles through their hands,
so that, from their very first hearing, great numbers of people suddenly received the fear of God anew into their souls.
But since it is not easy for us to list by name all those who received the first [?] of the apostles,
who became shepherds and evangelists in all the churches throughout the world, we have mentioned by name in this account only those
through whose writings we still possess the transmission of the apostles’ teaching, as with Ignatius in the letters we have listed.
Chapter Thirty-Eight. On Clement’s letter and the writings falsely said to be his.
And Clement, in the acknowledged letter that he wrote on behalf of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth,
included many ideas drawn from the meaning of the Letter to the Hebrews. He also reproduced its very words, writing them as they appear there.
He clearly showed that this Letter to the Hebrews had not been written recently. For this reason it was rightly counted among the apostle’s other letters.
For the apostle wrote to the Hebrews and addressed them in their ancestral language. Some say that Luke the evangelist translated it,
and others say that it was this same Clement. This seems to be true, because this Letter to the Hebrews and Clement’s own letter have the same style of expression,
and the ideas expressed in the two are not far apart. It should also be known that a second letter is attributed to Clement.
We do not, however, readily acknowledge it as his in the same way as the first, because we do not even know of earlier writers who used it.
Recently, some people have also brought forward another very lengthy book as though it were his. It contains a debate between Peter and Apion.
But none of the earlier writers mentions it at all. Nor does it bear any resemblance to the pure and true teaching of the apostles.
Clement’s universally acknowledged writing, however, is well known. We have also spoken of the writings of Ignatius and Polycarp.
Chapter Thirty-Nine. On the treatises of Papias. Papias has five treatises, bearing the title “Exposition of the Sayings of Our Lord.”
Irenaeus mentions these, writing only the following about them and saying this:
Papias too, he says, used to say that he had heard these things from John himself. He was a companion of Polycarp and was a man of ancient times.
He bears witness to this in writing at the beginning of his books, for he composed five books. These are the things Irenaeus said about him.
But Papias himself, at the beginning of his account, did not indicate that he had heard the holy apostles or seen them.
He did, however, explain that he had received the teaching of the faith from people who knew the apostles, in these words: “I will not hesitate to set down for you in these interpretations of mine
also the things that I learned well from the elders and remember well, and I vouch for their truth.
For I did not, like many people, take pleasure in those who say a great deal, but in those who teach the truth;
nor in those who recount the commands of outsiders, but in those who handed down what was given by our Lord for faith
and was conveyed and came from the truth itself. And whenever anyone came who had followed the elders, I would inquire into the elders’ words: what Andrew said,
or what Peter said, or what Philip, Thomas, James, John, or Matthew said,
or any other of our Lord’s disciples, or what Aristion or John the elder said. For I did not think that I could benefit as much from their writings
as from a living and enduring voice.” Here we need to recognize that he lists the name John twice.
He counts the first with Peter, James, Matthew, and the rest of the apostles, clearly indicating the evangelist.
But he distinguishes the other John in his account and places him separately, outside the list of the apostles. He puts Aristion before him
and plainly calls him an elder. Thus these statements show that the account given by those who said the following is true:
there were two men in Asia who were called by the same name, and their tombs are in Ephesus, both called John’s to this day.
We ought to consider this carefully. For the revelation called John’s, if someone does not accept that it belongs to John the evangelist,
was apparently seen by this other John. And this Papias himself, whom we have just discussed, acknowledges
that he received the apostles’ words from those who had followed them, and from Aristion and John the elder.
For he says that he himself had heard them. He frequently mentions them by name and sets down in his writings the tradition he received from them.
These things have not been said by us without benefit. It is fitting to follow these words of Papias that we have quoted with other words of his, in which he relates miracles
and other matters that he received through tradition. We have already explained that Philip lived in Hierapolis with his daughters.
Now we explain that Papias himself lived in their days and mentions accounts of miracles that he received from Philip’s daughters.
For he relates that a dead person rose in his days. He also relates another miracle concerning Justus, who was called Bar-Shealt [?]:
he drank a deadly poison, but because of our Lord’s grace, nothing harmful happened to him. After our Savior’s ascension, this Justus
was put forward along with Tolmai [?] to take Judas’s place in his ministry. The Acts of the Apostles relates this as follows.
that they put forward two men—Joseph, called Bar-Shealt, who was named Justus, and Talmai—and prayed.
This same man also recorded other things that he received, apparently from unwritten tradition, and strange wonders concerning our Savior and his teaching.
And also other parables, in which he says that there will be a thousand years after the earth [?]. But I think
that, concerning the accounts of the apostles that he received, which were told to them as symbolic illustrations, I think differently.
For he did not examine them according to their meaning. Indeed, from the evidence of his words, he appears to have been very limited in understanding.
Nevertheless, he also became the reason why many members of the church after him adopted this view,
because they looked to his antiquity, as Irenaeus did, and anyone else who holds such a view.
He also handed down other things in his book: Aristion’s explanations of the words of our Lord, and the tradition of John the elder.
Let us add to his words the tradition that he recorded about Mark the evangelist, which he set down in these words [?].
“The elder used to say this: Mark, who became Peter’s interpreter, wrote down fully whatever he remembered,
though not in order, of the things said or done by our Lord. For he had neither heard our Lord nor followed him.
But later, as I said, he followed Peter, who would teach according to his needs,
but did not arrange our Lord’s words into a connected account. Thus Mark made no mistake in writing down what he remembered.
For he had one concern: not to leave out anything he had heard, or to say anything false in his account.” This is what Papias related about Mark.
About Matthew he said this: “Matthew wrote the Gospel in the Hebrew language, and each person translated it as well as he could.”
This same Papias also used passages from the letters of John and Peter as testimonies.
He also recorded an account of a woman who was accused of many sins during the time when our Lord was in the world.
This account is written in the Gospel of the Hebrews. These things, together with what we said before, were set down [?].
The third book of the History of the Church is finished.
