Chapter 1: Who were bishops in Rome and Alexandria during the reign of Trajan. In the twelfth year of Trajan’s reign,
Cerdon, the bishop of the church of Alexandria, whom we mentioned a little earlier, departed from this world.
Rimus took over the ministry there. He was the fourth bishop in succession [?] the apostles. At this time,
when Evaristus had completed eight years as bishop of Rome, Alexander, who was fifth in succession from Peter and Paul, succeeded him.
Chapter 2: What the Jews suffered in the days of Trajan. The spread of our Savior’s teaching and his church increased and grew stronger every day.
The affliction of the Jews through evils of every kind also grew more severe. For when the emperor reached his eighteenth year,
an uprising of the Jews broke out again, and a great many of them perished. For in Alexandria, throughout Egypt, and in Cyrene,
they were driven as though by an evil spirit of unrest, and threatened the Gentiles who lived among them.
When they had greatly intensified the uprising, in the following year they waged a major war. At that time Lupus was governor over all Egypt.
In their first engagement, they happened to defeat the Gentiles, who fled and took refuge in Alexandria.
They seized all the Jews who were in the city and killed them. When those in the region of Cyrene were deprived of their assistance,
they pursued the Gentiles in Egypt and undermined its laws. Their leader was Lucuas.
The emperor sent Marcius the tribune with a force of infantry in ships, and also some cavalry.
For a long time he engaged in many battles in the war against them, and killed many tens of thousands of Jews,
not only those from Cyrene, but also those in Egypt who were supporting Lucuas their king. The emperor, however, supposed
that the Jews there in Mesopotamia were likewise rising against the inhabitants of the country, and ordered Lusius Quietus
to wipe them out of that province. He attacked them and killed a great many of them. Because of this victory that he won,
the emperor appointed him governor over Judea. Pagan historians who lived at that time also related these things in their accounts.
Chapter Three. Which men spoke in defense of the faith in the days of Hadrian. After Trajan had held the imperial throne for twenty years less six months,
Aelius Hadrian succeeded him. Quadratus wrote a discourse in defense of our faith and presented it to him,
saying that wicked men were devising ways to oppress our people. This discourse is still in the possession of many of the brothers, and of us as well.
From it we can see clear evidence of this man's understanding and of the simplicity of the apostolic faith.
He himself also shows how early he lived in the following words, which he relates:
"Our Savior's works continued to endure, for those who were healed and those who rose from the dead were real.
They were not merely seen being healed and being raised [?], but remained continually present,
not only while our Savior was in the world, but also for a long time after he had departed from the world,
so that some of them survived even to our own times." This is what he said. Aristides too, a faithful man who followed our teaching,
like Quadratus, composed a defense of the faith and presented it to Hadrian. This writing is still found in the possession of many people to this day.
Chapter Four. The bishops in Rome and Alexandria in the days of Hadrian. In the third year of his reign,
Alexander, bishop of Rome, departed from the world after completing ten years in office. Xystus succeeded him.
In the church of Alexandria, Primus departed from the world after completing twelve years, and Justus succeeded him as bishop.
Chapter Five. The bishops in Jerusalem, from our Lord down to these times. As for the bishops who were in Jerusalem,
I have not found the dates of their years in writing [?]. It is said, however, that each held office for only a short time. But I have received this from written records:
that down to the final destruction that took place in the days of Hadrian, there was a succession of fifteen bishops who held office there,
all of whom were Hebrews who had lovingly received the knowledge of Christ from the beginning.
From among them, those considered worthy of the ministry of bishop were selected by people capable of judging such matters.
For the whole church there was then made up of Hebrew believers, from the days of the apostles down to the final destruction.
For when the Jews rebelled against the Romans, they were devastated in great wars. Since the succession of bishops from among the circumcised came to an end at that time,
it is fitting that we now list them, beginning with the first. He was James, who was called the brother of our Lord...
The second was Simeon. The third was Justus. The fourth was Zacchaeus. The fifth was Tobias. The sixth was Benjamin... The seventh was John... The eighth was Matthias.
The ninth was Philip... The tenth was Seneca. The eleventh was Justus. The twelfth was Levi. The thirteenth was Ephraim. The fourteenth was Joseph.
And the last of them all, the fifteenth, was Judas. All these were bishops in the church of Jerusalem from the apostles down to this time, and all of them were from among the circumcised.
In the twelfth year of the reign, when Xystus had completed ten years as bishop of Rome,
Telesphorus succeeded him. He was the seventh in the succession from the apostles. When a year and a few months had passed,
Eumenes became the sixth bishop in the church of Alexandria, his predecessor having completed eleven years.
Chapter Six. The final devastation of the Jews during the years of Hadrian... When the Jewish rebellion had grown extensive and powerful,
Rufus, the governor of Judea, together with the army sent to his aid by the emperor,
dealt with their audacity through merciless punishment, suddenly destroying tens of thousands of men, women, and children.
Under the law of war, he seized their lands. At that time the Jews had a leader called Bar Kokhba.
In other respects he was a murderer and a bandit, but he glorified himself through his name, claiming that he had shone upon them from heaven as a savior,
as though they were oppressed captives. When the war intensified in the eighteenth year of the reign,
there was a small town on the edge of the country. It was very strongly fortified and was not far from Jerusalem.
The Jews rebelled there. After it had been besieged from outside for a long time, those rebels perished from hunger and thirst.
The man who had caused them to rebel received the punishment he deserved. Because of this, the entire Jewish people were barred altogether from setting foot in the area around Jerusalem,
in accordance with the law and command of Hadrian, who ordered that they should not even look upon their ancestral homeland from a great distance.
Ariston of the city of Pella related these things. When Jerusalem had been completely emptied of all the Jews who had lived there from ancient times,
and another city had been built by the Romans and settled by foreign peoples, in honor of the reigning emperor,
Aelius Hadrian, it was called Aelia. The church there, too, was gathered from the Gentiles.
After those bishops who had been from among the circumcised, Mark was the first to receive the bishopric there...
Chapter Seven. Who the leaders of the teaching of false knowledge were in those times.
While the churches throughout the world were shining like bright stars, and faith in our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, was growing strong throughout the whole human race,
Satan, the hater of good things and the enemy of truth, who is always opposed to the lives of human beings,
He plotted against the church everywhere, having long armed himself against it in every way through persecution at the hands of outsiders.
But when he was restrained from these things, he used wicked men and sorcerers as instruments for destroying souls and as servants of destruction.
He armed himself with other schemes and used every device so that sorcerers and deceivers too would take on the name of Christianity.
Those among the believers who imitated them, they dragged into the pit of destruction.
And through their wicked conduct they turned away those who had not yet approached the faith,
so that they would not approach the word of life. Now Menander, whom we mentioned a little earlier as having succeeded Simon—
the alien power first appeared in the likeness of a snake with two [?], in the two leaders who arose to establish two heresies:
Saturninus, who was of Antiochene origin, and Basilides, an Alexandrian. One of them in Syria and the other in Egypt
established the teaching of heresies hateful to God. Saturninus told many lies in the manner of Menander, as Irenaeus showed.
Basilides, under the guise of something inexpressible, also extended his schemes without limit, concocting insipid tales for his defiled heresy.
At that time there were many members of the church who fought for the truth
and wisely waged battle for the faith that the apostles had established in the church.
Many also left writings for those who came after them, warning against these heresies we have mentioned. Among these we ourselves have seen a forceful work of refutation,
which Agrippa son of Castor, one of the well-known writers of that time, composed against Basilides, exposing the wickedness of his error.
In revealing his secrets, he said of him that he had written twenty-four books against the Gospel.
He also named prophets for himself, Barcabbas and Barcoph, and other nonexistent barbarian names, to astonish those who are impressed by such things.
He also taught, he says, that they should eat food sacrificed to idols without distinction and deny the faith in a time of persecution without hesitation.
Like the Pythagoreans, he commanded those who joined him to remain silent for five hours.
He said other similar things about Basilides. Irenaeus too fully and openly exposed this heresy.
Irenaeus also wrote about another, which was called that of the Gnostics. These people did not conceal Simon’s sorcery as he had done,
but practiced it openly. They boasted, as though of some great achievement, of the things they did through love magic,
dream visions, the constant presence of demons with them, and other similar things.
They teach, he says, that those initiated into their mysteries must commit every kind of defilement—
that is, into their abominations—because otherwise, as they themselves say, they cannot escape the rulers of the world
unless they repay their debts to them through unspeakably abominable deeds, by means of these servants of evil.
Satan, who delights in evil, was making use of them. And those whom they held in their hands were being led captive, wretchedly, to destruction.
But the nations that had not yet believed were being taken captive. But the nations that had not yet believed—
they were speaking great blasphemies against the word of God because of those who conducted themselves under the name of Christianity.
It happened that, because of these false apostles, an impious suspicion against us grew stronger:
that, they said, we engaged in unlawful sexual unions with our mothers and sisters, and defiled ourselves with unclean foods.
But these things were not allowed to continue for long. For truth itself asserted itself and showed its light after a short time.
For the craft of the enemies was exposed by their deeds and was soon extinguished.
For the heresies kept changing and being renewed, while the earlier ones died out; and in every form and shape they were destroyed from time to time.
But the glory of the church's truth continually grew and became stronger, remaining unchanged.
It alone, everywhere, in chastity, clear-mindedness, freedom, and purity and holiness of conduct,
was shining with God's wisdom among the whole human race, among Greeks and barbarians.
With time, that slander against the entire Christian people also died away.
Our teaching alone remained victorious, and everyone acknowledged that it was glorious in its commandments of chastity and the holiness of God's wisdom.
No one dared to speak a filthy word against our faith or to utter slander against anyone belonging to us.

8. Which members of the church became writers.

Now, in those very times,
truth brought forward many who fought on its behalf. They rebuked the heresies and fought against them,
not only without writing, but also through written arguments. Among these, Hegesippus was well known.
We have already made extensive use of his words, and from his [?] we have set down various things about the apostles.
In five books, then, he recorded in simple words the unerring tradition of the apostles' preaching.
He also gave information, in the time in which he lived, about the idols that had been set up earlier, and wrote as follows:
“Those,” he says, “for whom they built tombs and temples, just as they are still being built to this day—one of them is Antinous, the slave of Emperor Hadrian,
for whom they also hold games. This Antinous lived in our own days. For he also built a city in his name, Antinoë.”
In his days there also lived Justin, a lover of true wisdom, who at that time was still occupied with the philosophy of the Greeks.
He indicates this period of his life in the defense he composed for Antoninus, writing as follows:
“It is fitting,” he says, “that along with these we should also mention Antinous, who has appeared in our own time.”
This man, whom everyone is eager to worship with reverence as God, although they know who he is and where he comes from.
This same writer also mentions the Jewish war at that time and writes as follows: “Also in the war involving the Jews,
Bar Kokhba, who was the leader of the Jewish rebellion, ordered Christians to be brought in for severe torture,
unless they denied and blasphemed Jesus Christ.” He also speaks about himself, describing how he turned from Greek philosophy to reverence for our Lord,
and how he did this through reflection and judgment. Explaining these things, he writes: “I too used to take pleasure in Plato’s teaching.
When I heard Christians being slandered, yet saw that they were not afraid of death or of anything considered terrifying,
I thought to myself that it was impossible for them to be living in wickedness and lust.
For who is there who loves pleasures and lacks the strength to endure, or who approves of eating human flesh,
and can consider death a good thing, when it deprives him of his pleasures? Rather, anyone like that would use every possible means
to keep living in this world forever and to escape the notice of the judges. He would not proclaim what he was so that they would kill him.”
Chapter Nine. The letter Hadrian wrote ordering that Christians should not be persecuted without a trial. Justin himself also relates
that Hadrian received a letter about the Christians from the distinguished governor Serennius Granianus, who had written to him
that it was not just to gratify the crowd’s shouting by unjustly killing them without any charge.
In response to this, the emperor wrote to Minucius Fundanus, the proconsul of Asia, and ordered
that he should execute no one without a charge and a just accusation. Justin included a copy of this letter, writing it in Latin as it originally stood.
Before it he says the following: “On the basis of the letters of the great and renowned emperor Hadrian, your father,
we also have grounds to ask you, as we have petitioned, to order that a trial be held.
We have made this petition not because Hadrian issued such an order, but because our request is just.
We have also included a copy of Hadrian’s letter, so that from it you may recognize that we have spoken truthfully.” Now this man
included the copy just as it stood in Latin. We, however, have translated it into Greek as well as we could. It reads as follows:
“To Minucius Fundanus. I have received a letter written to me by Serennius Granianus, a distinguished man,
whom you succeeded. I do not wish to leave the matter without investigation, so that people may not be troubled
and slanderers may not be given an opportunity for wrongdoing. Therefore, plainly, concerning this petition by the people of the provinces that Christians should be executed:
if they can demonstrate that the Christians have committed an act deserving death, they are to be heard on this ground alone.
We should not, however, listen merely to petitions or shouting. It is entirely proper that, if anyone wishes to bring an accusation against them, you should decide the matter.
But if anyone accuses them and shows that they are acting contrary to the law, issue your ruling according to the seriousness of the offense.
And I charge you by Hercules: if anyone does this maliciously, take care to judge the matter and turn the penalty for his wickedness back upon him...
Chapter Ten. Who were the bishops in Rome and Alexandria during the reign of Antoninus.
After Hadrian had ruled for twenty-one years and died, Antoninus, who was called Pius, succeeded him as ruler of the Romans.
In the first year of his reign, Telesphorus departed from this world after completing eleven years in his ministry.
Hyginus succeeded him as bishop of Rome. Irenaeus relates concerning Telesphorus that his departure from this world was glorified by martyrdom.
Chapter Eleven. The leaders of heresy who lived in those days. Irenaeus himself reports
that in the days of Hyginus, the bishop of Rome whom we have mentioned, Valentinus introduced his heresy.
And Cerdon was the founder of the error of Marcion's followers. Both of them became known in Rome at that time. He writes as follows:
"Valentinus came to Rome in the days of Hyginus, and his error grew strong in the days of Pius.
He continued until the days of Anicetus. Cerdon, who preceded Marcion,
also came to the church in the days of Hyginus, who was the ninth bishop.
He confessed that he had indeed gone astray. He continued acting in this way: sometimes he would teach in secret,
and sometimes he would again confess his error. At other times he was exposed for the wicked things he taught and was excluded from the assembly of the brothers."
He said these things in the third book of Against Heresies. In the first book, he also said the following about Cerdon:
"Cerdon, who received his starting principles from Simon's followers, came to Rome during the years of Hyginus,
who was the ninth bishop in the succession from the apostles. He taught
that the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets is not the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
For the former, he said, is known, but the latter is unknown; and the former is [?], but the latter is good.
Marcion received this teaching from him and expanded it, blaspheming without restraint." This same Irenaeus
with great patience exposed the unfathomable depth of Valentinus's error, which lurked hidden like a harmful creeping creature in its marshes.
Along with these, he also spoke about another man named Marcus, who lived in those same times
and was skilled in the art of sorcery. He also wrote and exposed the practices of their defiled mysteries in these words:
"Some of them prepare a wedding chamber and perform the rites of their mysteries with words that they pronounce over those being initiated.
They call what they perform a spiritual marriage, in the likeness of those pairings above."
They bring them to the water [?] and baptize them, saying these words over them: “In the name of the Father of all, who is unknown,
and in the name of Truth, the Mother of all, and in the name of the one who descended upon Jesus.” Others pronounce Hebrew names,
to greatly astonish those being initiated into their mysteries. After Hyginus had completed four years as bishop,
Pius took over the ministry of bishop of Rome. In Alexandria, Mark became the shepherd when Ammonius had completed thirteen years.
When Mark had completed ten years in his ministry and had passed away, Celadion succeeded him in the ministry of the church of Alexandria.
In the church of Rome also, after fifteen years as bishop, Pius departed from this world,
and Anicetus succeeded him there. Hegesippus related that he came to Rome in his days and remained there until the episcopate of Eleutherus.
Chapter Twelve. On the defense that Justin wrote to Antoninus. In those times Justin was becoming especially prominent.
Wearing the dress of a philosopher, he proclaimed the word of God, and in the works he wrote he fought on behalf of the faith.
In the work he wrote against Marcion, he mentions that Marcion himself was still alive at the time he composed it.
He says this: “Marcion of Pontus, who is still alive even now, teaches those who are persuaded by him to believe that there is a god greater than the Creator.
This man, in various places, has persuaded many people, through the demons who helped him,
to utter blasphemies and deny that the Creator of all is the Father of Christ, and to declare that there is another who is greater than he.
All who have followed these people are called Christians, as I said, just as, although the teachings of the philosophers do not agree with one another,
the name ‘philosophy’ is common to them all.” After this he adds: “We have works against all the heresies that have arisen.
If you wish to read them, we will give them to you.” This same Justin also diligently composed works against the pagans.
He also wrote other works containing a defense of our faith to the emperor Antoninus, who was called [?], and to the council of the Roman Senate.
For he was living in Rome itself, and he explains who he is and where he comes from
in the defense he wrote, in these words: “To the Emperor Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Pius Caesar Augustus,
and to Verissimus his son, the philosopher, and to Lucius, the son of Caesar, and to the entire Senate,
and to the whole Roman people, on behalf of those from every race of humanity who are unjustly hated and wronged:
I, Justin, son of Priscus, son of Bacchius, from Neapolis in Palestine, present this petition and supplication to you.”
Chapter Thirteen. The letter Antoninus wrote to all Asia concerning our teaching. When others also presented a petition to the emperor Antoninus,
saying that throughout Asia Christians were being oppressed with every kind of abuse by the local population, he issued the following decree throughout Asia:
“Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, to all Asia, greetings. I know that the gods are concerned about it.
that they do not overlook people like these. For they punish those who refuse to worship them more severely than you do.
For by stirring up disturbances against them, you confirm the conviction they hold.
You accuse them of having no God. But precisely because of this accusation, they choose
to die for their God rather than live. This is why they are victorious when they surrender their lives,
rather than submit to doing what you urge them to do. As for the earthquakes that have happened and continue to happen, it is proper that I remind you
that we are distressed whenever they occur. When we compare our situation with theirs, then, they have greater confidence before God than we do.
But throughout the time you remain in error, you also despise the other gods and offend against the worship of the one who does not die,
because you drive out the Christians who worship him and persecute them even to death. Many governors in the provinces wrote to my father about these matters.
He too wrote back to them that no one should harass people like these in any way,
unless they were found attempting some action against the Roman Empire. Many people have also informed me about these matters.
I too have written in agreement with my father's judgment. But if anyone persists in this attitude and brings one of these people to trial, saying that he is such a person,
the accused is to be released from the charge, even if he is found to be as alleged.
But whoever accused him is to be condemned. This decree was posted throughout Asia.
Melito, who was bishop of the church in the city of Sardis, testifies that these things happened in this way.
He was well known at that time for the defense he addressed to Emperor Verus on behalf of our faith.
Chapter Fourteen: What is recorded about those who knew the apostle. In the days of this Anicetus, whom we have mentioned as bishop of the church of Rome,
Irenaeus relates that Polycarp was still alive and came to Rome,
where he had a matter to discuss with Anicetus concerning the day of Easter. This same writer also handed down another account about Polycarp,
which it is proper for us to add to what is being said about him. It is recorded as follows in the third book that Irenaeus composed Against Heresies:
“Polycarp,” he says, “was not only taught by apostles and associated with many who had seen our Lord,
but was also appointed by the apostles themselves as bishop of the church in Smyrna in Asia. We too saw him in our youth.
He lived a very long time and grew very old. He suffered martyrdom gloriously and with distinction, and so departed from this world.
He constantly taught these things, which alone are true. All the churches in Asia bear witness to these things,
as do those who preserve Polycarp's tradition to this day. For he was a man of great excellence and a faithful witness to the truth,
far superior to Valentinus, Marcion, and the other corrupters of thought. And when he came to Rome,
In the days of Anicetus, he brought many of these heretics whom we have mentioned back to the church of God.
He taught and proclaimed that he had received only this truth from the apostles, the truth that the church hands down. There are people who heard him say:
“John, the disciple of our Lord, went to bathe at Ephesus. He saw Cerinthus inside and rushed out of the bathhouse without bathing.
Instead, he said, ‘Let us flee, so that the bathhouse does not collapse on us too, for Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is inside it.’”
Marcion himself once came before Polycarp and said to him, “Recognize us!” But he replied:
“I recognize you: you are Satan’s firstborn.” Such was the great caution exercised by the apostles and their disciples,
so that they would not share even a word with anyone who distorted the truth.
As Paul also said, “As for a man whose thinking is divisive through a different teaching,
after a first and a second warning, keep away from him, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins,
and condemns himself.” There is also a well-known letter of Polycarp, which he wrote to the Philippians.
From it, those of us who are willing and concerned about our own lives can learn the evidence of his faith and his proclamation of the truth. These are the words of Irenaeus.
Polycarp himself, in this letter that he wrote to the Philippians, which survives to this day, drew testimony from the first letter of Peter.
Chapter Fifteen: How Polycarp was martyred with others in the city of Smyrna during the reign of Verus. Now Antoninus, who was called Pius,
had ruled the kingdom for twenty-two years when his son Marcus Aurelius Verus Antoninus succeeded him, together with his brother Lucius.
At this time a great persecution broke out in Asia, and Polycarp was brought to perfection through martyrdom.
It is fitting that we include in the account of this history the document concerning his martyrdom, which has been preserved to this day.
The document is [?], in the name of the church that he led,
to the church in Pontus, and gives its account in these words: “The church of God, to those in Philomelium and to all the congregations of the holy church everywhere:
May the grace, peace, and love of God the Father and of our Lord Jesus Christ abound. We have written to you, brothers, about those who were martyred, and also about the blessed Polycarp,
who sealed it with his martyrdom, and the persecution ceased.” After these words, before the account of Polycarp,
they tell of other martyrs and record in writing the endurance they showed in their sufferings.
They astonished those who stood around watching them: at times they were stripped by scourging down to their inner blood vessels,
so that even their internal organs could be seen. At other times, sharp sea shells were spread beneath them,
and they were subjected to every kind of torture and scourging. Finally, they were given to the wild beasts as food.
They relate that the valiant Germanicus distinguished himself especially. Strengthened by the grace of God, he overcame the fear of death implanted in the body.
The proconsul wanted to persuade him. He drew his attention to his youth and said to him, “You are a boy, a young man. Have pity on yourself.”
But he paid no attention to him. Instead, he joyfully brought the wild beast toward himself, not merely by coaxing it, but even by force,
so that he might quickly depart from this world of injustice and wickedness [?]. At his glorious death, all the people were amazed
at the courage of this martyr, who loved God, and at the steadfastness of the whole Christian community.
Suddenly they began shouting, “Away with those who have no god! Let Polycarp be hunted down!” While their shouting was causing a great uproar,
a man named Quintus, a Phrygian by birth who had recently come from Phrygia, stood and saw the wild beasts and their threatening behavior.
He became afraid and sick at heart, and in the end he faltered out of concern for his life. The account in this book shows that this man was rash
and had thrown himself into trial with others, not out of fear of our Lord. Yet when this man perished, he left everyone a clear example
that no one should rashly throw himself into such circumstances without fear of our Lord. This was how these events ended.
When the admirable Polycarp first heard about this, he remained untroubled and kept his mind steady and unshaken.
He wanted to remain in the city itself. But when those who were with him asked him to go out to a farm a short distance from the city, he agreed.
He stayed there with a few people. Night and day he did nothing else but devote himself continually to prayer to our Lord.
In these prayers he petitioned and pleaded, asking that there might be peace for all the churches throughout the world. This was his constant practice.
While he was praying, three days before he was to be handed over, he saw a vision in the night concerning the pillow beneath his head:
suddenly fire caught it and consumed it. When he awoke at this, he immediately interpreted the vision.
He plainly foretold to those who were with him what was going to happen: “For Christ’s sake, I will depart from this world by fire.”
As those who were searching for him pressed their search with great eagerness, the love of the brothers again compelled him to move to another farm.
A little later, those who were searching for him caught up with him there. The love of the brothers again compelled him to move to another farm.
A little later, those pursuing him caught up with him there. They seized two boys from there and flogged one of them.
They took them and brought them to the house where Polycarp was staying. When they caught up with him there in the evening, they found him reclining in an upstairs room.
Although he could have moved from there to another house, he did not want to. Instead, he said, “Let God’s will be done.”
When he learned that they had arrived, as the account says, he went down to them and spoke with them with a peaceful and cheerful expression.
Those who did not know him felt that they were seeing something extraordinary, as they looked at his advanced age
and the modesty and composure of his face, and wondered whether such efforts had been made to arrest an old man like this.
He immediately ordered a table to be set for them and had excellent food prepared for them. He asked them for one hour in which to pray undisturbed.
When they gave him permission, he stood and prayed, filled with the grace of our Lord, so that those who had come were amazed.
They listened to him as he prayed, and many of them felt remorse,
because such a man was about to die—a chaste old man worthy of God. Besides these things, the book recounting his story also relates the following:
After he had remembered everyone in his prayer, even those he had never known, the small and the great, the honored and the lowly,
and the whole church throughout the world, he finished his prayer. When the time came to leave, they seated him on a donkey and brought him to the city.
It was the Great Sabbath. Herod, the chief of police, and his father Nicetes met him. They seated him with them in their carriage.
As they sat with him, they tried to persuade him, saying, “What harm is there in saying, ‘Caesar is my lord,’ and offering sacrifice and staying alive?”
At first he did not answer them a word. But when they kept pressing him, he said to them,
“I will not do what you advise me to do.” When they saw that he would not be persuaded by them, they began saying abusive things to him.
Suddenly they threw him out of the carriage. As he fell, his shin was scraped. But he did not turn back.
Instead, as though nothing had happened to him, he went on joyfully and eagerly. They brought him to the stadium.
There was such a great uproar in the stadium that many did not even hear that Polycarp had entered the stadium.
As he was entering, a voice came from heaven: “Be strong and courageous, Polycarp!” No one saw the one who said this,
but many of our people heard the voice. When they brought him forward, there was a great commotion, because they had heard that Polycarp had been arrested. When he was brought forward,
the proconsul asked him, “Are you Polycarp?” When he acknowledged it, he tried to persuade him to deny his faith, saying to him, “Have regard for your old age.”
He also said other similar things to him, as they customarily do: “Swear by Caesar’s fortune and repent.
Say, ‘Away with those who have no God!’” But Polycarp,
with a cheerful face, looked at all the people in the stadium and waved his hand at them. He sighed, looked up to heaven, and said,
“Take away those who have no God!” But the judge kept pressing him, saying, “Swear, and I will release you. Revile Christ!”
Polycarp said to him, “I have served him for eighty-six years, and he has never harmed me in any way.
How can I revile my King, the one who saved me?” When he pressed him again, saying, “Swear by Caesar’s fortune,” Polycarp said to him,
“You are mocking me when you tell me, ‘Swear by Caesar’s fortune,’ and you pretend not to know who I am. So hear it openly:
I am a Christian. If you want to learn the teaching of Christianity, appoint a day and listen.” The proconsul said to him, “Persuade the people.”
Polycarp said to him, “I considered you worthy of an answer. For we have been taught to give rulers and authorities appointed by God
the honor that is due to them, provided it does not compromise us. But I do not consider those people worth spending my breath on.”
The proconsul said to him, “I have wild beasts, and I will throw you to them unless you repent.” But he said, “Call them.”
“For we cannot change our minds and turn from good to evil. But it is good for someone to turn from evil to good.”
Again he said to him, “If you scorn the wild beasts, I will torment you with fire unless you repent.”
But Polycarp said to him, “You threaten me with fire that blazes for an hour and goes out after a little while.
For you do not know the fire of the coming judgment and the everlasting torment reserved for the wicked. But why are you delaying now?
Bring whatever you wish.” He said these things, and more besides, full of courage and joy, and his face was full of grace.
Not only was he not saddened or troubled by what was being said to him, but quite the opposite, so that even the proconsul himself was amazed.
He sent a herald, who proclaimed three times in the middle of the stadium, “Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian.”
When this was announced by the herald, the whole crowd of Gentiles and Jews living in Smyrna,
with uncontrollable rage and loud voices, shouted, “This is the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians, and the destroyer of our gods,
who teaches many not to sacrifice to them or worship them.” And when they had said these things,
they shouted and demanded that Philip, the ruler of Asia, release a lion against Polycarp. But he said, “I have no authority to do so,
because the spectacles have ended.” Then they agreed to shout together that Polycarp should be burned alive.
For the vision he had seen concerning the pillow beneath his head had to be fulfilled: he had seen it burning while he was praying.
He had turned and said prophetically to the believers who were with him, “I must be burned with fire.”
These things were carried out as soon as they were said: the crowds gathered wood and brushwood from the shops and baths and brought it.
The Jews were especially eager, rejoicing and busying themselves with such things, as was their custom. When the fire was ready,
he took off all his clothes and loosened the belt around his waist. He also wanted to untie what was on his feet,
though he had not done this before, because the believers used to compete over which of them would be the first to attend to his clothing.
For he was adorned with every kind of good conduct, even before his old age. Immediately, then, the equipment prepared for the fire was put in place.
When they were about to fasten him with nails, he said to them, “Leave me as I am. For the one who gives me strength to endure the fire
will also enable me to remain in the fire without struggling and without being fastened with nails.” So they did not nail him down.
They did, however, bind him. He put his hands behind his back and was bound like a distinguished lamb coming from a large flock,
an offering acceptable to God Almighty. And he prayed and said, “Father of Jesus Christ, your beloved and blessed Son, through whom we have received the knowledge of you,
God of angels and powers and all created things, and of the whole race of the righteous who live in your presence.
I bless you because you have judged me worthy of this day and this hour, to receive a share among the martyrs in the cup of Christ.
For the resurrection to eternal life, of soul and body, through the Holy Spirit, without decay. May I be offered among them before you today as a rich and acceptable sacrifice.
Just as you prepared beforehand and revealed, and are now bringing about, God of truth. Therefore, for everything I praise you and bless you,
through the eternal high priest, Jesus Christ, your beloved Son, through whom, to you and with him, together with the Holy Spirit,
be glory from now and forever and ever. When he finished the prayer and said, “Amen,” the men tending the fire lit it.
When the flame grew strong, we who were allowed to see witnessed a marvel. We were preserved to report to others what happened.
For the fire formed the shape of a vault, like a ship’s sail when it is filled with air.
It surrounded the martyr’s body, and he was inside it, not like flesh burning,
but like gold and silver being refined in a furnace. Such a sweet fragrance came to us, like the scent of frankincense
or one of the finest spices. Finally, when those wicked men saw that the fire could not burn his body,
they ordered an executioner to approach and stab him with a sword. When he did this, so much blood came out of him that it extinguished the fire.
The whole crowd was amazed that there was such a distinction between unbelievers and God’s chosen ones.
One of these was this blessed and remarkable man, who in our times became an imitator of the apostles and prophets, the bishop of the church of Smyrna.
Every word that came from his mouth has been fulfilled and is being fulfilled. But the evil adversary, jealous and envious, who opposes the race of the righteous,

when he saw the greatness of his martyrdom and his conduct, which had been blameless from the beginning, and that he had been crowned with an imperishable crown and had received an unquestionable victory,
schemed to prevent even his body from being given to us, although many longed to obtain it and to have a share in his holy body.
So people urged Nicetes, the father of Herod and brother of Alce, to approach the governor so that he would not give us his body.
“Otherwise,” they said, “they may abandon the one who was crucified and begin worshiping this man.”
They urged this, and the Jews also helped them [?]. These were the very people who had kept watch on us when we were preparing to take him out of the fire.
For they did not know that we could never abandon Christ,
who suffered for the life of the world—that is, for those who wish to live—nor do we worship anyone else.
For we worship Christ, who is the Son of God, but we love the martyrs as they deserve,
because they imitate the martyrdom of our Lord, and because of their good and excellent devotion to our King and Teacher. May we too be worthy to become their disciples and companions.
When the centurion saw the Jews’ contentious behavior, he placed the body in the middle, as was their custom, and burned it.
Then, at last, we gathered his bones, which are more precious than costly stones and far finer than refined gold.
And we laid them where the Lord allowed us, so that we could gather in joy and gladness and celebrate the anniversary of his martyrdom.
This was to commemorate those who had already triumphed and to prepare those who would follow their example.
Such were the things that happened to the blessed Polycarp, together with those twelve from Philadelphia who suffered martyrdom in Smyrna.
His memory alone is far more celebrated than that of all the others, so that he is spoken of even among the Gentiles.
Such, then, was the end of the admirable Polycarp, a disciple of the apostles. The brothers in the church of Smyrna wrote this account of him in the letter we have quoted.
In this same document, there is also material about other martyrs who suffered martyrdom in Smyrna at that same time.
They wrote about them together with the martyrdom of Polycarp. Along with these, they also tell
of Metrodorus, who was regarded as a presbyter of the heresy of Marcion's followers. He had no hope of relief.
Apparently out of zeal for God's martyrs, he too was handed over to the fire and died. Among the distinguished martyrs of that time was the well-known Pionius.
His confession in its several parts, the boldness of his speech, and his defense of the faith before the people and the judges,
his teaching in everyone's presence, his welcome to those who had fallen during the trial of persecution, and the comfort he gave in prison to the brothers who came to him,
together with the tortures he endured and their sufferings, his being fastened with nails, his endurance in the fire, and his end—all these in full
are recorded in the accounts about him. For those who are eager and wish to learn, these things are written in the records of the martyrs that we have already collected.
The records also contain accounts of those who suffered martyrdom in Pergamum, a city of Asia:
Carpus, Papylus, and a woman named Agathonice. They reached their end with a glorious and notable confession.

Chapter Sixteen. How Justin the philosopher suffered martyrdom while preaching the word of Christ in Rome.

At this time,
Justin too, whom we mentioned a little earlier, after presenting a second defense of our teaching to these same emperors, reached his end in martyrdom.
For Crescens the philosopher was a Cynic—that is, a dog—and strove in thought and deed to live up to the name he bore.
Justin repeatedly defeated him in debate before the listeners who were present. In the end, however, he devised a plot against Justin.
And for the truth that he proclaimed, Justin reached his end in martyrdom. This philosopher of truth himself stated this clearly in the defense he composed.
He foretold what was going to happen to him in these words: “I too expect to be handed over by one of those who are well known,
or by Crescens, the lying, glory-loving philosopher, and to be nailed to a stake. For we ought not to call him a philosopher—
a man who publicly testifies before the people about things he does not know, saying that Christians are godless and wicked.
He did this to win the favor of, and please, the many who were deceived.
For if he has not even read the teaching of Christ, yet dares to tell lies about us, it is clear that he is an evil man.
And he is far worse than ordinary people, for they at least may guard themselves against discussing or giving false testimony about something they do not understand.
But if he has read it and has not understood the greatness contained in it, or if he has understood it but has done these things so that he will not be thought to belong to it,
he proves to be still more weak and wicked, enslaved to ignorance, empty glory, and fear. And I asked him questions like these,
and learned from him and exposed him as truly knowing nothing. But I want you to know that I am speaking truthfully.
If these discussions themselves have not come to your attention, I am ready for these questions to be presented again before your eyes.
For this very undertaking is worthy of kingship. But if you know these questions of mine and his answers, this is clear to you:
he understands nothing of our teachings. Or, if he did understand but did not dare to speak because of those who were listening, then, as I said before,
he has shown himself to be no philosopher but a lover of empty glory. He does not even honor the teaching of Socrates, which deserves to be loved.
Justin said these things. As for what he said earlier, that Crescens brought against him the accusation through which he met his end, Tatian recounts this.
This man had formerly been a sophist trained in Greek learning, and he had gained no small reputation in it. He left many written discourses as records.
In the work he wrote Against the Pagans, he recounts the following: “The admirable Justin also rightly said
that those we mentioned earlier resemble robbers.” After saying a little about the philosophers, he then says the following:
“Crescens, who had recently entered the great city of Rome, surpassed everyone in his passion for corrupting boys.
He was deeply occupied with the love of money. And death, which he advised people to despise—he himself was afraid of that death.
Thus he schemed to bring death upon Justin, as though it were a great evil, because Justin proclaimed the truth
and rebuked the philosophers for being gluttons and deceivers.” This, then, was the cause of Justin’s martyrdom.
Chapter Seventeen. Which martyrs Justin mentions in his discourse. Justin himself, before his martyrdom, mentions others who suffered martyrdom before him,
in the first defense he composed for the emperors, because it suited the subject he had undertaken. He writes as follows:
“A certain woman was married to a depraved man. She too had formerly been depraved, but when she came to know Christ’s teaching, she became chaste.
She tried to persuade her husband to become chaste like her. She acquainted him with the teaching and told him about the fire of everlasting punishment
that awaits those who fail to live chastely and conduct themselves with sound judgment. But by persisting in his recklessness through his filthy actions,
he alienated his wife. For this woman considered it ungodly
to share her life with a man who wanted to use every means to satisfy his desires contrary to the law of nature and contrary to what is right.
She wanted to separate from him. But her relatives urged her not to, advising her to remain with him a little longer in the hope that he would change.
When her husband came home on one occasion, she forced herself to remain with him. But afterward he went to Alexandria, and it was reported that he was committing wicked acts.
So that she would not share in his wrongdoing and wickedness by remaining with him in marriage, living with him, and sharing his bed, she gave him a certificate of divorce and separated from him.
But this depraved and wicked husband of hers ought to have rejoiced that she had withdrawn from what she had previously done without restraint with her servants and hired workers,
and that, although she had delighted in drunkenness and every kind of wickedness, she had stopped all these practices and wanted to stop him from doing these things too.
Because she had left him, he brought an accusation against her, saying that she was a Christian. But she petitioned the emperor and asked to be allowed first to arrange her affairs,
and afterward, once she had arranged her affairs, to make her defense against the accusation brought against her. He granted her this.
But the man who had formerly been her husband, because he could bring no charge against her, turned against Ptolemy,
who had been this woman's teacher in Christian doctrine, and whom Urbicius put to death.
This was how the centurion had thrown Ptolemy into prison: he was a friend of her husband,
who had persuaded him to catch Ptolemy out in his words and ask him just this one question: whether he was a Christian.
But Ptolemy, because he loved the truth and was neither a deceiver nor a liar, acknowledged that he was a Christian.
The centurion immediately threw him into prison and tormented him there for a long time. Finally, when they brought this man before Urbicius,
he was asked only this: whether he was a Christian. But because he was convinced of the truth of Christ,
he openly acknowledged this glorious teaching of God. For anyone who denies it and turns away either doubts his faith,
or considers this teaching something [?] and avoids acknowledging it. Neither of these things is found among true Christians.
When Urbicius ordered him to be put to death, Lucius, who was also a Christian, saw that this judgment had been made without thought,
and said to Urbicius, “What is the reason for this? Although he has not been proved to be an adulterer or sexually immoral,
or a murderer, robber, or plunderer, or to have committed any of these crimes, you have condemned him merely because he acknowledged that he is a Christian.
You are passing a judgment, Urbicius, that is unworthy of the emperor Pius, of the philosopher who is Caesar's son, and of the illustrious Senate.”
Without giving him an answer to these things, he said to Lucius, “It seems to me that you too are a Christian.”
Lucius said, “Yes, indeed.” He then ordered this man also to be put to death. But Lucius gave thanks and said
that a great favor had been shown him, since he was being delivered from wicked masters and was going to God, the good King and Father.
Yet another man came forward, a third, and he too received the sentence of death. To these things Justin added the words that we mentioned earlier, saying:
“I too was expecting to be betrayed by one of those mentioned,” and so forth.
Chapter eighteen: Which writings of Justin have come down to us. ... This same Justin left us many writings, full of great benefit,
which show that he possessed a cultivated soul, eager for the teaching of God.
Let those who love learning examine them. We record those among them that seem to us useful.
He has one work written to the emperor Antoninus, who was called Pius, and to his sons and the Roman Senate: a petition on behalf of our teaching.
There is another containing a defense of our faith, which he addressed to Antoninus Verus,
who succeeded the earlier emperor whose times we have just discussed. There is also another work against the pagans,
in which he discusses at length the inquiry shared by us and the Greek philosophers. There is also another in which he undertakes to speak about the nature of demons,
which there is no need for us to present now. There is also another against the pagans, which he entitled Refutation.
There is also another, That God Alone Is the One Who Exists, which he establishes not only from our Scriptures,
but also from the writings of the Greek sages. There is also another entitled The Psalmist,
and another, On the Soul, in which he sets out distinct questions that he raises concerning this subject.
He presents the opinions held in the teachings of the non-Christian sages and promises to argue against them
and to set out his own opinions in other discourses. There is also a dialogue that he composed against the Jews,
which he held at Ephesus with Trypho, who was then a well-known man among the Hebrews.
In it he explains how the grace of God brought him to the message of faith,
how devoted he had previously been to the study of philosophy, and how he had searched for the truth with his whole soul.
In it he also tells how the Jews plotted against the teaching of Christ, speaking to Trypho as follows:
“Not only do you refuse to repent of the evil things you have done, but at that time you also chose well-known men from Jerusalem
and sent them throughout the earth to say, ‘A godless sect of Christians has appeared.’ They spoke evil things about us,
which are repeated today by everyone who does not know us. Thus you are the cause of ruin not only for yourselves,
but also for all humanity.” He also wrote and showed that the gift of prophecy was present in the church even down to his own days.
He mentions the Revelation of John and plainly says that it belongs to the apostle. He also cites passages from the prophets and demonstrates to Trypho
that the Jews cut them out of the Scriptures. So highly esteemed by the ancients were this man's discourses, filled with zeal,
that Irenaeus even quotes his words in the fourth book that he composed against heresies.
He quotes his words as follows: “Justin spoke well in the discourse he composed against Marcion:
‘I would not have believed even the Lord himself if he had proclaimed that there was another God besides the Creator.’”
Again, in his fifth book on this same subject, he says the following: “Justin spoke well.”
Before the coming of our Lord, Satan had never dared to blaspheme against God, because he did not yet know his condemnation.
These things were rightly said to encourage those who love learning to examine his writings diligently. This man's story was as follows.
Chapter Nineteen: Which bishops served in Rome and Alexandria in the days of Verus.
In the eighth year of the reign of Antoninus Verus, when Anicetus, bishop of Rome, had completed eleven years,
Soter succeeded him. Likewise, in the church of Alexandria, after Celadion had served for fourteen years, Agrippinus succeeded him.
Chapter Twenty: Which bishops served in Antioch. In the church of Antioch, Theophilus was known as the sixth bishop after the apostles.
After Heron, Cornelius had been the fourth bishop there. After him, Eros received the office of bishop as the fifth.
Chapter Twenty-One: The church writers who were distinguished in those times. Hegesippus was distinguished in the church in those times.
We have learned that he belonged to the earlier generation. There were also Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and Pinytus, who was a bishop in Crete,
and along with them Philip, Apollinaris, Melito, Musanus, Modestus, and Irenaeus.
Through their writings, the true faith of the apostolic tradition has been handed down even to us.
Chapter Twenty-Two: Hegesippus and those whom he mentions. Hegesippus, in the five books he composed concerning our teaching,
left a full record of his thinking. In them he relates that he met many bishops while traveling on his way to Rome,
and received this same teaching from them all. Let us hear what he says, after other matters, also about the letters that Clement wrote to the church of Corinth.
He recounts it as follows: "The church of Corinth continued in simplicity of teaching until Primus, who was bishop in Corinth.
When I was setting out for Rome, I met the Corinthians and stayed with them for many days,
and together we found comfort in sound teaching. When I went to Rome, I traced the succession of bishops there as far as Anicetus,
who was succeeded by Soter, and after Soter by Eleutherus. And so it is in every succession and in all the churches,
in accordance with what the Law, the Prophets, and our Lord proclaimed." This same man also described the leaders of the heresies that arose in his days in these words:
"After James the Just was martyred, as we have already said, Simeon son of Clopas, who was his cousin, became the second bishop.
Everyone favored him because he was a relative of our Lord. For this reason they called the church a virgin,
for she had not yet been corrupted by empty teachings. Thebuthis was the first to begin corrupting her there,
because he had not become bishop. He belonged to one of the seven sects, and he was [?]. From these came Simon,
which is why they are called Simonians; Cleobius, from whom came the Cleobians; Dositheus, from whom came the Dositheans;
and Gorthaeus, from whom came the Gorthaeans and Masbotheans. From these came the Menandrians, Marcionites, and Carpocratians.
And the Basilidians and Saturnilians—each of them [?] on his own—and others introduced teachings according to the designs of their own minds.
From these arose false messiahs, false prophets, and false apostles, who divided the unity of the church
through the blasphemous words they spoke against God and his Christ. Again, Hegesippus himself also discusses the sects that existed among the Jews in ancient times, saying:
“There were differing opinions among the circumcised in Israel, among those who opposed the tribe of Judah and the Christ.
These were the Essenes, the Galileans, those who are baptized every day,
the Masbotheans, the Samaritans, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees.” He also wrote many other things, some of which we have included under their respective periods in this history.
He quotes some things from the Gospel of the Hebrews and of the Syrians, and independently includes some things from the Hebrew language.
He indicates that he himself was one of the Hebrews and came to believe. He also mentions other things from the unwritten tradition of Judaism.
He, Irenaeus, and all the early writers used to call the Proverbs of Solomon “All-Virtuous Wisdom.”
Concerning the writings called “revelations,” he relates that some of them were compiled in his own time by people belonging to heretical sects.
Chapter twenty-three. On Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and the letters he wrote.
Let us now speak first about this man also: Dionysius, who was bishop of the church of Corinth.
In his zeal for the teaching of God, he taught not only those who were under his authority,
but also benefited distant regions through the letters he wrote to the churches.
There is one that he wrote to the Lacedaemonians about instruction in the true faith, peace, and unity, and another to the Athenians
about vigilance in faith and conduct according to the gospel. In it he rebukes them because they had lost heart and were close to abandoning their faith.
In connection with this, the bishop who led them, whose name was Publius, suffered martyrdom in the persecution that occurred at that time.
He mentions that Quadratus became their bishop after Publius suffered martyrdom.
He testifies concerning Quadratus that through his diligence they were gathered together and their faith was rekindled. Along with these things, he makes known
that Dionysius the Areopagite, who came to believe through Paul, as is written in Acts,
became the first bishop of the church of Athens. There is also another letter of his, which he wrote to Nicomedia.
In it he fought against the heresy of Marcion and upheld the teaching of the truth. He also wrote a letter to the church in Gortyna and the other churches in Crete.
He praises Philip, their bishop, since many noble achievements bear witness to the church that was under his care.
He reminds him to beware of the schemes of the heretics. He also wrote letters to the church in Amastris, together with the other churches in Pontus.
He indicates that Bacchylides and Elpistus had urged him to write. In these letters he set down an explanation of the divine Scriptures.
He also makes known that they had Palmas as their bishop, and he teaches them many things about marriage and chastity.
He also instructs them to welcome those who turn back from transgressions, failings, or the error of heresy.
Following these is another letter that he wrote to the people of Cnossus. In it he urges Pinytus, the bishop of the church there,
not to impose the heavy yoke of sexual abstinence on the brothers by compulsion, but to take account of the weakness of many.
In response to this, Pinytus himself wrote to him, expressing admiration for him and praising Dionysius.
He asked him also, from time to time, to nourish the people under his care with solid food through more mature writings,
so that they would not remain occupied with words of milk to the very end and grow old in an infantile way of life.
In this very letter, evidence is given of the soundness of Pinytus’s true faith,
his concern for the welfare of those under his care, and his eloquence and understanding in the fear of God.
Dionysius also has another letter to the Romans, addressed to the bishop at that time, whose name was Soter.
We will quote a few words from it to show how he praises the custom of the Romans, which was maintained until this persecution that took place in our own days.
He says as follows: “From the beginning you have had this custom of helping the brothers in every way
and sending provisions to many churches in every city. In this way you relieve the needs of the poor
and supply the needs of the brothers in the mines with the provisions you have long been accustomed to send.
The Romans preserve this custom as an inheritance from their fathers. Your blessed bishop Soter
not only maintained it but even increased the gift that was being sent to the saints.
With kind words he encouraged the brothers who went up there, like a compassionate father encouraging his children.”
In this same letter he also mentions the letter that Clement wrote to the Corinthians, and makes known that, according to an ancient custom, it is read there before the whole church.
He therefore says: “Today we observed the holy day of Sunday and read your letter during it.
We ought always to gain wisdom by reading it, just as we do from the earlier letter written to us by Clement.”
Speaking about his own letters and how some people had tampered with them, he says: “The brothers urged me to write letters to them, and I wrote them.
But Satan’s apostles filled these letters with weeds by taking things away from them and adding things to them. Woe is reserved for these people.
It is therefore no wonder if some people have also altered the writings of our Lord, since they have dealt deceitfully with writings that are not of that kind.”
Dionysius also has another letter, similar to these, which he wrote to Chrysophora, a faithful sister.
He gave her the nourishment of instruction that was suitable for her. These, then, are the things concerning Dionysius.
Chapter Twenty-Four. On Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, and on Philip and Modestus.
And on Melito and those whom he mentioned, and on Apollinaris and Musanus. Now Theophilus, whom we have spoken of as bishop of Antioch,
has three discourses against Autolycus, and another bearing the title Against the Heresy of Hermogenes,
in which he uses testimony from the Revelation of John. He also has other books useful for instruction.
Even at that time, those who belonged to the teaching of heresy were corrupting the pure seed of the apostles’ teaching like weeds.
But the shepherds in the churches everywhere drove them away from Christ’s flock like wild animals.
Sometimes they did this through teaching and appeals to the brothers; at other times they openly confronted them, fighting against them in debate and pressing them hard.
They also carefully set out and published their thoughts in written discourses.
Theophilus himself fought against them along with others. This is evident from one discourse that he composed forcefully against Marcion,
which is itself preserved along with the other works we have mentioned. After him, Maximinus received the bishopric of the church of Antioch.
He was the seventh after the apostles. As for Philip, of whom we learned from the words of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth,
that he was bishop of the church in the city of Gortyna, he too carefully composed a discourse against Marcion.
So did Irenaeus and Modestus, who exposed this man’s error more openly than the others,
and many others whose discourses are preserved among many of the brothers to this day.
At this time Melito, bishop of the church of Sardis, and Apollinaris, bishop of the church of Hierapolis, were also flourishing with distinction.
Each of them independently composed a defense of the faith, and they presented them to the Roman emperor of that time.
The discourses of these men that are known to us are as follows. By Melito: two works On Passover; On Conduct; and On the Prophets;
another On the Church; another On Sunday; another On the Faith of Man; and another On His Formation;
another On the Hearing of Faith; and, along with these, On Soul and Body; also On the Birth of Christ, and On the Word of His Prophecy;
and again On Soul and Body; another On Hospitality; On Satan; and On the Revelation of John;
another On God Who Put On a Body; and another that he wrote to the emperor Antoninus.
When he wrote about the time of Passover, he began his work by reporting the following: “In the time of Servilius Paulus, proconsul of Asia, Agris [?] was martyred.
There was a great inquiry at Laodicea about Passover, a question that kept arising in those days, and these things were written.” This discourse
is mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in his own discourse that he wrote about Passover. He says that he himself wrote in response to Melito’s discourse.
In the defense that he presented to the emperor, he relates things like these that happened [?] in our world.
“Something that has never happened before is happening now: the people who fear God are being persecuted in Asia under new decrees.”
For shameless informers and people who covet the possessions of others,
on the pretext that they have an official order, openly plunder and rob, night and day, people who have done nothing wrong. And after other remarks, he said again:
“If you ordered this to be done, then it is being done rightly, for a just king never makes an unjust decision.
We too gladly endure the honor of such a death. But we present only this request to you:
that you first examine those responsible for this dispute and judge justly whether they deserve death and punishment, or life and peace.
But if this intention and this new decree do not come from you—for it is not fitting to act this way even toward barbarians who are enemies—
we ask you all the more not to neglect us in this persecution by the world.” After this he said:
“Our philosophy first flourished among the barbarians, but it also sprang up among your people in the days of Augustus.
It brought great power to the Roman Empire, and especially beneficial growth to your own reign.
For from that time the dominion of the Romans has grown and prospered—the dominion that you inherited and enlarged, and will strengthen further together with your son—
as you preserve the philosophy that grew up alongside your empire, which began with Augustus. Your ancestors also honored it along with the other religions.
And this is great evidence that our message sprang up for the good of the empire, together with its auspicious beginning:
since the days of Augustus, nothing bad has befallen your empire. Rather, it has become increasingly glorious and strong in every respect through the prayers of us all.
Of all the emperors who have reigned, only Nero and Domitian were persuaded by envious people and accepted slander against our teaching.
From them it came about that this false accusation against us was handed down as an unthinking custom.
But your ancestors corrected their error. For on various occasions they warned [?] many people in writing,
those who wished to act insolently and cause trouble over this. Your grandfather Hadrian wrote to many people about this,
including Fundius, the proconsul of Asia. Your father also wrote about us to the cities, ordering that no one should mistreat us, while you too were administering everything with him,
including to the [?], the Thessalonians, Athens, and all the peoples. We are confident that you have an even more favorable opinion of these matters than they did.
And we are confident that you will order everything we ask of you with still greater wisdom.”
These passages have been set down thus far. In the Extracts written by Melito, at their beginning,
he recorded the number of the books of the Old Testament and indicated which are accepted. It is fitting to list them here. He writes as follows: “Melito to Onesimus, my brother, greetings.
Since you have often urged me, in your zeal for the word, to make extracts for you from the Law and the Prophets concerning our Savior and our entire faith,
and since you also wished to learn precisely about the ancient books, how many they are in number and which they are in their order,”
I made it my concern to do this very thing, since I was convinced of your zeal for the faith and for the teaching of the word.
For you prize the love of God above everything else, and you struggle for eternal life.
So when I went up to the East and reached the very place where these things were proclaimed and took place, I carefully investigated the books of the Old Testament.
I wrote them down and sent them to you. Their names are these: the five books of Moses—Genesis, Exodus,
Numbers, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy; also Joshua son of Nun; the book of Judges; Ruth; the four books of Kings;
the two books of Chronicles; the Psalms of David; and those of Solomon—Proverbs, which is Wisdom, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs;
Job; and of the prophets, Isaiah and Jeremiah, the twelve prophets together, Daniel, Ezekiel, and Ezra.
From these I made extracts and arranged them in six books. All these are the works of Melito.
There are also many works of Apollinaris preserved by many people. Those that we have seen are these:
One, a defense [?], which he composed for this emperor whom we mentioned earlier; and five against the pagans;
two against the Jews; and those he later composed concerning the heresy of the Phrygians, which had recently sprung up a short time before.
For at that time Montanus, together with the false prophetesses who followed him, was beginning to turn away from the truth.
Twenty-five: On the heresy of Tatian. Musanus, whom we numbered among those we have listed,
has a work which he composed for brothers who had inclined toward the heresy called that of the Encratites, to bring them back to the truth.
For it was just then beginning to appear and to introduce into the world a false, foreign, and destructive way of thinking. It is said,
however, that Tatian was responsible for the beginning of this error. A little earlier we quoted some of his words about Justin, the glorious martyr,
and related that he was his disciple. Irenaeus gives information about this in the first book of his work against heresies,
concerning Tatian and his heresy. He writes as follows: “After Saturninus and Marcion, those called Encratites
preached and rejected marriage, repudiating God's original creation and indirectly accusing him who made male and female for the propagation of the human race.
They also teach that one should abstain from eating anything that has life.
They deny thanksgiving to God, the maker of all, and oppose the salvation of the human being who was formed first.
This has only now appeared among them: Tatian was the first to introduce this blasphemy.
He was a disciple of Justin, and as long as he remained with him, he displayed nothing of this sort.
But after Justin's martyrdom, Tatian withdrew from the church, becoming conceited and boastful, because he imagined that he could be a teacher superior to others.
He devised for himself a different form of teaching, and he too told tales like those of the followers of Valentinus.
“Of the invisible aeons,” he says. He called marriage corruption and fornication, like Marcion[?] and Saturninus, and opposed the salvation of Adam.
Irenaeus said these things. A short time later, a man named Severus reinforced this heresy.
He was the reason that those who became its disciples were called Severians, after his name.
These people use the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, but interpret the meaning of the Scriptures according to their own ideas.
They blaspheme against Paul the apostle and reject his letters. Nor do they accept the Acts of the Apostles.
This Tatian, their first leader, collected and combined material and composed a gospel, which he called the Diatessaron, that is, “the combined version.”
Many people still have this to this day. It is said of him that he dared to alter some words of the apostle in order to improve the arrangement of the wording.
He left many discourses. Among them is one discourse widely known as Against the Gentiles.
In it he mentioned the famous people who had lived among the Gentiles from ancient times, and showed that Moses and the prophets of the Hebrews preceded them all.
This discourse appears to be excellent and more useful than all his other discourses. These things have been said about these people.
Chapter twenty-six. On Bardaisan the Aramean and his discourses. During the reign of Antoninus Verus, heresies multiplied.
In Mesopotamia, at Edessa, Bardaisan, a well-known man who was highly skilled in the Aramaic language,
opposed in his discourse the followers of Marcion and others who upheld various teachings.
He wrote the discourse in his own language, along with many other discourses that he wrote. He had many learned followers who were powerful speakers.
They published his discourses. There is a particularly distinguished dialogue of his, On Fate, which he wrote to Antoninus.
They say that he also wrote many other works because of the persecution that took place at that time. He had originally followed the teaching of Valentinus.
But when he came to despise this teaching and refuted its many fables, he thought that he was moving of his own accord to a better belief.
Yet he did not entirely wipe away the stain of that earlier heresy. At this same time, the bishop of the church of Rome died.
The fourth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished.

Book Five of the History of the Church.
Chapter 1. How many martyrs there were in Gaul in the days of Verus, and where they endured the struggle for the sake of devotion to God.
Soter, the bishop of the church of Rome, departed this world after serving for eight years, and Eleutherus succeeded him.
He was the twelfth bishop after the apostles. It was the seventeenth year of Emperor Antoninus Verus.
At that very time, persecution against us flared up fiercely in various regions, stirred up, it seems, by the populace.

One can discover that there were tens of thousands of martyrs everywhere by comparing what happened among a single people, which was written down and handed on to those who came after them as a memorial never to be forgotten.
We have recorded the full account of their history in the collection of accounts of martyrs that we compiled. We have presented it not only as history but also as instruction.
Now, however, let us gather and set down what is needed for the subject before us. Others who recount and write the histories of the world
hand down accounts of victories won in wars against enemies, the triumphs of military commanders, and the bravery of warriors
who were stained with blood, with the slaughter of many young men of their own country, and with the wealth of others. But in our historical account of a life devoted to God, we speak
about the battle for the peace of the soul and about those who triumphed in it. They fought not for their country but for the truth,
and not for their loved ones but for devotion to our Lord. We have recorded, as an everlasting memorial, the endurance of the champions of truth,
what they bravely suffered, and the victory they won over demons and invisible enemies. We proclaim their crowns as an everlasting memorial.
It was in the land of Gaul, then, that this struggle took place—the contest of these martyrs whom we have mentioned.
Two well-known cities there are called metropolitan cities, standing above the other cities in that land: Lyon and Vienne.
The river Rhône flows past both these cities and through their entire district, with its abundant waters.
The well-known churches in the land of Gaul wrote and sent to the churches in Asia and Phrygia an account of these martyrs and of what had happened among them.
They tell the story in this manner. I will set down their very words: “The servants of Christ who live in Vienne and Lyon in Gaul,
to the brothers in Asia and Phrygia who have faith in our salvation and our hope: peace, grace, and glory
from God the Father and from Jesus Christ our Lord.” After this they said a little by way of introduction to the account, and began their narrative as follows:
“Concerning the greatness [?] of the persecution that took place here, the fury of the nations against the saints, and how much the blessed martyrs endured,
we cannot give an exact account, nor can it be fully contained in writing.
For the enemy rose against us with all his strength and gave us a foretaste of his coming, which will take place openly.
He used every device to stir up those who belonged to him and train them beforehand against the servants of God.
They not only drove us out of houses, baths, and marketplaces, but also threatened us so that none of us should be seen anywhere at all.
But the grace of God stood against them and rescued those who were weak.
It raised up firm pillars who, through their endurance, were able to take upon themselves the enemy’s entire assault.
Together they endured every insult and every torture, and great sufferings seemed small to them.
For they were eager to go to Christ and showed that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy
of the glory that is to be revealed in us. First, they courageously endured whatever befell them at the hands of the whole assembled crowd:
blows, stoning, imprisonment, and everything that savage people are accustomed to inflict
on those they hate and on their enemies. Then they were brought to the marketplace and questioned before all the people by the military commander and the authorities who governed the cities.
When they confessed that they were Christians, they were confined in prison until the governor’s arrival.
Afterward they were brought before the governor, who treated our people with exceptional harshness.
One of the brothers, whose name was Vettius Epagathus, was filled with love for God and for his neighbor.
He was so blameless in his conduct that, although he was young, he could be compared to Zechariah according to the testimony given about him.
For he walked blamelessly in all the Lord’s commandments and righteous requirements, and tirelessly performed every service for his neighbor.
He had zeal for God and was fervent in spirit. Such was his character that he could not bear to see the trial being conducted against us so recklessly.
But he protested vehemently and pleaded to be heard in defense of the brothers.
He argued that they had committed no act of wickedness, as godless people do.
