But everyone standing around the judgment seat shouted at him, for he was a well-known man.
The governor himself would not accept the appeal for justice that he presented to him. He asked him only this: whether he too was a Christian.
He openly confessed it in a loud voice. He too was numbered among the martyrs and became a comforter of the Christians.
For he had within him the Spirit, the Advocate, to an even greater degree than Zechariah. He showed his abundant love by being willing to lay down his own life as well in defense of the brothers.
For he was a true disciple of Christ, following the Lamb of God wherever he went. From this point onward, many began to be distinguished from one another.
The first [?] martyrs were clearly recognizable and ready. They wholeheartedly fulfilled their confession of martyrdom.
Those who were unprepared and untrained were also recognizable, because they were still weak.
They could not endure the intensity of the great struggle. Ten of them in all renounced the faith.
They caused us much distress and great pain, and weakened the resolve of the others who had not yet been arrested.
These others were enduring every kind of mistreatment from the pagans alongside the martyrs, and did not separate themselves from them.
Then we were all deeply troubled, because we did not yet know what would happen in the confession of the faith.
It was not that we feared the tortures that were coming upon us, but that we were looking toward the outcome of these events.
We were afraid that someone might renounce the faith. Yet every day people who were worthy were arrested.
They filled up the number of those who had fallen, so that all the zealous members of these two churches were picked out.
This included those whose efforts did most to sustain the churches here. Some pagan members of the households of our people were also arrested.

For the governor had publicly ordered, in the sight of all the people, that all of us should be investigated. These people, through Satan’s influence, became afraid of the iron combs used for torture,
which they saw the saints enduring. The soldiers incited them to make false accusations against us and say
that we ate our children and had sexual intercourse with our mothers, along with other things that we are not permitted to speak or think about, or even to believe
that anything like them had ever happened among human beings. When this report spread, everyone became enraged against us like wild beasts.
Even people who had previously shown us affection because of family ties then became deeply embittered and gnashed their teeth at us.
The words of our Lord were being fulfilled: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is serving God.”
From then on, the blessed martyrs endured indescribable tortures, for Satan was devising ways to make even them utter some blasphemy.
The anger of all the people, the governor, and the soldiers grew especially fierce against Sanctus, the deacon [?] from Vienne.
And about Maturus, who had recently received baptism and was a valiant athlete; and about Attalus, who came from the city of Pergamum.
He was always a firm pillar for everyone in that region. And about Blandina, through whom Christ showed
that those who appear insignificant, ugly, and despised among human beings are considered worthy of great glory before God because of their love for him.
He is known by his power and does not boast in outward appearance. For while we were all afraid,
even the woman who was her earthly mistress—for she too was among the martyrs engaged in the struggle—was anxious about this slave of hers,
fearing that she might be unable to confess openly because of her bodily weakness. But Blandina herself was filled with such strength
that those who took turns torturing her in every way from morning until evening became exhausted and worn out. They admitted that they had been defeated
and had nothing more they could do to her. They were amazed that there was even any breath left in her, since her whole body was torn and pierced.
They testified that a single kind of this suffering would have been enough to take her life, let alone all this torture.
But this noble woman, like a valiant athlete, was renewed through her confession.
This was her relief and rest, and kept her from feeling pain in what she suffered: she would say, “I am a Christian,
and nothing evil is done among us.” Sanctus too endured the tortures inflicted by human beings courageously, exceedingly more than anyone else.
Those wicked men hoped that, because of the intensity and severity of the tortures, they would hear him say something improper.
But he resisted them with such endurance that he would not even tell them his name,
nor what people he belonged to, nor what city he came from, nor whether he was a slave or free.
Instead, in answer to everything they asked him, he replied in Latin, “I am a Christian.”
He made this confession in place of his name, his city, his ancestry, and everything else alike. The pagans heard nothing else from him.
Because of this, great anger arose against him from the governor and those who were torturing him. When they had nothing else they could do to him,
they finally heated bronze plates and placed them on the tender parts of his body. Although his body was burning, he endured
and did not bend or give way. Instead, he was strengthened in his confession by the heavenly spring of living water that flowed from Christ’s side,
which shed dew upon him and made him radiant. His body itself bore witness to what he had endured, for it was entirely covered with wounds and sores.
His whole appearance was mangled and disfigured beyond human likeness. Yet Christ, suffering in him, accomplished great glory through him,
defeating the enemy and showing others an example in him: there is nothing fearful where the Father’s love is,
and nothing painful where Christ’s glory is. But after a day those wicked men again tortured the martyr.
They thought that, since his body was decaying and festering, if they subjected him to the same tortures again, they would exhaust his strength.
For not even a human hand could touch it. Or, if he died under his tortures, he would strike fear into others...
But not a single one of these things happened to him. Instead, something happened that people had not imagined.
His body was healed and restored through the [?] subsequently brought upon him, and it regained its former appearance and the use of its limbs.
For that second torture served not to torment him but to heal him, by the grace of Christ.
And a woman named Biblis, who was among those who had previously denied the faith—when the enemy thought that she had fallen,
he wanted to condemn her through blasphemy as well. He brought her back to the tortures and pressed her to say improper things about us,
so that he might see her weakness and frailty. But amid those very tortures she came to her senses and awoke as though from a deep sleep.
[?] through these temporary tortures, the eternal torment of hell. She answered those blasphemers, saying, “How can they eat children,
when they are not even permitted to eat the blood of animals?” From that moment she openly declared herself a Christian,
and she was added to the number of the martyrs. But when Christ had brought the tyrants’ tortures to nothing through the endurance of the blessed ones,
the enemy devised another scheme: to torment them by confinement in dark, cramped places in prison,
to stretch their feet in the stocks as far as the fifth hole, and to inflict other blows that people habitually use in their rage.
These attacks were carried out by the enemy against those who were imprisoned.
Thus many of them were suffocated in prison—those whom the Lord wished to depart from the world in this way, to reveal himself.
For those who had been bitterly tortured, who were thought unable to survive even if every medical treatment were given to them,
remained in prison, deprived of all human care. Yet they were healed by our Lord and strengthened in body and soul,
and they encouraged and comforted others. But those who had recently been arrested, whose bodies had not yet been beaten,
could not endure the burden of confinement, but died inside. Now the blessed Pothinus, who had been entrusted with the ministry of bishop in Lyon,
was over seventy years old and very weak in body. He could barely breathe because of his bodily weakness,
but he was strengthened by his spiritual resolve because of his steadfast desire for martyrdom. They dragged him too and brought him before the tribunal.
Although his body was failing from old age and illness, his soul was preserved within him so that Christ might be glorified through him.
When the soldiers brought him before the tribunal, the city authorities accompanied him, and the whole crowd shouted all kinds of cries, saying, “This is Christ!”
But he made his confession with a good testimony. When the governor pressed him to say who the God of the Christians was,
he spoke. And he endured blows of every kind. Those who were near him
abused him in every way with their hands and feet, showing no respect for his old age. And those who were far from him,
Each one of them threw at him whatever he was holding in his hand. They all had this thought in their minds:
“I am committing a great sin and acting wickedly if I hang back and do not defile myself with him.” For they thought that vengeance would be [?] upon him. He was thrown into prison.
After two days he died. But God's great providence was at work,
and Christ's immeasurable mercy toward those [?] who had fallen. They were not abandoned by Christ's providence.
For those who had been arrested earlier and had denied the faith were also kept in prison and endured afflictions.
Their denial had brought them no benefit even in this world. For those who had confessed what they were were imprisoned as Christians,
with no other charge brought against them. But these others were now held as murderers and defiled people,
and were tortured twice as much as the others. For the joy of martyrdom lightened the burden for those who had confessed,
as did the hope of Christ's promise, his love, and the Spirit, the Advocate. But those who had denied the faith were severely tormented by their consciences.
Thus everyone could recognize them by their faces in the streets. For whenever the martyrs came out, they were joyful,
and glory and abundant grace were mingled in their faces. Their chains were like beautiful ornaments upon them,
like an adorned bride whose clothing is decorated with fine gold. And Christ's fragrance wafted from you,
so that some of them seemed to have been anointed with earthly perfumes. But those who had denied the faith
were gloomy, downcast, disfigured, and utterly filled with shame. The pagans reviled them as weak and cowardly,
and they were accused as murderers. They had lost the name that is honored above all, glorious, and life-giving. After saying a little,
they went on to say: “After this, at their departure, their martyrdom took every form.
For they wove a crown from every kind of blossom and flower and offered it to the Father.” Now it is fitting to speak about the mighty athletes
who endured the contest in all its variety, won a great victory, and received the great, imperishable crown. So Maturus, Sanctus, Blandina, and Attalus
were brought before the wild beasts in the sight of all the people, for the merciless spectacle of the pagans, on the day set aside on our account for the spectacle of combat.
Maturus and Sanctus were brought into the theater again for every kind of torture, as though nothing had happened to them.
Rather, through many [?], they were overcoming the adversary, for their contest was for the [?].
They again endured the wounds from the blows inflicted on them there and the bites of the wild beasts,
and everything that the crowds in their madness shouted from this side and that, ordering them to be tortured.
Besides all this, they seated them on an iron chair. As their bodies were being roasted,
the smell of their burning reached the crowds. But even then the crowds did not relent.
But they became still more frenzied and wanted to overcome the endurance of the blessed ones.
Yet even then they heard nothing else from Sanctus except that statement of confession
which he had been accustomed to utter from the beginning. These, then, endured a great contest, because they had such great patience within them.
In the end they were slaughtered. In place of the various spectacles of combat held that day, they themselves became a spectacle to the whole world.
Blandina was hung on a wooden stake and was made ready to become food for the wild beasts that were being released against her.
She hung there looking like a cross, and through her powerful prayer she gave great encouragement to those engaged in the contest.
For in their contests, through this sight, they saw with their own bodily eyes the one who had been crucified for them,
to assure all who believe in him that everyone who suffers for the glory of Christ has fellowship with the living God.
When none of these beasts approached her, they took her down from that stake and threw her into prison again, to be kept for another contest,
so that through many trials she might defeat Satan the adversary and bring lasting condemnation upon him, while encouraging the brothers.
For this small, weak, despised woman had been clothed like a great, undefeated athlete, and in many rounds she overcame the adversary.
And in the contest she was crowned with an imperishable crown. The crowd also demanded Attalus with great insistence.
For he was well known, and because of his good conscience he entered like a well-prepared athlete.
For he was fully trained in the promise of Christianity and had always been a witness to the truth among us.
As they led him around the theater, a placard went before him with this written on it in Latin: “This is Attalus the Christian.”
While the people were raging fiercely against him, the governor learned that he was a Roman citizen.
He ordered him to be confined in prison with the others who were there, about whom he had written to Caesar, and he was awaiting Caesar’s decision.
The intervening time was neither idle nor fruitless for them. Rather, through their endurance,
the immeasurable mercy of Christ was revealed. For through those who were alive, even those who had died came to life.
The martyrs restored those who had not become martyrs, and there was great joy for our virgin mother,
because she received alive those whom she had cast out as dead. For through the hands of those martyrs,
many of those who had denied the faith were conceived and born again. They were awakened and learned to confess.
Alive and [?], they were brought before the tribunal to be questioned by the governor, by the permission of God, who does not desire the death of the sinner,
but is kind to those who return to him. … Caesar wrote that those who did not deny the faith should die, and those who denied it should be released.
At the festival held here, for which many people from every nation gather, when the gathering began, he brought them before the tribunal.
to make the blessed ones a spectacle and a show for that whole crowd. For this reason he questioned them again.
He ordered those who held the status of Roman citizens to be beheaded, but sent the rest to the wild beasts.
Christ was greatly glorified through those who had previously denied him, for they now confessed him, contrary to the pagans’ expectations.
For these were questioned separately, on the understanding that they were now to be released. But when they confessed, they were added to the number of the martyrs.
Those who had never had even a trace of faith remained outside, having no knowledge of the wedding garment,
nor even any thought of reverence for God. Instead, by their conduct they also blasphemed the way of truth.
These are the children of destruction. All the others were added to the church. And while they were being questioned,
there was a man named Alexander, a Phrygian by birth and a physician by training and profession,
who had lived in Gaul for many years and was known to everyone for his love for God and his boldness in speaking.
Nor was he without the gift of apostleship. This man stood before the tribunal and encouraged them by gestures to confess.
He was like someone gripped by labor pains, and he was noticed by those standing beside the tribunal. The whole crowd was grumbling because those who had denied had turned back and confessed.
They shouted against Alexander, saying that he had brought this about. When the governor had him brought forward and made him stand before him, he asked him what he was.
He said, “I am a Christian.” The governor became angry and sentenced him to be thrown to the wild beasts. The next day he entered the arena with Attalus.
For the governor, wishing to do the crowd a favor, had handed Attalus over as well to be thrown to the wild beasts.
After they had been put through all the instruments prepared for torture in the theater and had endured a great struggle,
they too were finally slaughtered. Alexander did not even groan, nor did he open his mouth to say anything.
Instead, he spoke with God in his heart. As for Attalus, after they seated him on the burning iron chair, when an odor began to rise from his body,
he said in Latin to that whole crowd, “This is what it means to eat human beings—what you are doing to us.
For we neither eat human beings nor do anything vile.” When they asked him what name God had, he said,
“God does not have a name as a human being does.” ... After all these things, on the last day of the contests, they brought in Blandina,
together with a boy named Ponticus, who was about fifteen years old. These two had been brought in every day to watch the torture of the others.
They tried to force them to swear by the idols. But because they remained steadfast and treated them with contempt,
the whole crowd became enraged against them, showing no pity for the boy’s youth and no consideration for her being a woman.
Instead, they subjected them to every torture and put them through every kind of torment, trying to force them to swear by the idols.
But they could not make them do this, for Ponticus himself was strengthened by that sister of his.
Those pagans saw that she was encouraging and strengthening him. So he bravely endured every torture.
He gave up his spirit and departed from the world. But blessed Blandina, last of them all,
like a courageous mother who had encouraged her children and sent them crowned to Christ the King, had brought all her children's contests to completion.
She was eager to go to them, full of joy and gladness, as though she had been invited to enjoy a banquet. They threw her to the wild beasts.
After the beatings, the wild beasts, and the frying pan, they finally threw her into a net, and she fell prey to a bull. While she was being tormented by it,
she seemed not even to feel what was happening to her, because of her hope and expectation of what she believed in, and because of her conversation with Christ.
Finally she too was slaughtered. All the pagans admitted that no woman had ever endured these or comparable sufferings.
Yet even this did not satisfy their madness and cruelty toward the saints. For by the savage beasts—that is, by Satan—
these savage and barbarous peoples had been stirred into a frenzy, and they did not know how to stop.
Instead, they made yet another beginning of outrages against the bodies of the saints. Their defeat did not restrain them, for they had no human understanding.
Rather, their rage against us was stirred up still more, like that of wild beasts. The governor and all the people alike displayed their unjust hatred toward us,

so that the scripture might be fulfilled which says, “Let the evildoer continue to do evil, and let the righteous continue to act righteously.” For they threw to the dogs those who had been suffocated in prison,
and guarded them carefully night and day so that we could not bury them. Then they laid out the remains left by the wild beasts and the fire:
some torn apart and some burned, and the heads of the others, together with the severed pieces of their remains.
For many days they kept them under the soldiers' careful guard so that they would not be buried.
Some of the pagans raged and gnashed their teeth at them, wanting to take still greater vengeance on them.
Others laughed and mocked them, magnifying their idols and saying that it was from them that they had received these punishments.
Others, who seemed to be gentle and sympathetic toward them,
reproached them, saying, “Where is their God, and what benefit has their worship brought them—
the worship they chose over their own lives?” Such were the different ways those people behaved...
But we were in deep mourning because we could not bury their bodies in the ground.
Not even the night helped us do this. Money did not persuade the guards, nor did pleading restrain them.
They guarded them by every possible means, as though they would gain something great if these bodies were not buried... After saying this,
they added other things, saying, “The bodies of the martyrs, after they had exposed them in every way, were left in the open air for six days.
Afterward those wicked people burned them until they became like ashes, and threw them into the river Rhône [?], which flows there,
so that not even a remnant of them would be seen on earth anymore. They did these things as though they could defeat God
and take away from them even the renewal of their resurrection from the dead. For these people used to say:
“Let them not even have any hope of the resurrection on which they relied. They introduced among us the practice of a strange and new religion, despised every affliction,
and went joyfully to death, prepared for it. Now let us see whether they rise, and whether their God can help them and rescue them from our hands.”
Chapter Two. How the martyrs, God's friends, welcomed and healed those who stumbled during the persecution.
The churches of Christ endured the things we have described above in the days of the emperor Verus.
From these things a person can form an idea of what happened at that time in other places as well.
It is right, however, that we should also record some other statements from this same document,
which reveal the humility and compassion of these martyrs whom we mentioned earlier.
These words are written there: “These martyrs were such zealous imitators of Christ,
who, although he is the likeness of God, did not consider equality with God something to seize,
that although they possessed this glory, having borne witness not once or twice but many times,
and having been taken away from the wild beasts, covered with burns, bruises, and wounds,
they neither called themselves martyrs nor allowed us to call them by this name.
But if anyone ever happened to call them martyrs, either in speech or in a letter,
they sternly rebuked the person who called them that. For they gladly reserved this title of martyrdom for Christ,
who is the faithful witness of the truth, the firstborn of the dead, and the beginning of life. They remembered the martyrs who had departed from the world and said,
‘Those are the martyrs: those whom Christ deemed worthy to be taken away while confessing him, sealing their witness by their departure.
We, however, are poor and lowly confessors.’ With many tears they pleaded with the brothers and asked them
to offer earnest prayers for them, so that they might be made perfect. And although they demonstrated the power of martyrdom in their actions,
through the [?] boldness they showed toward the pagans, and displayed their endurance by bearing suffering without fear or trembling,
they declined the title of martyrs before the brothers, because they were filled with the fear of God.”
Again, further on, they said: “They humbled themselves beneath the mighty hand by which they have now been exalted.
They gave everyone relief and accused no one. They released everyone and bound no one.
They prayed for those who made them suffer evil: ‘[?] hold this sin against them.’
But if he prayed for those who were stoning him, how much more for the brothers! ... And a little later they said again:
“This whole great battle that they fought against Satan was for the sake of perfect love, so that the evil serpent might be strangled
and they might restore alive those whom they thought had fallen. For they did not boast over those who had fallen.
Instead, with what they had in abundance, they supplied what others lacked. They had compassion like a mother for her children.
They poured out many tears for them before the Father. They asked him for life, and he gave it to them, and they shared it with their neighbors.
In everything they clothed themselves in victory and went to God. They always loved peace and entrusted peace to us, and in peace they reached God.
They left no sorrow for their mother, nor turmoil and conflict for their brothers, but joy and peace, harmony and love.”
These things were said about the love of those blessed people toward the brothers who had fallen, and have been placed here for our benefit,
because of the attitude of those who are without compassion or mercy and who attack the members of Christ without pity.

Chapter 3. The visions that Attalus the martyr saw in his dream.

This same account of the martyrs whom we discussed above
also contains another story worth remembering. There is no reason to withhold it from the knowledge of those who read.
It goes as follows: “Alcibiades, one of them, practiced a very austere way of life.
He had previously eaten or drunk nothing but bread and water, and he wished to follow the same way of life in prison.
But after the first ordeal that Attalus had endured, it was revealed to him that Alcibiades was not acting rightly in refusing to make use of God's creatures
and was leaving others an example that could cause them to stumble. Alcibiades was persuaded to eat everything, and he accepted food and gave thanks to God.
For they were not left without the working of God's grace, but the Holy Spirit was their teacher.” Let this suffice concerning these matters.
Chapter 4. How the martyrs commended Irenaeus in their letters.
As for Montanus, Alcibiades, and Theodotus and their followers in Phrygia, many people at first believed that they possessed the gift of prophecy.
For glorious signs of God's grace were still being performed in many churches up to that time.
For this reason, many people believed that these men too were indeed prophesying.
But there was division over them. The brothers in Gaul also wrote their judgment about these matters, expressing their reverence for God and their true faith.
They also included separate letters from the martyrs who had met their end among them, which they had written while in prison
to the brothers in Asia and Phrygia. These were addressed not only to them,
but also to Eleutherus, who was bishop of Rome at that time. They appealed to him for the peace of the church. These same martyrs
also commended Irenaeus, who was then a presbyter in the church of Lyons, to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome.
They testified to many things about him, as their words show when they say this: “May you rejoice in God again.”
“And we continually pray for you, our father Eleutherus. We have appointed our brother and companion Irenaeus to bring you these writings mentioned above.
We appeal to you and commend him to you, for he is zealous for the covenant of Christ.”
But why must we repeat the list of the names of the martyrs recorded in this letter, written by them and addressed to them:
those who were beheaded and crowned, and those who became food for wild beasts,
and also those who died in prison, and the number of confessors who were still alive?
Anyone who wishes can easily learn the full details by obtaining their letter, which we have also included in the collection of martyrdoms that we have compiled.

Chapter Five: How God sent rain down from heaven for Marcus Aurelius Caesar through the prayers of the Christians.

The events that took place during the years of Antoninus
were those we have described above. Now the story is told that his brother, Marcus Aurelius Caesar,
while preparing for battle against the Germans and Sarmatians, found that his army was suffering from thirst, and he had no way to do anything about it.
But the soldiers of the legion called Melitene, which from that time until now has been made up of believers,
while drawn up against their enemies, knelt on the ground, as is our custom when praying, and pleaded with God.
This action seemed something astonishing to their enemies. And while they were marveling,
an even greater wonder overtook them: a violent thunderstorm pursued their enemies and drove them into flight and destruction.
Through the rain, however, God brought relief to the whole army because of those who were pleading with him, for the entire army had been close to dying of thirst.
This account is also found among those writers who are far removed from our teaching, in whose midst this event took place.
Some of our own people also reported it. But as for the outside writers of history,
being strangers to the faith, they recorded the miracle but did not acknowledge that it happened through our prayers. Our own writers, however, as lovers of truth,
handed down what happened plainly and clearly. One of them is Apollinaris, who said concerning this legion,
through whose prayers this miracle occurred, that from that time it received from the emperor a name in Latin corresponding to what had happened.
A trustworthy witness to these things is Tertullian, who wrote in Latin an impassioned defense of our faith addressed to the Senate.
We have already mentioned this man. He confirms this account with substantial evidence that it actually happened.
He too writes and says as follows: “… Letters of Marcus, the wise emperor, still exist to this day, in which he testifies
that in Germany his army was close to perishing for lack of water, and that they were saved through the prayers of the Christians.
He says of him that he even threatened death against those who wished to bring accusations against our people. After this, the same man goes on to say:
What, then, are these laws of wickedness, injustice, and cruelty that are imposed on us alone? Even Vespasian did not observe them, although he had defeated the Jews.
Trajan also rejected them to some extent, forbidding Christians to be hunted down.
Hadrian too dismissed them, although he investigated everything. Nor did Antoninus, who was called Pius, observe them.
Chapter Six. The bishops who were in Rome. Let us now return to the sequence of the history.
Pothinus, having completed the full span of his life, ninety years, was brought to his end together with those martyrs of Gaul.
After him, Irenaeus received the bishopric of the church of Lyons. In his youth he had been a disciple of Polycarp.
He recorded the succession of the bishops who were in Rome in the third book that he composed against heresies.
He listed them down to Eleutherus, in whose time he was eagerly engaged in composing those books.
He speaks about them and sets them out in order as follows: “The blessed apostles laid the foundations of the church and built it.
They appointed Linus as its bishop. The apostle Paul mentions this Linus in his letter to Timothy.
Anacletus succeeded him. After him, Clement received the bishopric, the third after the apostles.
He had seen the blessed apostles and associated with them, and the apostles’ preaching was still firmly established in him.
Their tradition was before his eyes. Nor was he alone,
but many who had been disciples of the apostles were still living at that time. In the days of this same Clement,
there was great dissension among the brothers in Corinth. The church of Rome sent a letter to Corinth to bring them to peace
and to renew their faith and the tradition they had received together from the apostles.” A little later he says again:
“After this Clement, Evaristus succeeded. After Evaristus came Alexander. Then Sixtus took office, the sixth after the apostles.
After him came Telesphorus, who suffered martyrdom gloriously. After him came Hyginus, and after Hyginus, Pius.
Then, after him, came Anicetus. Soter succeeded Anicetus, and after him Eleutherus succeeded, the twelfth after the apostles.
They continued in the same order and in the same teaching, and the tradition that the church received from the apostles and the proclamation of the truth have reached us.”
These are the words of Irenaeus, which agree with the accounts we have already related.
Chapter Seven. Glorious signs continued to be performed through believers until those times.
In the books that Irenaeus wrote, five in number, On the Refutation and Overthrow of False Knowledge,
he wrote in his second book on this subject that even in his own days demonstrations of miraculous power remained in the churches.
He makes this known in these words: “They fall far short of raising the dead as our Lord did, and as the apostles did through their prayers.”
And many times, even within the brotherhood, when it was necessary and the church in our regions [?] petitioned God with fasting and much supplication,
the spirit of the dead person returned, and the person was granted to the prayers of the saints. After these things, he said again:
If they say that our Lord too performed such things only in appearance, let us lead them to the prophets and show them from their writings
that everything had been foretold about him and was truly accomplished, and that he alone is the Son of God.
For this reason, those who are truly his disciples, in his name and through the gift received from him,
perform such things to help other people, according to the gift each has received from him.
For some of them faithfully and truly drive out demons, so that often, after people have been cleansed of evil spirits,
they come to believe and join the church. Others also have foreknowledge of things to come, visions, and prophetic utterances.
Others heal the sick by laying hands on them and restore them to health. Indeed, as we said before, even the dead have risen
and remained with us for many years. But why speak of these things? For there is no counting the gifts that the church throughout the world has received from our Lord.
And in the name of Jesus Christ, who was [?] in the time of Pontius Pilate, she brings help to the nations every day,
without deceiving people or giving her gift for money. For just as she received freely from God, she also gives freely.
Elsewhere, the same writer writes: We have heard of many brothers in the church who have the gift of prophecy,
who speak in all languages through the Holy Spirit and bring people's hidden things to light for their benefit,
and who recount the mysteries of God. We have said these things to show that, down to those prophets, various gifts continued among those who were worthy.
Chapter Eight: How Irenaeus refers to the divine Scriptures. ... Since, when we began this history,

we promised to set down what the early elders and writers in the churches said in their own times about the accepted Scriptures, according to the tradition they received and handed down in their writings,
and Irenaeus is one of them, let us therefore set down his words, beginning with what he said about the holy Gospel.
He spoke as follows: Matthew also produced a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own language,
while Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome and establishing the church. After their departure, Mark, Peter's disciple and interpreter,
also handed down to us in writing what Peter had preached. ... But [?], who accompanied Paul,
set down in writing the Gospel that Paul himself preached. Afterward, John, our Lord's disciple, who had reclined on his chest,
also wrote a Gospel while living in Ephesus in Asia. He said these things in the third book of the work we mentioned earlier.
In the fifth book, he spoke as follows about John's Revelation and the numerical value of the deceiver's name:
Since these things are so, and this number is given in all the early copies that were carefully written,
And all those who had seen John face to face testify to this, and the statement itself teaches us.
The numerical value of this serpent’s name, according to Greek reckoning, is known from its letters. A little later he says about him again:
“We are not compelled to make a definite pronouncement about the deceiver’s name and state it with certainty.
For if his name needed to be proclaimed openly at this time, it would have been declared through the one who saw that revelation.
For it was seen not very long ago, but almost in our own generation, toward the end of Domitian’s reign.”
The man we have mentioned related these things about that revelation. He also mentions John’s first letter and brings forward many testimonies from it.
He does the same with Peter’s first letter. As for the book called The Shepherd, he is not merely acquainted with it,
but also accepts it. He quotes it as follows: “The scripture has rightly said, ‘First believe that there is one God, who created and established everything.’”
And [?]... He also uses the words of the Wisdom of Solomon and quotes it as follows: “The vision of God produces life,
and life brings one near to God.” ... He also recounts something that a certain elder had mentioned, which the elder had received from the apostles, though he has not passed on his name to us.
He also provides his own interpretations of the divine Scriptures. He further mentions Justin Martyr and Ignatius,
and uses their writings as testimony. He also promises, in the efforts he has undertaken, to oppose Marcion using Marcion’s own writings.
As for how the Scriptures of the Spirit of God were translated by those seventy translators, listen to what he writes in his own words:
“God became a human being, and the Lord himself gave us life and gave a sign: ‘Behold, the virgin will conceive and give birth.’
It is not as some who now presume to translate the Scriptures have said: ‘Behold, the young woman will conceive and give birth to a son,’
as Theodotion of Ephesus and Aquila of Pontus translated it. Both of them were converts to Judaism.
The Ebionites followed them and say that our Lord was born of Joseph.” ... A little later he says again:
“Before Roman rule was firmly established, while the Macedonians still controlled Asia,
Ptolemy was eager to enrich the library he had established in Alexandria with the writings of all peoples, wherever they were worth the effort.
He asked the people of Jerusalem to let him acquire their books and translate them into Greek.
Since they were subject to the Macedonians at that time, they sent Ptolemy seventy elders who were trained in the Scriptures and knew both languages.
God was doing what he willed. The king, however, wanted to put them to the test,
for he feared that they might agree on a common plan and conceal in their translation the truth contained in the Scriptures.
He separated them from one another and ordered them all to write a translation of the same text. He did this for all the Scriptures.
When they had assembled and all came together before Ptolemy, he compared each one’s translation.
God was glorified, and the Scriptures were recognized as truly belonging to God, because they all alike spoke the same words and names, from beginning to end.
And all the peoples who were there recognized that the Scriptures had been translated through God's prompting.
And this deed of God was not astonishing. For he also, during the captivity of the people that took place in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, when the Scriptures had been destroyed,
and after seventy years, when the Jews returned to their land in the time of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,
put the Spirit in Ezra the priest, of the tribe of Levi, so that he would write down all the words of the former prophets
and give the people the Law that had been given through Moses. Irenaeus said all these things.
Chapter Nine. The bishops who lived in the days of Emperor Commodus. When Antoninus had completed nineteen years of his reign, Commodus succeeded him.
In his first year, Agrippinus had completed twelve years of service as bishop of the church of Alexandria, and Julian succeeded him.
Chapter Ten. Pantaenus the philosopher. At that time, the head of instruction for the believers in Alexandria was
a man renowned for his learning in philosophy, whose name was Pantaenus.
For, following an ancient custom, instruction in the sacred words had been established among them, and it has continued down to our own time.
It was maintained by people who were powerful in speech and zealous in reverence for God. It is reported that, among all those who were distinguished at that time,
this man of whom we have spoken stood out. He came from the philosophical school of those called Stoics. They say of him
that he showed such zeal for the word of God that he even became a herald of the gospel of Christ to the peoples of the East.
He traveled as far as the land of India. For even at that time there were many evangelists of the word of God,
who, in their zeal for God, had taken on the likeness of the apostles and were working eagerly for the growth and strengthening of the word of God.
Pantaenus himself was one of them. It is said of him that he traveled as far as India and found the Gospel of Matthew there.
Before his arrival there, it had been in the possession of people there who had believed in Christ, to whom Bartholomew, one of the apostles, had [?].
He had left them the book of the Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew letters, and it had been preserved among them until that time.
Pantaenus himself, after all his good deeds, finally became the head of instruction in Alexandria.
Through his living voice and his written discourses, he laid up a treasure of instruction in reverence for God.
Chapter Eleven. Clement of Alexandria. In the days of Pantaenus, Clement was known in Alexandria as someone trained in the Scriptures of God.
He bore the same name as the bishop who had been in Rome, who was a disciple of the apostles—the one who had been in Rome,
who was a disciple of the apostles. This Clement, in the discourses he wrote under his own name, mentions Pantaenus as his teacher.
He also mentions him in other discourses, and in the first discourse he alluded to this Pantaenus.
While describing certain well-known men who had received what had been handed down from the apostles, he says this: “This account which we have undertaken...
“It is not a book skillfully prepared for display. Rather, we are storing up recollections as a treasury for old age,
“and a portrayal of those living and powerful images of the words of blessed men whom I was privileged to hear [?] and see.
“They are truly worthy of honorable remembrance. One of them was from Greece [?], and another from Syria,
“another from Egypt, and another from the East. Of these last, one was from the land of the Arameans, and another was a Palestinian,
“who was originally one of the Hebrews. Last of all, I encountered the one who was foremost in ability.
“I found him living in obscurity and unknown, and I found rest with him in Egypt [?]. These men preserved the tradition of the teaching of truth,
“directly from Peter, James, John, and Paul, those holy apostles.
“They received it like children from their fathers. Yet few are those who resemble their fathers.
“By the will of God, they reached even us and sowed in us the holy seed of our fathers, the apostles.”
Chapter Twelve: The Bishops Who Were in Jerusalem. ... At that time, Narcissus was well known as bishop of the church in Jerusalem.
He remains renowned even now. He was the fifteenth in the succession after the destruction of the Jews in the years of Hadrian.
From that time, a church composed of Gentiles first began to be established there, after those who belonged to the circumcision.
We have reported that Mark was the first Gentile bishop there. After him came Cassianus, as the order of succession there shows.
After him came Publius, and after him, in turn, Maximus. After these came Julian, and after him Gaius.
After him came Symmachus and another Gaius, and then another Julian. After these came Capito, and after him Valens.
Then came Dolichianus, and last of all Narcissus. In all, they numbered thirty in the succession after the apostles. ...
Chapter Thirteen: Rhodon and the Division He Mentioned Concerning Marcion. ... At that time there was also Rhodon, who was a native of Asia.
He had studied in Rome under Tatian, whom we mentioned earlier, as he himself related. This man composed various books.
Among these, he also wrote against the heresy of Marcion, which in his days had split into differing opinions, as he relates,
writing about those who caused the division and carefully exposing the false statements that each of them had devised and invented.
Listen, then, to what he writes: “They have therefore become divided among themselves because they base themselves on an opinion that has no firm foundation.
“From their own flock, Apelles, who prides himself on his gray hair and old age, acknowledges one first principle.
“He says that the prophecies come from an opposing spirit, because he is persuaded by the utterances [?] of a certain demon-possessed virgin named Philumena.
“Others, however, introduce two first principles, as Marcion did. Among them are Potitus and Basilicus.
Others followed Pontintus, but they could not explain the matters, just as he himself could not explain even the simple ones.
They turned to saying that there are two first principles, simply asserting this without proof. Others among them, however, fell into things still worse than these.
For they posit not only two natures but even three. Their chief and leader is Syneros,
according to those who hold to his teaching. Rhodon himself wrote that he also entered into a debate with Apelles.
He said this: “The elderly Apelles spoke with us, and in many of the things he said he was shown to be badly mistaken.
For this reason he said that the matter should not be brought into question, but that everyone should remain as he had believed. For he said
that all who place their hope in the crucified one will be saved, provided only that they are found doing good works. But the most difficult thing of all that he taught, as I said before,
concerned God: he posited one first principle, as we also say. After positing it, he went on to say that he based it entirely on his own thinking.
When we challenged him, saying, ‘Where do you have proof of this? Or how can you speak of one first principle? Explain it to us,’
he said, ‘The prophecies refute themselves, because they say nothing true. For they do not agree with one another,
and they are false and contradict themselves.’ But as to how there was one first principle, he said that he did not know,
but that this was simply his conviction. Again I put him under oath to tell the truth, and he swore and affirmed, saying,
‘I do not understand how there is one self-existent God; I simply believe it.’ But I laughed and inwardly despised him,
because he claimed to be a teacher, yet did not know how to establish what he taught.”...
In this same work he wrote to Callistion and acknowledged that he had been taught by Tatian in Rome.
He said that Tatian had taken pains to compose a book of Questions, in which he promised to demonstrate
what was hidden and unknown in the things written in the divine Scriptures. Rhodon himself, however, promised in his own work to compose solutions to Tatian’s questions.
He also has a book on the six days. Apelles, of whom we have spoken, uttered many blasphemies against Moses.
Along with him, he also blasphemed the words of God in his many writings. And, as he imagined,
he devoted great effort to refuting and disproving the Scriptures. Let this suffice concerning these people.
Chapter Fourteen. On the false prophets who belonged to the heresy in Phrygia. Now the enemy of the knowledge of God, who hates good things and loves evil things,
leaves no opportunity unused to practice deceit against human beings. Once again he strove to bring heresies into being against the church.
Some of these crept through Asia and Phrygia like a venomous reptile spewing poison. Montanus boasted that he was the Paraclete.
Prisca and Maximilla were women who belonged to his following, and they too boasted that they were Montanus’s prophetesses....
Chapter Fifteen. On the schism of Florinus and Blastus that arose in Rome. There were also others in Rome who were flourishing.
Their leader was Florinus, who had fallen from his office as a presbyter of the church. With him was also Blastus, who had likewise fallen.
These men were drawing many members of the church over to their own way of thinking. Both were striving, on their own initiative and for their own ends, to oppose the truth…
Chapter Sixteen: What is said about Montanus and the false prophets who were with him. Against the heresy called that of the Phrygians.
The power of truth raised up at that time a mighty, unconquerable opponent to fight against them: Apollinaris of Hierapolis, whom the account mentioned earlier.
And with him many others skilled in speaking. From these men, many historical accounts [?].
From these men many historical accounts have been left to us. This Apollinaris, as he begins writing against them, makes it known that he had also exposed their error without written works.
At the beginning of his discourse he writes something like this: “A long time ago, our beloved Avircius Marcellus, you instructed me
to compose a discourse against the heresy called that of Miltiades. I have held back until today, not because I was unable to expose falsehood and bear witness to the truth,
but because I hesitated and was afraid that some might think I wished to add something to the teaching of the new covenant of the gospel.
For anyone who wishes to live according to the teaching of the gospel cannot add anything to it or take anything away from it.
For [?], I went to Ancyra in Galatia and found the church of Pontus disturbed by this ‘new prophecy,’ as they call it.
As the facts make clear, however, it is false prophecy. As far as I was able, with the strength granted by our Lord’s grace,
we spoke in the church for many days about these matters and about what they professed. As a result, the church rejoiced, and our opponents were driven back for the time being,
while those who supported them were distressed. The presbyters throughout that region urged us
to leave them a written record of what had been said against those who oppose the word of truth. The presbyter Zoticus was with us, sharing in our ministry.
We did not do this, but we promised that, by God’s grace, we would diligently write these things here and send them to them.”
After this he says other things. At the beginning of his discourse he tells about the man who caused this heresy, introducing the account as follows:
“This was the reason their heretical schism arose against the church.
There is said to be a village in Mysia in Phrygia named Ardabau. There, it is said, a man named Montanus, who had recently come to believe,
in the days of Gratus, proconsul of Asia, through an intense desire for leadership,
suddenly went out of his mind and began prophesying and speaking strange words, contrary to the customary tradition of the church.
Some of those present at that time who heard his strange words were distressed.
They treated him as a man under the influence of a demon and a spirit of error that stirs up the people.
They rebuked him and ordered him not to speak, remembering our Lord’s relevant commands to be watchfully on guard against false prophets.
Others, however, took pride in him as though he possessed the Holy Spirit and the gift of prophecy, and they became complacent within themselves.
They did not remember our Lord’s command. And that spirit which harms the mind, blinds it, and leads the people astray—
since they were being led astray and [?] by it, they encouraged it not to remain silent any longer. This came about through the skillful cunning of the enemy,
who devised a scheme for the destruction of those who listened to him, because they honored him beyond what was right.
He awakened and inflamed their minds, which had been asleep to the true faith. He also raised up two other women and filled them with a lying spirit.
They spoke in madness, at inappropriate times and outside the proper order, just like Montanus.
That demon himself pronounced blessed those who looked to him and yielded to him, and made them proud through great promises.
At times he also condemned others, apparently only for show, so that he might be considered trustworthy and thought to be someone who also rebuked wrongdoing.
Only a few Phrygians were led astray. In his insolence, that demon taught them to blaspheme the whole church under heaven,
because it did not receive him with honor. Nor did that demon have any means of introducing his false prophecy into it.
For all the believers in Asia gathered many times in many places about this matter.
They subjected these utterances that were being spoken [?] to examination and ruled that they were unclean words.
They rejected this heresy, and so its followers were cast out of the church and excluded from its fellowship. ... Apollinaris first related these things.
Throughout his discourse he refuted this error. In his second discourse he spoke as follows about the end of these people: ...
“Since they call us despisers of the prophets because we have not accepted their false prophets—
for they say that these are the ones whom our Lord promised to send to that people—let them answer us as before God:
Was anyone among the followers of Montanus, or among those women who began speaking falsehoods, persecuted by the Jews or killed by the lawless?
There was not even one. Nor was any of them arrested and crucified on account of this name. Nor, in the synagogues of the Jews,
was any one of these women of theirs ever flogged or stoned. Rather, they are said to have died a different death.
For Montanus and Maximilla were both driven by that destructive spirit and killed themselves,
not together, but each at the time of their own death. The report is that they died in this way, like the death of Judas the betrayer.
And a story is told about the leader of what they call prophecy, namely Theodotus, who acted as their steward:
he lost his mind and trusted that spirit of deception, believing that he was being raised and carried up to heaven. He fell and died a terrible death.
They say that this is what happened. But until we ourselves see, or you are convinced about this, let us not pronounce judgment, blessed ones.
For whether it happened this way or not, Montanus, Theodotus, and Maximilla certainly died.” In this same discourse he also said
that the holy bishops of that time wanted to rebuke the spirit that was in Maximilla, but others prevented them.
those who were helping that spirit. He wrote as follows:
“Do not let the spirit that was in Maximilla say, as it said to Asterius Urbanus, ‘I am being driven away like a wolf from the sheep.
I am not a wolf. I am word, spirit, and power.’ But if there is power in this spirit, let it show itself in action and expose
and, through that spirit, compel those who came to silence and rebuke the spirit while it was speaking to acknowledge it.
These were distinguished men and bishops: Zoticus from the village of Comana and Julian from Apamea.
The followers of Themison restrained these men and did not allow them to rebuke that spirit and show that it was false and was misleading the people.”
In this same discourse he also said other things to expose Maximilla’s false prophecy. He also spoke about the time when he wrote these things.
He also mentions the words of her prophecy in which she predicted that there would be war and upheaval. He exposes her falsehood, saying:
“How, then, has this falsehood of hers not also become known? For it is now more than thirteen years since this woman died,
and there has been no war, either throughout the world or in any particular place. Rather, through God’s mercy, there has been a long peace, especially for Christians.”
These things are from the second discourse. From the third discourse I will set down a few words about those who boast that there have also been many martyrs among them.
He says as follows: “When they have been refuted on every point and have nothing to say,
they take refuge in the martyrs and say, ‘We have many martyrs, and this is a reliable sign.’
But that spirit of prophecy said to be among them is false. For this claim, above all the others, is without truth.
For there are also other heresies that have many martyrs. Yet we do not say on that account that their beliefs are sound,
nor do we acknowledge that they possess the truth. Foremost are those of the Marcionite heresy, who say that they have many martyrs,
but do not truly acknowledge Christ himself.” A little later he says again: “For this reason,
when those of the church who hold the true faith are called to martyrdom together with martyrs from the so-called Phrygian heresy, they separate themselves from them
and meet their end without entering into fellowship with them, because they are unwilling to believe in the spirit that is in Montanus and these women.
This is true. It happened even in our own days in the city of Apamea, which is on the river Maeander, in the case of Gaius and Alexander and their companions, who suffered martyrdom from Eumenea.”
Chapter Seventeen: Miltiades and the Discourse He Wrote. In this discourse written by the man we have mentioned,
he also mentions Miltiades, a writer of the church, who likewise wrote a discourse against this heresy.
After setting down some of their words, he adds: “I found these things in one of their discourses,
in which they oppose the discourse of our brother Alcibiades, in which he demonstrates that a prophet ought not to speak while out of his mind.”
As he proceeds briefly with his discussion, he lists those who prophesied under the new covenant.
Along with these he counted a woman named Ammia and Quadratus. He speaks as follows:
“The false prophet,” he says, “is out of his mind, and for this reason he acts without restraint or fear. He begins willingly in ignorance,
but is then driven unwillingly into madness, as I said before. They cannot show that any of the prophets acted in this manner,
either in the Old Testament or in the New, among those who were clothed with the Holy Spirit—not Adda, nor Judas,
nor Silas, nor Philip’s daughters, nor Ammia of Philadelphia, nor Quadratus,
nor any of the others. So let them no longer boast of these people, since they cannot count themselves among them.” Again, a little later, he says:
“For if, as these people say, the women belonging to Montanus received the gift of prophecy after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia, let them show
who received it from these followers of Montanus and their women.
For the gift of prophecy must remain in the church until the final coming, as the apostle said.
But they have no one to show. For fourteen years have now passed since Maximilla’s death.”
This writer said all these things. As for Miltiades, whom he mentioned, he too left us a record of other efforts concerning the words of God,
in a discourse he wrote against the pagans and in another he composed against the Jews.
On each of these two subjects he composed two discourses, addressing each group separately. He also composed a defense against the pagans concerning the philosophy he followed.

Chapter Eighteen: How Apollonius Refuted the Heresy of the Phrygians, and Whom He Mentioned.

Against the heresy called that of the Phrygians,
Apollonius too, a writer belonging to the church, composed a discourse of refutation while it was still flourishing in Phrygia.
He proved that the women whom they called prophets were false prophets.
He also exposed the conduct of the leaders of this heresy. Now listen to what he says about Montanus:
“His deeds and his teaching show who this new teacher is. He is the one who taught the dissolution of marriage and laid down a law of fasting;
the one who called Pepuza and Tymion ‘Jerusalem’—these are small towns in Phrygia—
and wanted to gather there everyone from every place who obeyed him; the one who appointed collectors of money
and devised a way to receive gifts under the name of offerings; the one who paid wages to those who proclaimed his teaching,
so that through their greed the teaching of his message might be established.” These things he said about Montanus.
As he proceeds in his discourse, he writes as follows about Montanus’s women prophets: “First, we show concerning these women prophets of his
that, after they were filled with a spirit of falsehood, they abandoned their husbands. How, then, can they lie about Prisca and call her a virgin?”
Again he adds: “You know that all the Scriptures forbid a prophet to accept gifts and money.”
So when I see that the prophetess has taken gold, silver, and fine clothes, how can I fail to question her?
Again, as he continues his discussion, he says the following about one of their confessors:
“Then there is Themison, who clothed his wrongdoing in a respectable appearance and obtained the distinction of being a confessor only by paying a large sum of money.
He had his chains removed. Although he ought to have humbled himself because of this, he boasted as though he were a martyr.
He even dared to imitate the apostle and write a general epistle, to instruct those who had believed more faithfully than he had, so that they would engage with him in empty arguments
and blaspheme our Lord, his apostles, and the holy church.” Again, concerning another man whom they honored as a martyr, he said:
“Not to speak of many others, let the [?] tell us about Alexander, who used to call himself a martyr,
with whom she used to lodge, and whom many worship, as they also worship her. As for his robberies, his insolence, and the other things for which he was tried,
it is not we who need to speak, but the breach in the wall. Who, then, forgave whose sins? Did the prophet forgive the martyr his robberies,
or did the martyr forgive the prophet his wrongdoing? For although our Lord said, ‘Do not acquire gold or silver, or two tunics,’
these people act contrary to all these commands, sinning by acquiring the very possessions he forbade them.
For we can show that those whom they call martyrs and prophets collect money not only from the rich,
but also from the poor, orphans, and widows. If they are confident, let them stand up to this charge
and pronounce judgment if they are convicted, even if from now on they cease their offenses. For a prophet’s fruits must be examined.
A tree is known by its fruits. But to make the facts known to those who want to learn about Alexander, we will explain them plainly.
This man was tried by Aemilius Frontinus, the proconsul at Ephesus, not because of the Name, but because of the robberies he brazenly committed.
He became a denier of the faith, swore and lied in our Lord’s name, and deceived the believers there. His own church, in the place he came from, would not receive him because he was a robber.
Those who want to learn about him have the archives of Asia available to them. Yet this prophetess does not know him,
although he has been with her for many years. We expose this man to her, and through him we also expose her possessions.
Likewise, we expose this prophet, and we can show many things openly. But if they are confident, let them endure the exposure.”
Again, elsewhere in the same treatise, he adds the following about the prophets in whom they boast:
“If they deny that their prophets accept bribes, let them at least acknowledge this: if they are convicted of accepting them, they are not prophets.
I can produce countless witnesses to these things. But all the fruits of a prophet ought to be examined. Tell me, then:
Does a prophet bathe? Does a prophet adorn himself? Does a prophet love finery? Does a prophet play at gaming tables and dice? Does a prophet lend money?
Let them acknowledge whether these things are permissible or not. For my part, I will show that they have done them.” Apollonius himself also relates these things in this same treatise.
Forty years had passed by the time this treatise was written, since Montanus embarked on this supposed prophecy. And he also said:
Zoticus, whom the earlier writer had mentioned, when Maximilla was pretending to prophesy in Pepuza,
stood up to rebuke the spirit that was stirring within her, but those who shared her views prevented him.
He also mentions Thraseas, a martyr of that time. He also says the following, as something handed down by tradition:
Our Savior commanded his apostles not to leave Jerusalem for twelve years.
He also uses the Gospel of John as testimony, and relates that John even raised a dead man in Ephesus by the power of God.
He said other things as well, in which he thoroughly refuted this heresy we have discussed. These things Apollonius said.
Chapter nineteen. What Serapion said about the heresy of the Phrygians.
Serapion, who succeeded Maximinus as bishop in the church of Antioch, mentions what Apollinaris said against this heresy of the Phrygians.
He mentions it in his letter to Caricus and Pontius, in which he too refuted this heresy. He added the following in it:
“So that you may know that the activity of the falsehood called the new prophecy is abhorrent to the whole brotherhood throughout the world,
I have also sent you the writings of the blessed Claudius Apollinaris, who was bishop in Hierapolis in Asia.”
This letter of Serapion also bears the signatures of many bishops. Some of them signed as follows:
“Aurelius Quirinius, martyr. I pray that you may be in good health.” Another signed in this manner:
“Aurelius Publius Julius, bishop of Debeltum in Thrace. As the God in heaven lives,
the blessed Sotas of Anchialus wanted to drive out the demon that was in Prisca, but the partisans would not allow him.”
Many other bishops who agreed with these also put their signatures to this letter. Such, then, were these matters.
Chapter twenty. What Irenaeus said in his writings against the schisms that existed in Rome.
There were people in Rome who were altering the true character of the church’s laws. Irenaeus wrote separate letters.
One he entitled Against Blastus, Concerning Schism; another, Against Florinus, On the Sole Principle, and That God Is Not the Author of Evil.
For this man was defending that opinion. And again, because he had been swept into the error of the followers of Valentinus,
Irenaeus diligently composed a treatise On the Ogdoad, in which he noted that he himself had received the original tradition of the apostles.
At the end of this treatise I found another note, which it is fitting to reproduce in this book. It reads as follows:
“I adjure you who copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he comes to judge the living and the dead,
to compare what you have copied and correct it against the manuscript from which you copied it. And carefully copy this adjuration as well.”
And include it in that book you wrote. These things were said by that man for our benefit.
We repeat them so that we may have a complete demonstration of the zeal and diligence of those holy men of earlier times.
In the letter we mentioned, which Irenaeus wrote to Florinus, he again reminds him of his association with Polycarp and speaks confidently as follows:
“These teachings are not in harmony with the church, and they plunge anyone who accepts them into great wickedness.
Even the heretics outside the church have never dared to express these teachings. These teachings
the elders who came before us, who were disciples of the apostles, did not hand down to you. For when I was a boy, I saw you in Lower Asia with Polycarp, at the royal court.
You conducted yourself splendidly and were eager to gain his approval.
For I remember the things of that time more clearly than things happening now. For what is learned in childhood
grows along with the soul and becomes interwoven with it. For this reason, I can even describe the place where the blessed Polycarp used to sit and teach,
his going out and coming in, his way of life, his physical appearance, and the teaching he gave to the people,
and his association with John and with others who had seen our Lord, as he used to recount it,
and how he remembered their words, and what he had heard from them about our Lord, the miracles he performed, and his teaching.
Polycarp had received these things from those who had seen the living Word with their own eyes, and everything he recounted agreed with the Scriptures.
Even at that time, because of God's mercy toward me, I listened eagerly to these things and committed them to memory,
not on paper, but in my heart. And continually, by God's grace, I recall them with affection.
And I can testify before God that if that blessed elder, who learned from the apostles, had heard anything like these things,
he would have cried out and covered his ears, saying, as was his custom, ‘O our good God! For what times have you kept me alive, that I should endure these things!’
And he would have fled even from the place where he was standing or sitting if he heard such words.
And from the letters he wrote, whether to the neighboring churches to strengthen them, or to some of the brothers to instruct and encourage them,
what I have said can be established.” These were the words of Irenaeus...
Chapter Twenty-One: How Apollonius suffered martyrdom in Rome. During the reign of Commodus, the persecution had subsided,
and by God's grace there was tranquil peace for all the churches throughout the world.
The teaching of life was turning souls from every part of the human race to the service of God,
so that even among those in Rome distinguished by wealth and ancestry, many had turned toward their salvation, together with all their households and relatives.
But the envious demon, who hates good things, could not endure this. Instead, he devised ways to deploy various schemes against us once again.
And he brought Apollonius to trial, a man renowned among the [?] of that time for his education and wisdom.
For he had incited one of his servants, who were ready for such things, to accuse this man. But this wicked man himself,
because he had brought the charge at the wrong time—for those who informed about such matters could not show that they were acting on the emperor’s orders—had his legs broken.
Perennis the judge had pronounced this sentence against him. But this martyr, who loved God, when the judge earnestly and persuasively asked him
to make a statement before the council of the Senate, delivered a wise defense of the faith for which he was bearing witness.
But by order of the Senate he was sentenced to be beheaded, and his martyrdom was completed. For they had an ancient law
that those who had once come to trial and did not change their convictions should not be released. Anyone who wishes to learn his words
and the defense he delivered in response to the questions put to him by Perennis, and his entire defense before the Senate, can learn them from the book we have compiled.
Chapter Twenty-two. Which bishops were prominent at that time. In the tenth year of his reign, [?] the episcopate of Eleutherus.
Victor succeeded him. At this time, when Julian had completed ten years of service in the church of Alexandria, Demetrius succeeded him.
At this same time, Serapion was known as the eighth bishop of the church of Antioch after the apostles.
He is the one we spoke of earlier. Theophilus was governing the church of Caesarea in Palestine.
Narcissus too, whom the account mentioned a little earlier, was still holding office in the church of Jerusalem at that time.
At this same time, Bacchylus was bishop in Corinth in Greece. They were renowned in the church at that time
and for their steadfast faith, as we have learned from written accounts. We have listed these men by name because it was appropriate.
Chapter Twenty-three. The dispute that arose at that time concerning Passover. A major controversy arose at that time.
For the churches throughout Asia, following an ancient tradition,
observed the fourteenth day of the lunar month and celebrated it as the day of the saving feast of Passover, on which it is written that the Jews slaughtered the lamb.
They said that the fast must in every case be ended on that day, whatever day of the week it fell on.
But this was not practiced in all the churches throughout the world. For this custom has been observed as something handed down from the apostles until today:
that no one should end the fast on any day other than the day of our Savior’s resurrection. The bishops therefore gathered together about this matter,
and all, with one mind, wrote letters to all the churches everywhere, stating that, according to the rule of the church,
the mystery of our Lord’s resurrection from the dead should be celebrated only on Sunday, and that care should be taken to end the Passover fast on that day alone.
The writings of those who gathered at that time in Palestine still exist even now.
At their head were listed Theophilus, bishop of the church of Caesarea, and Narcissus of the church of Jerusalem.
There is also another document from those who had assembled in Rome concerning this dispute. It names Bishop Victor,
and the bishops of the other regions, with Palmas at their head, and those of the churches in Gaul, whose head was Irenaeus.
There is also one from the churches of Mesopotamia and the cities there, and likewise one from Bacchylus, bishop of Corinth, and from many others.
They had agreed with one mind and reached a single decision. All these held the same judgment that we have mentioned.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Disagreement That Arose in Asia. … Now the bishops in Asia were making every effort
to preserve the original custom that had been handed down to them. Polycrates was their leader.
In the letter he wrote to Victor and the church of Rome, he too set out the tradition he had received in these words:
“We observe the day without alteration, neither adding to it nor taking anything away from it.
For in Asia too great lights lie asleep. They will rise on the day of our Lord’s coming, when he comes in glory from heaven and seeks out all the saints.
There is Philip, who was one of the twelve apostles, who fell asleep in Hierapolis,
and his two daughters, who grew old in virginity. Another daughter of his lived under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and came to rest in Ephesus.
There is also John, who leaned against Jesus’ chest, who was a priest and wore the holy crown, and who was a witness and teacher.
He fell asleep in Ephesus. There is also Polycarp in Smyrna, who was a bishop and martyr,
and Thraseas, who was a bishop and martyr from Eumenia and fell asleep in Smyrna.
Why need I speak of Sagaris, the bishop and martyr who fell asleep in Laodicea, or again of the blessed Papirius,
and of Melito the eunuch, who lived under the guidance of the Holy Spirit at all times, who lies in Sardis
and awaits the visitation from [?] heaven, when he will rise from the dead? All these observed the fourteenth day of Passover, as the Gospel says,
and did not deviate in any respect, but followed the rule of faith. And I too, Polycrates, the least of them all,
observe it as I received it from my relatives, some of whom I followed. Seven of my relatives were bishops, and I am the eighth.
These relatives of mine always observed this day when the people removed the leaven. So I, brothers,
have been in the Lord for sixty-five years, have associated with brothers throughout the world, and have read through all the holy Scriptures.
I am not intimidated by those who threaten me. For those greater than I have said, ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’” To this he adds,
speaking about the bishops who shared his opinion and were with him as he wrote: “I could mention the bishops who have gathered here,
whom you urged me to summon, and I summoned them. If I were to write their names, they would be many, and I summoned them.
If I were to write their names, they would be many. Those who know my humble standing have agreed to this letter.
They know that my hair has not turned gray in vain, but that I have always conducted myself in Jesus Christ.
Chapter twenty-five. How agreement concerning Easter came about everywhere. Now Victor, the bishop of Rome,
suddenly wanted to take all the churches in Asia, together with all the congregations associated with them,
and cut them all off together from the common unity as people who caused division.
Through letters he publicly declared all the brothers there together to be excommunicated. But this did not please all the bishops.
Instead, they wrote and urged him to consider what made for peace, harmony, and brotherly love.
Their words also survive in letters in which they wrote sharply to Victor. Among these men was Irenaeus,
who also wrote on behalf of the brothers in Gaul who were under his authority. He maintained this position:
that the mystery of our Lord’s resurrection should be celebrated at Easter only on Sunday. But he wrote to Victor
that he ought not to cut off all these churches of God because they preserved the tradition of the ancient custom. He also made many other appeals to him.
In these same words he went on to say: “The disagreement is not only about the day itself, but also about the manner of fasting.
For some think that they ought to fast for one day, others for two, and others for several.
Others measure that day as forty hours of daytime and nighttime. All this variation exists among those who observe the fast.
This did not arise only in our own days, but also in the years of those before us, who did not hold strictly to the custom,
but simply and informally. All these people were at peace with one another, as we also are. Although there was disagreement about the fast,
the unity of faith was [?].” To this he adds an account that is appropriate to include here. It runs as follows:
“All the bishops of this church that you govern who came before Soter—Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Sixtus—
did not themselves observe this day, nor did those who came after them permit its observance.
Although they did not observe it themselves, they were at peace with people from other churches who observed it and came to visit them,
even though observance and nonobservance were opposed to each other. Nor was anyone ever cast out over this matter.
Rather, although the bishops before you did not observe it, they sent communion to those in other churches who did observe it.
When the blessed Polycarp came to Rome in the days of Anicetus, although they had a slight disagreement with one another over other matters as well, they immediately made peace with one another.
They did not quarrel with one another over this matter. For Anicetus could not persuade Polycarp not to observe this day,
because he had associated with John, our Lord’s disciple, and with the apostles, and had observed this day with them. Nor did Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe it,
for he told him, ‘We must preserve the custom of our fathers, the bishops who came before us.’ Although matters stood this way, they shared communion with one another.
