And in the church Anicetus allowed Polycarp to offer the Eucharist with his permission. They parted from one another in peace, while there was peace throughout the whole church.
Both among those who observed it and among those who did not observe it. Irenaeus, who lived up to his name, was indeed a peacemaker in his actions, for that is the meaning of his name.
He made these requests and appeals for peace. And he himself addressed not only Victor, but also many leading men in the churches.
He wrote similar things in his letters concerning this question. Now the bishops in Palestine—
Those whom we mentioned a little earlier, Narcissus and Theophilus, together with Cassius, bishop of the church of Tyre, Clarus of Ptolemais, and those who assembled with them—
Wrote at length about the tradition of the apostles that they had received concerning Easter. At the end of the document they add these words:
“Make every effort to send a copy of this letter to the other churches, so that we may not become a cause of error for those who easily lead themselves astray.
And we inform you that they also celebrate in Alexandria on the same day that we celebrate.
For letters go from us to them, and from them they also come to us, so that together, in agreement, we may celebrate this holy day.”
Chapter Twenty-Six. How many writings have come down to us from the diligent work of Irenaeus. Besides the treatises and letters that we have said belong to Irenaeus,
He also has a brief treatise against the pagans, which is very useful and bears the title On Wisdom.
And another, written to a brother named Marcian, On the Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching; and another book of various discussions,
In which he mentions the Letter to the Hebrews and the Wisdom of Solomon, and includes quotations from them. These, then, are the writings of Irenaeus that we know.
Chapter Twenty-Seven. About the many men who were well known in those times.
When Commodus had reigned for thirteen years and died, and Pertinax had reigned for six months after the death of Commodus, Severus succeeded him.
Many writings by numerous ancient members of the church, composed with great care, still survive even to this day.
Among those we know are the work of Heraclitus on the Apostle, and that of Maximus on the question debated by members of the heresies:
Where evil comes from, and on the fact that matter is created. There are also the work of Candidus on the six days, and that of Apion on the same subject,
And that of Sextus on the resurrection from the dead, and another work by Arabianus, as well as works by many others.
Because we have no evidence concerning them, we have not established their dates in this book or recorded any account of them in this history.
We have also seen writings by many others whose names we cannot give. They were members of the church who held the true faith, as their interpretations show.
But they are unknown because the names of those who wrote them are not recorded.
Chapter Twenty-Eight. About those who originally belonged to the heresy of Artemon, and what sort of people they were,
And how they dared to corrupt the Holy Scriptures... And among these learned men whom we have mentioned,
In a treatise carefully composed by one of them against the heresy of Artemon, which Paul of Samosata has attempted to revive in our time,
It contains an account relevant to the subject before us, for this heresy says that our Savior is a mere human being.
He demonstrates, however, that it broke away from the church not very long ago,
because its leaders boasted that it was ancient. He also set down many things to refute the false statements of their blasphemy.
He relates this in his own words as follows: “They claim that all the earlier teachers, even the apostles themselves, accepted and taught these very things that we say,
and that the truth of the preaching was preserved until the time of Victor, who was the thirteenth bishop of Rome after Peter.
But under Zephyrinus, who succeeded him, the truth was falsified. Now this might perhaps have been persuasive,
if, in the first place, the Holy Scriptures did not stand against them. There are also writings by some of our brothers that are older than the time of Victor,
who wrote against the pagans in defense of the truth, and against the heresies that existed at that time.
I mean the writings of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement, and many others, all of whom speak of the divinity of Christ.
For who does not know the writings of Irenaeus, Melito, and the others, which proclaim that Christ is God and a human being?
The hymns and songs written long ago by faithful brothers praise Christ, the Word of God, and speak of his divinity.
How, then, when the truth of the church is evident throughout all these years, can what these people say be true—that this opinion was preached until the time of Victor?
Or how are they not ashamed to slander Victor in this way, when they know for certain that Victor
excluded Theodotus from communion, the leader and father of this apostasy that denies God?
For he was the first to say that Christ was a mere human being. For if Victor, as they say, believed according to their blasphemous teaching,
how could he have expelled Theodotus, the very man who originated this heresy?” These things he said about Victor.
After Victor had served in his ministry for ten years, Zephyrinus succeeded him, in the ninth year of the reign of Severus.
The author of this treatise against the man who began the heresy we have mentioned goes on to relate
another incident that happened in the time of Zephyrinus. He writes in these words:
“I will remind the brothers of something that happened in our own days, which, I think, might have taught even Sodom wisdom if it had happened there.
There was a man named Natalius who was a confessor—not one from long ago, but from our own times.
At one time he was led astray by Asclepiodotus and another Theodotus, who was a banker.
Both of them were disciples of the Theodotus whom we mentioned earlier,
whom Bishop Victor had excluded from communion because of this foolish opinion, as I said before.
They persuaded Natalius to be called bishop of this heresy in return for a fixed salary that they would pay him.
And he was to receive from them one hundred and fifty denarii every month. But when he joined them,
he was often warned by our Lord through visions. For the merciful God and our Lord Jesus Christ
did not want him to remain outside the church and perish, because he had been a witness to his suffering. But because he paid little attention to the visions,
because he was ensnared by his position as their leader and by the filthy profits that bring many to ruin, he was finally scourged by holy angels.
And he suffered terribly all night. At once he rose early in the morning, put on sackcloth, and scattered ashes over himself.
With great earnestness and tears he fell at the feet of Bishop Zephyrinus. He threw himself down before everyone, before the people,
and poured out his tears before the merciful church of the merciful Christ. He pleaded and begged earnestly, showing the bruises from the blows he had received.
Only with difficulty did they grant him communion. To these statements he also added other words by this same writer, as follows:
"They have corrupted the holy Scriptures without fear," he says, "and rejected the original rule of faith. They do not know Christ,
nor do they investigate what the Scriptures of God say, but rather what form of argument they can find that strips the Son of his divinity.
They diligently occupy themselves with this. And if someone asks them about a passage from the Scripture of God,
they first ask what form of argument that passage can produce: a conjunctive or a disjunctive argument.
They have abandoned the holy Scriptures of God and study earthly measurements, since they belong to the earth and speak from the earth.
They do not know the one who came from above. For Euclid is diligently studied by some of them.
Aristotle and Theophrastus are greatly admired by them. Indeed, Galen is practically worshiped by some of them.
They employ the art of unbelievers to support the thinking behind their own heresy,
and mix the craftiness of the godless with the simple faith of the Scriptures of God.
Since they do not even come near the faith, what need is there for us to say anything about them?
For this reason they have fearlessly laid hands on the Scriptures of God, saying, 'We are correcting them.' And that I am not falsely accusing them
anyone who wishes can discover. For if someone wishes to bring out a copy belonging to each of them and compare them with one another,
he will find that they disagree with one another. For the copies of Asclepiades disagree with those of Theodotus.
Many of their copies can be found, because their disciples diligently copy them,
the 'corrections' of each of them, as they call them, though they are corruptions. Again, the copies of Hermophilus do not agree with these.
The copies of Apolloniades do not even agree with one another. For if someone compares those they corrected earlier with those they transcribed later,
he will find that these too disagree with one another. It seems that even they themselves know how brazen this sin is.
For either they do not believe that the holy Scriptures were spoken by the Holy Spirit, [?] they are wiser than the Holy Spirit.
What else, then, are they but demon-possessed? For they cannot deny responsibility for this audacity, since the texts are written in their own hands.
They did not receive the Scriptures in this form from those under whom they studied, and they cannot show where they copied their texts from.
Some of them did not even wish to alter them, but rejected the Law and the Prophets altogether.
Through their lawless and godless teaching, and under the pretext of grace, they were thrown into the pit of destruction. We have said this much about these people.
The fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History is completed. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
While he was a fugitive in the regions of Palestine, they saw him for seven years. As for the church of Jerusalem, after Bishop Hymenaeus,
whom we mentioned earlier, Zabdas took over the ministry there. After a short time, when he had passed to his rest,
Hermon, the last, received the throne of the apostles, which was preserved there until the time of the persecution.
In Alexandria, after Marcus had held the episcopate for eighteen years following the death of Dionysius, Theonas succeeded him.
In his days, along with the elder Phanarius [?], Achillas was also well known in Alexandria, and held the teaching office of the holy faith there.
Few could be found like him: he devoted himself vigorously to the practice of philosophy and to conduct shaped by the teaching of the gospel.
After he had served on the throne for nineteen years, Peter succeeded him as bishop of Alexandria.
He distinguished himself greatly during twelve years in the episcopate. He led the church for three years before the persecution,
and for the remainder of his leadership he conducted himself with great patience, and, for the benefit of the churches,
took very great care of these matters. There, then, in the ninth year of the persecution, he was beheaded and adorned with the crown of martyrdom.
Thus far the account of the succession has been brought down from the days of our Savior’s birth
until the destruction of the churches during the persecution, a period of three hundred and five years. From now on, we will recount the deeds of those who showed courage in the struggle
for devotion to God. We will leave in writing a record for those who come after us of who these people were and what they were like.
The seventh book is completed.

Chapter 1. On what happened before the persecution in our days. [?] The reception of the tradition handed down from the apostles.
We have brought this to a close in seven books. And in this eighth book, it is no ordinary task to hand down in writing what happened in our days,
for the instruction of those who come after us. Let us begin our account here: how great, and of what kind, were the freedom and glory
enjoyed by the message of devotion to God, which was proclaimed through Christ to all humanity,
among Greeks and among barbarians, before the persecution that took place in our days. It is beyond our ability to describe it as it deserves.
Let us take as evidence the honor that emperors showed to those who belonged to us: they gave them authority to govern nations.
And because of the great love they maintained for the teaching of our faith, they spared the nations the ordeal of sacrifices.
And what shall we say about those who belonged to the households of emperors, and also to those of high officials?
They allowed the members of their households, in their very presence, freedom in matters concerning God,
in speech and conduct—their wives, children, and servants. They not only encouraged them to take pride in the freedom of their faith, but also received them with honor,
and esteemed them more highly than those who had grown up with them. Such was Dorotheus,
who more than anyone maintained truthfulness and fidelity toward them. For these qualities he was honored above all those who held positions of leadership and distinction.
And Gorgonius, who was similarly renowned, and all those like them, were honored because of the word of God.
And how the leaders of the church were received on this account with exceptional honor by all the administrators and governors!
Chapter 2. On the destruction of the churches. How could anyone describe the vast gatherings of people that took place, growing numerous in every city,
and the eagerness of the crowds that gathered in the churches on the appointed days? The former buildings were no longer sufficient for them.
Instead, they expanded and enlarged them anew, building churches like cities. While these things were flourishing in those times,
and daily growing more numerous, stronger, and greater, there was no envy to hinder them. Nor could an evil demon display its jealousy,
or hinder them through human schemes, so long as the hand of God from heaven sheltered and guarded his people, as they deserved.
But when our affairs changed because of the abundance of peace and freedom, many grew envious and insulted one another. And not only this,
but we were, as it were, fighting against ourselves with the weapons and spears of words, and leaders were battling against leaders.
The people were stirred up against one another, showing boundless partiality. Mockery amid wickedness grew and became stronger. But God's justice, with patience, as befits it,
while the congregations were still standing, quietly and gradually stirred into action, and persecution began
among the brothers serving in the army. Yet we neither took notice nor considered how God might be reconciled to us and forgive us.
Instead, like people without God, we thought that our affairs had no one to care for them or oversee them.
We kept adding further evils to evils, and those who were thought to be shepherds
cast away the rule of reverence for God and burned with strife against one another. They fostered only things that led to strife and conflict,
jealousy, fighting, and hatred toward one another. Tyranny and the love of leadership
they pursued with their whole minds. Then, according to the saying of Jeremiah, which says, “The Lord darkened the daughter of Zion
and cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth, and did not remember his footstool on the day of his anger.
Instead, the Lord swallowed up everything desirable in Israel and overthrew all his strongholds.” And as it is said prophetically in the psalm,
“He rejected the covenant of his servant and cast his sanctuary to the ground,” through the destruction of the churches, “and tore down his fences and overthrew his strongholds.
All who passed along the road trampled him, and with all this he became a reproach to his neighbors. He raised the right hand of his enemies and turned back the help of his sword.
He did not support him in battle. He put an end to his victories and overthrew his throne to the ground. He shortened the days of his youth and clothed him in shame.”
All these things were fulfilled upon us when the houses of prayer were being demolished from top to bottom, down to their foundations.
With our own eyes we saw God's holy books burning in the middle of the marketplace, while the shepherds of the church hid shamefully here and there.
Some of them were disgracefully arrested and mocked by their enemies. As it says in another prophetic saying,
“He cast calamity upon rulers and made them wander in a trackless wasteland.” But it was not for me to recount these things. Nor were the divisions
among us and the evils before the persecution things for us to hand down to remembrance. Therefore we do not wish to say anything more about these matters,
except those things through which we acknowledge God's righteous judgment. Nor did I wish to recount the things concerning those who were tested in the persecution,
or those who sank completely and utterly and, of their own will, threw themselves into the depths of the storm.
We will add to the full account only those things that will benefit us first, and those who come after us.
Chapter Three. How those who underwent persecution fought their contest. Let us therefore now proceed
and briefly record the glorious contests of the martyrs of the word of God.
It was the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, in the month of Adar, when the day of the feast of our Savior’s passion was drawing near.
Imperial decrees were published everywhere, ordering that the churches be razed to the ground,
that the Scriptures be burned, that those who held positions of honor be disgraced, and that those who had been slaves and had been freed,
if they persisted in their Christian convictions, be deprived of their freedom. Such was the first decree issued against us.
A little later, other decrees arrived, ordering that all those who presided over the churches everywhere
first be handed over to imprisonment and afterward be compelled by every means to offer sacrifice. Then many leaders of the churches
were seen to be the first to undergo cruel tortures. Other shepherds, however, lost heart through fear and were easily defeated at the very beginning of the struggle.
As for the rest, each underwent different kinds of torture in succession. Some had their bodies beaten with blows,
while others received punishment through unbearable tortures and lacerations,
through which many met an unhappy end to their lives. Others, again, came through the contest in a different way.
Chapter Four. Concerning God’s glorious martyrs: how their memorials filled every place, and how they received distinguished crowns for their devotion to God.
For there were some who, when others forcibly subjected them to judgment and brought them forward to the defiled and unclean sacrifice, were released as though they had offered sacrifice,
although they had not sacrificed. Another had not even approached or come into contact with anything defiled, yet because others said that he had sacrificed,
he silently accepted the injustice and went away. Another, struggling between death and life, was thrown aside as though dead.
Still another lay on the ground and was dragged by his feet for a long distance [?], and they counted him among those who had sacrificed. Another cried out
and testified in a loud voice, rejecting the defiled sacrifices. Another shouted that he was a Christian
and gloried in confessing our Savior’s name. Another cried out that he had not sacrificed and would not sacrifice. But many were beaten
and silenced by the many measures employed by the Roman military force assigned to this task. They were struck on their faces and cheeks
and forcibly thrown outside. In this way, the enemies of devotion to God took great pains, using every means,
to make it appear that their wishes had been carried out. But their efforts did not succeed with the holy martyrs, of whom words cannot give an adequate and accurate account.
For there were tens of thousands about whom one could tell, who displayed an extraordinary resolve for the sake of devotion to God,
not only after the persecution was stirred up against everyone, but also long before, while there was peace.
For immediately, at the outset, the man who had received imperial authority was profoundly stirred,
and secretly and covertly began a persecution against the churches, after the interval that had elapsed since Decius and Valerian.
Suddenly he set himself against us to wage war on us. First, however, he put those serving in the army to the test.
For he expected that in this way the rest would be easily overcome, if he first fought and defeated those many men serving in the army.
One could see them gladly agreeing to be discharged and to become like the rest who lived as ordinary civilians, rather than deny the worship of God, the Creator of all.
For the commander who held office at that time [?] first undertook the persecution of those serving in the army.
He was separating out and purging those enrolled in military service.
He required them to choose either to comply and remain in the rank they held, or, if they refused to comply and opposed the command, to be stripped of it.
And many who were soldiers of Christ's kingdom readily and without hesitation valued their confession of faith
more than that apparent glory and the advantage they enjoyed. There were, however, a few among them
who not only gave up their rank but also endured death for their steadfast commitment to the worship of God.
For the accomplice in the evil plot was then still venturing to shed the blood of only a few.
It seems that he was still afraid of the great number of believers and hesitated to threaten war against everyone.
Chapter Five. Concerning those who suffered martyrdom in Nicomedia. But when it broke out openly, no one could describe in words
how many martyrs of God, and what kind of people they were, one could see before one's own eyes in every city and village. Then one of the prominent men,
one of those most distinguished in the ranks of what the world considers honor, as soon as the decree against the churches was posted in Nicomedia,
was stirred by zeal for God and acted boldly in the fervor of faith. While this decree was posted in a prominent place in the marketplace, he took it down and tore it apart,
because it had been issued in impiety and wickedness. Two emperors were then in that very city,
namely, the most senior of them all and the one who held the fourth rank in the government.
This man was the first champion among the martyrs of that time, who won glory in this way.
And they immediately endured the consequences appropriate to such boldness. Without distress or agitation, he kept his composure until his last breath.
But more than all the martyrs who at various times received extraordinary praise and became renowned for their courage, [?] among the Greeks as well as among the barbarians,
there were at this time the glorious martyrs of God associated with Dorotheus, who were members of the emperors' households.
They enjoyed great honor from their masters, who made no distinction between them and their own sons in the genuine love they showed them.
But they regarded as truly greater wealth, beyond the glory and luxury of this world,
the disgrace and suffering endured for the worship of God, and the deaths of every kind that were devised against them. Of these men I will mention one,
and describe how his life ended, so that those who read this book may also gain from his experience some understanding of what happened to the others.
They therefore brought one man forward in the city we mentioned earlier, before these emperors, and he was ordered to offer sacrifice.
But as he continued to endure, orders were given that he should be hung up naked and his whole body torn by blows until he gave in.
Thus, even against his will, he was to do whatever he was commanded. While he suffered these things, he remained unchanged, and by now his bones were visible.
They mixed vinegar with salt and poured it over the places where the flesh had been stripped away. But when he also held out against these pains,
they brought a brazier into the middle, and, like meat intended for eating, what remained of his body was scorched over that fire little by little,
not suddenly, all at once, so that he would not escape easily. Those who had placed him over that fire would not allow him to get away from it
until he agreed, even by a gesture, to do what he was commanded. But he would not be moved from his resolve.
Clothed in victory amid those tortures, he surrendered his life. Such was the martyrdom of [?] of those members of the royal households,
who was truly worthy of his name, for his name was Peter. What happened to others was [?] no less severe than this.
But to avoid saying too much, let us leave the rest and say this: Dorotheus and Gorgonius, together with many others
who belonged to the royal household, after enduring a struggle involving every kind of suffering, received in return life and the crown of victory in God.
Chapter Six. Concerning those members of the royal households who suffered martyrdom. At this time Anthimus, who presided over the church of Nicomedia,
was beheaded because of his testimony to Christ. Suddenly a great number of martyrs were added to his company. For in those days,
I do not know how, a fire broke out in the royal palace at Nicomedia, and on the basis of suspicion,
a false report spread that our community was responsible for this act. Then, as though at a signal from the emperor,
the entire community of those who feared God there suffered together: some were killed by the sword, and others were consumed by fire.
It is reported that, through the working of God's inexpressible will, men and women alike leaped into that fire and entered it.
The enemies put many others to the sword and threw them into the depths of the sea. As for those members of the royal households,

after their deaths, once their funeral rites had been performed and they had been properly laid in the ground [?], they dug them up again and brought them out, and ordered that they too should be thrown into the sea.
Their masters, the emperors, thought that if they lay in their graves, people would worship them
and consider them gods. Such were the things that happened to the martyrs at the beginning of the persecution, along with other things like them.
A short time later, in the region called Melitene, and also in Syria, rebellions arose against this imperial rule.
They devised a plan to have all the leaders of the churches everywhere thrown into prison by an order.
The spectacle of what happened in these circumstances was beyond all description, for tens of thousands were imprisoned everywhere.
The prisons in every place, which had previously been prepared for murderers and grave robbers, were then filled with bishops, elders, deacons,
readers, and exorcists, so that no room was left there for those convicted of criminal acts.
Then other written orders followed the earlier ones. In them it was written concerning those who were imprisoned that, if they offered sacrifice,
they should be released and go freely wherever they wished. But if they persisted and would not comply, it was ordered that they should be torn by many tortures.
And now again, how could anyone count the multitude of martyrs everywhere, especially those in Africa and among the people of the Moors,
and in the Thebaid and Egypt, who afterward also went out to other cities and regions and gained glory through martyrdom?
Chapter Seven. Concerning the Egyptians who suffered martyrdom in Phoenicia. We are acquainted with those who came from Egypt and gained victory in Palestine,
and we know those in Tyre in Phoenicia. Whoever saw them was seized with amazement at their countless blows,
and at the endurance of these glorious champions in the steadfastness of their devotion to God, and at the contests they undertook
immediately after their beatings against beasts that eat human beings, amid the menace of leopards, bears, wild boars, and bulls,
which were subjected to burning brands and driven around them, and at the glorious endurance of the valiant men in facing each of the beasts.
We ourselves were also present when these things happened, as the power of God and of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,
for whose sake they were bearing witness, stood beside them and showed itself in action to the victorious martyrs.
We saw fierce beasts remaining for a long time without daring to attack
or approach the bodies of God's friends. Yet against other outsiders who were brought from somewhere,
they rushed with only a little provocation. But the glorious champions alone, even when they stood naked

and waved their hands to draw the beasts toward them—for this was what they had been ordered to do—the beasts would not touch at all. Sometimes they did rush at them, but they were driven back as though by a power from God,
and turned back again. As these things continued for a long time, they caused great amazement among the spectators.
And when the first beast did nothing, they released a second beast against them.
One must marvel at the untroubled steadfastness of these glorious martyrs and the unshakable endurance that dwelt in youthful bodies.
For I saw a young man, not yet twenty years old, standing without bonds,
stretching out his hands in the shape of a cross. With a mind neither frightened nor troubled, he directed himself toward God in prayer.
He did not move or turn aside from the place where he stood, while bears and leopards breathing deadly fury
came close to touching his body. Yet their mouths were shut as though by the power of God, and they turned back again.
Such was the case with this man. I also saw others who were thrown before a savage bull,
which tossed into the air with its horns other people from outside who approached it, tearing them apart and leaving them half dead.
But the holy martyrs alone, although it threatened them with fury and menace, it could not even approach. Instead, it struck here and there with its feet and horns.
Because it was being goaded with heated irons, it breathed rage and fury. But through God's providence it turned back.
Since even this did nothing to them, they again released other wild beasts against them. Finally, after these terrible threats of every kind,
they were all killed with the sword, and instead of being laid in the earth in graves, they were thrown into the depths of the sea.
Such was the contest of these Egyptians, who fought for devotion to God in Tyre.
Chapter Eight. Those who were martyred in Egypt. We should also marvel at those who were martyred in their own land [?].
Tens of thousands of men, together with women and children, despised this temporary life for the sake of our Savior's teaching,
and endured death in every form. Some, after being torn with claws, whipped, and cruelly beaten,
and after ten thousand kinds of dreadful torture, were thrown into the fire. Others were drowned in the depths of the sea.
Others confidently stretched out their necks to those who cut off their heads. Others died under torture.
Others perished from hunger. Others were crucified, some in the manner customary for criminals,
while others, treated worse than these, were fastened upside down. They were kept alive until they perished from hunger on those pieces of wood.
Chapter Nine. Those who were martyred in the Thebaid. Beyond description were
the injuries and pains endured by the martyrs in the Thebaid. Their whole bodies were scraped with potsherds instead of claws [?],
until they finally died. Women, too, were bound by one foot
and hoisted high into the air by a device, and were whipped while stripped naked. They were a shameful and merciless sight,
more dreadful than anything else for those who saw them. Others, again, were bound to trees and branches and died on them.
For they used a device to draw the strong branches of trees together into one place, from this side and that.
The martyrs' legs were stretched out, one on this side and one on that, and they let the branches return to their places.
They devised this to tear their limbs apart in an instant. These things went on not merely for days or a short time,
but over a period of years. On some days more than ten were killed, and on others more than twenty,
and sometimes thirty. On some occasions there were as many as sixty, and at other times as many as a hundred.
In a single day, men and women together with children would die, condemned to various punishments of every kind. We ourselves also saw with our own eyes,
when we went to those regions, many people suddenly put to death in a single day: some had their heads cut off,
while others received the punishment of fire. The sword grew blunt from cutting and could no longer cut,
and the executioners themselves grew weary and exhausted, taking turns with one another. Yet an astonishing determination was to be seen, with a resolve filled with the power of God.
of those who believed in the Christ of God. For as soon as the saints received their sentence, others immediately began coming in from another side before the judgment seat.
They declared themselves to be Christians and despised and scorned their persecutors amid those afflictions and tortures of every kind.
Without sorrow, they openly remained steadfast in the fear of God, and with joy and glad delight they received the final sentence of death.
As they sang, they offered praises and thanksgiving to the God of all until their last breath. These people were indeed remarkable.
Still more remarkable were those who were distinguished for their wealth, ancestry, reputation, and philosophical learning.
Above everything else they prized the fear of God and faith in our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ. Such a man was Polycarp,
who held no ordinary office of leadership, but was entrusted with the administration of Alexandria.
While he still held his rank and the honor granted him by the Romans, and was attended by soldiers,
this very man was brought to trial every day, as was Phileas, bishop of the city of Thmuis,

a man distinguished in his own country by his rank of worldly honor and his philosophical learning. Many of their relatives and other friends appealed to these men, as did those who held positions of authority.
Even the judge himself urged them to have mercy on themselves and spare their children and wives. But they would not yield to any of these appeals
to choose and cherish this temporary life, despise the law of confessing their faith, and deny our Savior.
Instead, with a strong and sound resolve—that is, one grounded in the fear of God—and with a soul that loved God,
they endured all the judge’s threats and insults. Finally, both of them were beheaded.
The tenth. [?] From the writings of Phileas to the people of Thmuis. For all these things, proofs, examples, and further fine indications
are set before us in the holy Scriptures of God. The holy martyrs among us were disturbed by nothing, but directed the eye of their soul with purity toward the God of all.
They accepted death in the fear of God and did not turn away from their calling, because they had found our Lord Jesus Christ, who put on humanity for our sake
to put an end to all sin and establish this for us as the way of life. For he did not regard being equal to God as something to be seized,
but emptied himself, took the likeness of a servant, and was found in human form. He humbled himself to the point of death—death on a cross.
For this reason, the martyrs who had put on Christ were richly endowed with great gifts. And all the pains and every means of torture
they endured not just once; some endured them even twice. And every kind of threat, not merely in words,
but also in deeds, they bore, as the armed men multiplied these against them. Yet they did not waver in their resolve,
because perfect love casts out fear. But to recount their victory and their courage amid every kind of torture,
what words could suffice us? For everyone who wished was free to abuse them. Some were beaten with clubs,
others with rods, others with whips, others with leather straps, and others with ropes.
The forms of their tortures varied. [?] They came to be without fear after its end, through their fear of Christ.
Chapter Eleven. Those who suffered martyrdom in Phrygia. Why, then, must we say much more and add fresh accounts upon fresh accounts
of the contests and struggles of the martyrs throughout the whole world, who were being attacked under a general law as though in a war?
For consider an entire town of Christians in Phrygia, its men together with its women and the children in it:
armed soldiers surrounded it, set it on fire, and burned it down, while the people called out and bore witness before God.
For all the people living in the town—the chief financial officer together with the military commanders, and the leading citizens together with all the people—
confessed that they were Christians and would not yield in any way to those who ordered them to worship idols.
There was also a man who held a position of honor among the Romans, whose name was Adauctus.
He belonged to a distinguished family in Italy and had passed through all the ranks of honor bestowed by the emperor,
so that he had also administered public affairs without reproach in the offices they call magistrate and comptroller.
And he, who had gained distinction in all these things, finally, through the victory of devotion to God and through his confession of Christ,
while still holding the office of comptroller, endured the contest for devotion to God and was adorned with the crown of martyrdom.
Chapter Twelve. The many men and women who contended with great distinction. Why must I now mention the rest by name,
or count the great number of men, or describe the various tortures of the wonderful martyrs? Some were cut apart with axes, as happened in Arabia.
Some had their legs broken, as happened to those in Cappadocia. Others, in turn, were hung up high by their feet,
and a slow-burning fire was placed beneath them, so that they were suffocated by the smoke rising from it, as happened
to those in Mesopotamia. Others had the tips of their noses, ears, and fingers cut away little by little,
and the rest of their limbs and parts of their bodies were cut off, as happened to those in Alexandria.
And why must we recall those in Antioch who, on a fiery gridiron, were roasted not to bring about death,
but to inflict prolonged punishment? Others had their right hands immediately placed in the fire because they would not offer a defiled sacrifice.
Others, fleeing these trials, before they could be seized and fall into the hands of their enemies,
threw themselves down from high rooftops, considering a sudden death preferable to the cruelty of the wicked.
There was a certain holy woman in Antioch, remarkable for her resolve and distinguished in other respects:
in wealth, in family background, and in her reputation with everyone. She had virgin daughters who were beautiful in body and graceful in stature,
and she had raised them according to the laws of devotion to God. And because the tyrant was stirred to great envy against them,
He went about using every means to track down the women who were hiding. But when he heard that they were in another place,
he took care to summon them to Antioch. When they had been caught in the soldiers’ trap, and she saw that she had no means
for herself and her daughters to [?], she weighed in her mind the evils that people could inflict, and considered that the worst of all was forced sexual intercourse.
She could not bear even to hear of such things, nor, indeed, could they surrender themselves to the worship of demons,
which, she said, was more bitter than any death and worse than any destruction. She held that there was one solution to all these things,
namely, refuge in our Lord. This was the counsel she gave herself and her daughters. Once they had agreed on this plan,
they all secured their clothing modestly around their bodies. When they were midway along the road, they asked the guards to withdraw a little.
Then they threw themselves into the river that flowed there. These women, then, cast themselves in.
But there were other virgins in Antioch itself who lived in harmony and were pleasing to God in everything.
They were sisters by birth, distinguished in ancestry, admirable in their conduct, and young in years.
They were beautiful in body, chaste in soul, beloved for their fear of God, and admirable in their zeal.
As though the earth could not bear to carry such lovely flowers, the servants of the demons ordered them to be thrown into the sea.
Such things were being done to these women. Others in Pontus were enduring things dreadful even to hear about.
They drove sharp reeds into their fingertips beneath their nails. Others melted lead in a fire,
and when it had melted in the fire, they poured it over their backs and roasted those parts of the body that are held in greater honor.
Still others endured hideous, merciless, and unspeakable sufferings in their private parts and their wombs.
The illustrious judges, the enforcers of the laws, displayed their ingenuity through these things. As though it were splendid wisdom, they devised ways of outdoing the demons.
They were constantly finding new ones, and competed to surpass one another in victory, as though in a contest. But the end of the afflictions came
when they finally grew weary of their excessive wickedness, became tired of killing, and were sated and filled with the outpouring of blood.
They turned, as they imagined, to kindness and mercy, intending from then on to do nothing cruel to us.
They said, “It is not right for us to defile our cities with the blood of the people under our rule, nor to dishonor through cruelty the exalted sovereignty of the emperors,
which is kind and gentle toward everyone. For it is right,” they said, “that the mercy of imperial authority should extend to everyone and bring them help.”
They were no longer to be condemned to death; instead, this punishment imposed on us was to be abolished because of the emperors’ mercy.
But orders were given that their eyes should be gouged out and one leg of each of them crippled.
For these were their acts of mercy and the light punishments imposed on us. And so, because of this mercy of the wicked,
I could not recount the multitude of things they endured. Some had their right hands cut off with a sword.
Afterward, the wounds were cauterized with fire. Others had their left legs cauterized at the joints and were crippled.
After these things, they were sentenced to be sent to the copper mines in various regions, not for any useful service,
but to inflict pain and humiliation on those who were condemned. Besides all these things, others were victorious in other contests,
which we cannot recount, for their victories surpass words. Through these things the victorious martyrs of Christ gained glory throughout the world.
Everywhere, those who saw their courage were amazed, and they openly demonstrated God's hidden power through their steadfast faith in our Savior.
Chapter Thirteen. Concerning those who led the churches, who demonstrated the truth of the devotion to God that they proclaimed,
by the outpouring of their blood. To mention them all by name would make a lengthy account,
and perhaps would not even be possible. But let us mention those leaders of well-known churches who suffered martyrdom. First in the remembrance of the faithful,
let Anthimus, bishop of the church in the city of Nicomedia, be recorded as a witness to Christ's kingdom. He was beheaded for his confession.
Among the martyrs from Antioch was Lucian, a priest of the church there, who was outstanding throughout his life.
He too suffered martyrdom at Nicomedia while the emperor was there. He first proclaimed Christ's heavenly kingdom in words,
through an utterance inspired by the Spirit, and afterward also in deed. Among those who suffered martyrdom in Phoenicia were notable men,
who were in every respect friends of God and shepherds of Christ's flock: Tyrannion, bishop of the church of Tyre;
Zenobius, a priest of the church of Sidon; and Silvanus, bishop of the church of Emesa. This last man, along with others, became food for wild beasts
in the city of Emesa and was raised to the company of the martyrs. Those who honored the word of God in Antioch itself
both gained glory through endurance to the point of death. The bishop was thrown into the depths of the sea.
Zenobius, who was a skilled physician, died under the tortures themselves, courageously enduring the scraping of his sides with hooks.
Among those who suffered martyrdom in Palestine was Silvanus, bishop of the church of Gaza. At the copper mines in Phaeno,
he was beheaded along with others who numbered thirty-nine. Among the Egyptians, too,
the bishops Peleus and Nilus, together with others, endured death by fire. Among these let us also remember the priest Pamphilus, the great glory of the church of Caesarea,
who was an outstanding man among those who lived with us. The glory of his victories will be recorded at the appropriate time. Among those in Alexandria,
let Peter the bishop, a man of God, be recorded among the teachers of devotion to Christ, along with the priests who were with him: Faustus, Dius, and Ammonius,
Christ's perfected martyrs; also Phileas, Hesychius, and Theodore, bishops of the churches in Egypt, and with them many other notable men,
who are remembered by the churches in their various regions and places. But as for what happened to all those throughout the whole world,
The struggles for the fear of God, so that we may give a precise written account of the victories of each one of them.
It is not for us to recount these deeds, but for those who saw them with their own eyes. As for those whom I myself received,
we are making a memorial in another book for those who know us and come after us. In this history, however, an account of the change in what happened to us will follow what has already been said.
What happened from the beginning of the persecution [?] for those who read these histories.
Chapter fourteen. What the enemies of the fear of God were like. Concerning the government of the Romans before their war against us.
For as long as their rulers lived in friendship and peace with us, what great prosperity and abundance [?].
What words could describe it? When [?] those who held sovereign authority completed ten years,
they lived amid festivals, celebrations, joyful festivities, and abundant peace. And thus, without disturbance, it continued to grow,
and their authority grew stronger every day. But when they suddenly abandoned peace with us and stirred up a bitter war, before they had completed even two years in this war,

something new happened within their empire itself and overturned all their affairs. Severe illnesses attacked the head of their entire empire, and because of these illnesses his mind also turned to madness.
Together with the other man who ranked second in honor after him, he adopted the life of a private citizen, like other people.
While these things were still happening in this way, their empire was divided completely in two—a thing that had never
happened before. After a short interval, Constantius, who was gentle in all his conduct
and was kind toward those under his authority and loving toward God, left behind a beloved son as his successor,
Constantine, emperor and Augustus, and ended his life according to the law of nature [?]. He was the first to be proclaimed a god.
Even after his death, he received every honor owed to an emperor, this gentle and kindest of emperors,
who alone in our days completed the term of his rule in a manner worthy of imperial government.
In other matters too, he devoted himself to honorable conduct and to the benefit of everyone. He took no part whatsoever in the war against us.
Instead, he protected those who feared God under his authority from injury and oppression. He did not demolish church buildings or introduce any new measure against us.
For this reason, he received a good end, full of blessings. He alone departed from this world while still reigning, amid harmony and glory,
with his beloved, self-controlled, God-fearing son Constantine succeeding him. Immediately upon his accession, he was proclaimed full emperor and Augustus
by his soldiers; and before they proclaimed him, he had been appointed by God himself, the King of all.
He committed himself to following his father's example in matters concerning the fear of God. Such, then, was his situation.
Chapter fifteen. Concerning what happened besides these things. Along with these events, Licinius too was proclaimed emperor and Augustus by the unanimous decision of those who held imperial power.
Maximinus the Great [?] voices and demons. He was very zealous for the error of idolatry, besides divination and the prophecies of demons.
He was unwilling to budge even a fingernail’s breadth. For this reason he also intensified the persecution, pursuing it more fiercely and relentlessly than his predecessors.
Thus he built temples in every city, and the idol temples that had long been demolished
he ordered to be diligently restored. He appointed priests of the idols in every region and city. Along with these,
he ordered that in every province one priest should be appointed from among the well-known civic leaders, someone who had distinguished himself by serving in an honorable office,
with a company of soldiers and armed men. All the sorcerers, however, as though they were righteous men who loved God,
he honored with governorships and high positions of authority. While he was engaged in these things, in every region and city, throughout every province under his rule,
he oppressed and harassed people by exacting gold, silver, and incalculable amounts of property, and by imposing the heavy burden of financial loss. From the wealthy
he took the property they had inherited from their fathers, and he gave his flatterers sudden riches and heaps of possessions.
He indulged so excessively in drunkenness that at drinking parties he even lost his reason. In his drunkenness he issued such orders
that, when his wine had worn off, he regretted them the next day. In his gluttony he prepared extravagant meals for everyone.
He himself was a teacher of wickedness to his officials and subjects. He encouraged those serving in the army to grow slack through luxury and debauchery.
He urged the governors and military commanders [?] to assert their power over those under their authority through plunder and oppression,
so that they would practice tyranny along with him and as he did. But why should we recall this man’s abominable deeds, or count the multitude of women with whom he committed adultery?
For he passed through no city without violating women there and also abducting virgins. In these things he succeeded against everyone
except the Christians, who despised death and regarded all his tyranny as nothing.
For the men endured at his hands fire, the sword, the driving in of nails, being thrown to wild beasts, and being cast into the depths of the sea,
the cutting off of limbs, burns, the gouging out of their eyes, and the gradual mutilation of their entire bodies. Along with these things they also endured hunger, the mines, and imprisonment.
Through all these things they demonstrated endurance for the sake of reverence for God, rather than exchange the worship of God for idols.
The women endured no less than the men, for they were strengthened by the teaching of the word of God. Some endured struggles just like the men
and won crowns of victory like them. Those who were being dragged away to be violated quickly surrendered their lives to death rather than their bodies to violation.
One woman, however, who was a Christian from Alexandria, stood out above all the women with whom the tyrant committed adultery.
She was well known and highly regarded, and by her courageous resolve she overcame the lust of Maximinus’s soul. She was distinguished in other respects as well:
in wealth, noble birth, and education in wisdom. Yet she considered everything secondary to chastity. Although he tried hard to entice her,
he could not bring himself to kill her, because his desire overpowered his anger, though she was ready to die.
Instead, he banished her and took all her property. Many other women, however, who could not endure or listen to threats of sexual violation,
They endured every kind of torture, affliction, and torment at the hands of the judges among all nations. These women were remarkable.
Especially remarkable was one chaste woman of Rome, distinguished by her noble birth, whom Maxentius, the tyrant there, wanted to dishonor.
He was scheming to commit an outrage like Maximinus. For when she heard that the servants had come and were standing at her door—
those who served [?] the tyrant in such matters—and saw that her husband, out of fear of him, had consented to their taking her away,
although he himself was the prefect of Rome, she, because she was a Christian, asked for a little time, supposedly to adorn herself.
She went into her bedroom, and when she was alone, she took a sword and stabbed herself in the heart. When she died, she left her corpse to those who were standing there to take her away.
Through deeds that proclaimed it more loudly than words, she showed that, above all possessions, the resolve of Christians is unconquerable and incorruptible,
to all people, both those who now exist and those who will come afterward.
Such an abundance of evil was gathered together and perpetrated at the same time by the two tyrants who held power in the East and the West.
For if anyone investigates the source of these things, he cannot doubt it when he says that it arose from the persecution against us. All this turmoil did not cease
until the Christians received freedom. Throughout the ten years of persecution, they never stopped plotting and waging war against one another.
For no one could travel by sea: wherever someone traveled, if he was arrested, he fell prey to every kind of torture and affliction.
They were flogged, had their sides raked, and were questioned about whether they had been sent by the enemy.
In the end they were crucified or sent to torment in the fire. Shields and armor were made ready,
as were arrows, spears, and the rest of the weapons of war; and ships were being deployed everywhere for war at that time.
There was nothing else for anyone to expect each day except war. Along with these things, a deadly famine then overtook them,
about which we have related what was appropriate in its proper place. These and similar things were what unfolded throughout the persecution.
Chapter Sixteen. On the favorable change in circumstances. When these ten years had been fully completed, by the grace of God—
though things had begun to ease after eight years—God’s heavenly grace showed its work toward us in peace.
Chapter Seventeen. On the change in the rulers. Then those rulers who had opposed us,
those through whose hands the war against us had first been carried out, underwent a remarkable change of mind.
They reversed their declarations and, through gracious letters addressed to us and lenient decrees, extinguished the great fire that had blazed up in the persecution.
The cause of this did not come from human beings, nor from the compassion or mercy of the rulers, for they fell far short of this.
Indeed, every day, from the beginning until that time, they had been devising increasingly evil things against us.
For they were constantly using their ingenuity to devise every variety of torture against us. Rather, this was the evident work of God’s providence.
who showed favor to his people. Upon that chief of the power of evil he brought the anguish of torment, which began in his body and penetrated as far as his soul.
For suddenly an abscess developed in the hidden parts inside him, and afterward a deep ulcer, that is, a fistula.
Gangrene from an incurable ulcer developed in his bowels, from which countless worms streamed without ceasing.
And a stench of death came from his body, which, through excessive eating before his illness, had become enormously fat.
Then, as he rotted away, his appearance brought indescribable horror to those who approached him.
The physicians who could not endure his foul smell were put to death. And as his body wasted away,
and he had no hope of surviving, other physicians were put to death without mercy because they could not help him.
While he lay amid all these afflictions, he became aware of the outrages he had committed against those who feared God, and he collected his thoughts.
First he acknowledged the God of all. Afterward he summoned those close to him and told them that those persecuting the Christians must stop without delay.
He commanded that, by law and imperial decree, they should hurry to rebuild their churches, follow their customs, and offer prayer on behalf of the empire.
Then action followed the word, and imperial decrees were published in every city. Translations of their wording follow.
They contained the following: Emperor Caesar Maximianus [?], Maxentius, and Augustus; Emperor Caesar
Constantine, Pious and Augustus. Among the other affairs of the empire concerning measures for the common good,
we previously wished that everything should be set right according to the ancient laws and the established order of the Roman Empire,
and that we should also take care that the Christians, who had abandoned the religion of their ancestors, should return to it. But through some manner of thinking,
such great arrogance had taken hold of them that they would not follow what their predecessors had prescribed, although their ancestors had adhered to these things from ancient times.
Instead, they acted according to their own judgment and as each one of them wished, so as to observe their own law. Accordingly, a decree of this kind had been issued:
that they should return to the practices established by their predecessors. Many of them were exposed to danger, and many were harassed
and endured every kind of death. And since we see that many have persisted in the same condition, neither offering the gods in heaven the worship due to them,
nor taking part in Christian worship, we, in our mercy and according to our constant custom, by which we are accustomed
to forgive everyone's offenses, have decided in this matter too, of our own free will, to grant them pardon, so that they may once again be Christians
and restore the buildings in which they used to assemble, provided they do nothing contrary to public order. In another letter we will inform the governors what
they are required to observe. Therefore, in return for this pardon of ours, they are bound to entreat their God for our lives and for the affairs of the empire,
and for themselves, so that in every way well-being may also be granted to the affairs of the empire,
and they may be able to live without anxiety in their own homes. These things were translated from Latin into Greek as well as was possible.
that this was how things stood in it. But it is time for us to consider what happened along with these things.
The eighth book is finished.
