Chapter One. On the temporary respite that occurred. The written statement of the emperor’s change of will had been circulated throughout every province in Asia.
While these things were happening in this way, the man who was above all a persecutor of reverence for God was displeased with what he had written.
Instead of issuing written orders, he verbally commanded the rulers under his authority to stop their warfare against us.
For he had no authority to act otherwise in opposition to the command of those greater than himself.
He kept silent about this law that had been enacted and took care that it should not become public in the territories under his authority.
Without putting it in writing, he commanded the rulers under his authority to stop persecuting us. They, however, made his command known to one another in writing.
Sabinus, who was honored in the empire with the eminent authority of the prefecture, disclosed and explained the emperor’s intention to the governors in every nation in a letter written in Latin.
They believed that the intention communicated to them in writing was genuine, and to the financial administrators, the military commanders, and those in charge of the villages
they disclosed and made known the emperor’s will through written communications. And not merely in writing: to comply with the emperor’s command,
they brought out into the open and set free all those whom they had confined in prison because of their confession of Christ.
They did the same for those in the mines who had been condemned to punishment there, for they believed that this was truly the emperor’s will.
While these things were happening in this way, light suddenly dawned, as though out of a gloomy night.
In every city one could see churches gathering, large congregations, and worship being conducted according to their former customs.
Everyone who belonged to the unbelieving pagans was greatly astonished and amazed at these things,
at this remarkable change that had occurred. They cried out and said that the God of the Christians alone was the true God.
And those of our people [?] who had distinguished themselves faithfully and courageously in the struggles of the persecution
regained the freedom to speak openly with everyone that they had formerly enjoyed. But all those whose souls had grown weak in faith and who were caught in the storm,
They lovingly concerned themselves with the healing of their souls and sought help from those who were healthy.
They asked them for a helping hand and pleaded with God to be reconciled to them. Moreover, the victorious champions of godliness,
once they had been freed from the blows of the sufferings inflicted on them, all returned to their own lands. Rejoicing and glad, they passed through every city
with great delight. The confidence they enjoyed cannot be expressed in words. A crowd of many people, meanwhile, in the roads and streets,
went along praising God with hymns and songs. And those who, under harsh punishments,
had shortly before been driven from their own lands in chains were welcomed into their homes, so that even those who had formerly been their executioners,
when they saw the astonishing thing that had happened, which they had not expected would happen, rejoiced with us over what had taken place.
Chapter Two. On the change that took place afterward. But the tyrant who hated what was good could not endure the things we have described.
He was an enemy of everything good—the man whom we said was ruler over the lands of the East.
He could not endure this state of affairs for even six months, but worked very cunningly to put an end to the peace.
First, he contrived to use a pretext to prevent gatherings at the shrines of the martyrs.
Then, through wicked men, he became his own envoy against us. He incited the people of Antioch to petition him to issue an order
that no Christians at all should live in the territory under their jurisdiction, as though he were bestowing a great favor on them.
He also gave others permission to do the same. The first to take the lead in this at Antioch was Theotecnus,
a wicked man and a sorcerer whose character belied his name. He was the financial administrator in that city.
Chapter Three. On the statue newly erected at Antioch. This man whom we have mentioned armed himself vigorously to make war on us.
By every means, he strove to hunt down our people as though they were defiled men hiding in darkness.
He employed every device in slandering and accusing us and caused the death of many. Finally, a statue of Zeus
Philius was erected by him. Through the art of [?], defiled worship, unlawful mysteries, and unclean rites of purification, he contrived and succeeded,
to the point that he even displayed to the emperor the astonishing art of divination. This same man, to gratify what was desired
by the one who held power, raised up the demon against the Christians, declaring, “Look! The god has commanded
that the Christians be driven beyond the boundaries of the city and its surrounding countryside, because they are enemies of the god.”
Chapter Four. On the plans devised against us. Now when this man first thought things were going according to his wishes,
all the other officials living in the cities under this emperor’s authority also resolved to carry out a similar plan.
For the provincial governors saw that the emperor took pleasure in this, and they urged those under their authority to do the same.
The tyrant also gladly granted permission through his letters for their intention to be carried out. Then the persecution was rekindled once again.
Priests and high priests of the idols were appointed in every city by Maximinus himself.
These were the men most distinguished in every respect by their ranks of honor, men who had great zeal
for the worship of the idols they served. The tyrant’s boundless wickedness urged all the rulers
and those under their authority to do everything against us that would please him.
They did him this favor in return for the benefits they wished to receive from him.
As a gift in exchange for a gift, they offered our slaughter, and they renewed their hostility toward us.
Chapter Five. The records they fabricated against our Lord. They fabricated records concerning our Savior and Pilate,
which were full of blasphemy against Christ. They were sent throughout his dominion as though by the emperor’s will, and he commanded in writing
that everywhere, in the cities and marketplaces, they should be publicly displayed for everyone, and that they should be handed over to all the teachers who taught reading and writing,
so that their pupils would study these instead of their lessons and learn them by heart. While these things were being done,
another military commander, whom the Romans call a dux, seized some immoral women from the marketplace in Damascus in Phoenicia and brought them in.
He ordered the torturers to deal gently with them, and compelled them to declare in writing that they had formerly been Christian women,
and that they had seen unlawful acts among the Christians, claiming that they committed filthy acts in their houses of prayer,
and other things that he wanted them to say to disgrace our way of life. This same man
put these statements into official records and informed the emperor. He ordered these writings to be proclaimed in every place and city.
But a short time later this military commander killed himself with his own hands, paying the penalty for his wickedness.
Chapter Six. Those who suffered martyrdom at this time. Once again our expulsion and a cruel persecution were set in motion.
The governors in every province again rose harshly against us, and many were arrested who were known
for teaching the fear of God, and readily received the sentence of death. Three of them, in Emesa, a city of Phoenicia,
who confessed that they were Christians were thrown to the wild beasts. One of them was Silvanus, a bishop who was advanced in years
and had carried out his ministry for forty years. At this same time Peter, the bishop who had presided with distinction over the church of Alexandria,
who was a vessel of God because of his distinguished service in the word of God, was seized without cause,
when there had been no expectation of anything beforehand. Suddenly, without a trial, at [?] the command of Maximinus,
he was beheaded. With him were also many other bishops from Egypt who suffered in the same way.
Lucian, too, was a man distinguished in every way by his chaste conduct, and he was well trained in sacred learning.
He was a priest of the church in Antioch. They brought him to the city of Nicomedia, where the emperor was staying at that time.
After he had given an account before the judge concerning the teaching he proclaimed, he was committed to prison and put to death.
Thus, in a short time, the treacherous scheme of Maximinus, the hater of good things, grew stronger, and the persecution he stirred up against us was worse than the former one.
Chapter Seven. Concerning the inscriptions set up against us on pillars. Now the resolutions of the cities against us,
together with the emperor’s commands, were inscribed on bronze pillars in the middle of the cities—something that had never happened before.
And the children at school, using the records they had fabricated concerning our Savior and Pilate, as an insult, every day
would recite them aloud. Here, however, it seems to me appropriate to include the document of Maximinus,
which he set up on pillars, so that this man’s insolence, arrogance, boasting, and hatred toward God may all be openly known,
along with the righteous judgment that immediately overtook him, which did not sleep in repaying the wicked. When he was tormented by it, after a short time
he adopted the opposite policy toward us and issued other laws concerning us in writing. A copy of this translation of the decrees of Maximinus the Younger,
which he issued in response to the resolutions [?] against us that were submitted to him, copied from the pillars that stood in Tyre.
Look, even before now, the feeble audacity of human thought has gained strength and has driven away and abolished from itself all the darkness of the gloom of error,
which, a short time ago, was wrapped in the ruinous darkness of error and took the wicked captive.
And especially for those among us who are godless to recognize this: that through the benevolent providence of the immortal gods,
everything is governed and put in order. Yet this matter cannot be believed when it is told: how we received this favor with joy and love,
and how you demonstrated your god-loving disposition, although even before this everyone knew
with what care and reverence you regarded the immortal gods,
who recognize people’s devotion not through ordinary, empty words, but through evident, glorious, and steadfast deeds.
Therefore [?] your city is fittingly established and may be called a dwelling place of the immortal gods. It is therefore clear from many proofs
that it flourishes through the presence of the heavenly gods [?] because of your devotion. Therefore that great and exalted god Baalshamin, who dwells in your splendid city,
who rescued the god of your ancestors, of your wives, and of your children, as well as your dwelling place and your houses, from every destructive calamity,
stirred up in your souls this life-giving [?] desire, revealing and showing how excellent, glorious, and pleasing it is
to approach, with the worship that is due, the service and ministry of sacrifices to the immortal gods.
For who is so senseless that he can be wholly a stranger to the sun?
He does not perceive that this happens through the zealous benevolence of the gods, so that the earth should not reject the seeds entrusted to it,
and empty the farmers’ hope and disappoint their expectations; nor that the warfare of the wicked should [?] be settled upon the earth without restraint,
and the balance of the heavens be upset, and bodies be swept away to death through destruction; nor that the sea should rage with its waves at the blowing of powerful winds,
nor that whirlwinds should suddenly sweep through and bring a destructive winter; nor, again, that the earth, the mother who nurtures all,
should sink at its edges through the terror of its tremors; nor that the high mountains should be cast into the chasm that opens. For all these evils, and others worse than these,
everyone acknowledges were happening a short time ago. All these things happened together because of the ruinous error arising from the impudence of those people
who were without law, when it overflowed beyond their own souls, and it was as though shame had seized the whole inhabited world.
And a little later he says again: “Let them look at the great plains, whose fields rejoice in abundant harvests of grain,
and the meadows that rejoice in the growth of flowers, because of the abundance of rain and the favorable condition of the air, granted in a gentle balance.
Let everyone rejoice in our good religious devotion and in the service of sacrifices and burnt offerings. The divinity of the air, its power, and its stability have been appeased.
Therefore let them rejoice as they rest in the brightness of peace, truly at ease. And all those who have turned away from that blindness of error,
and have been fully helped and have come to a right and excellent understanding, let them rejoice greatly that they have escaped as though from a storm,
or as though from a severe illness, and from now on find rest in the fruits of life’s enjoyment. But if they persist in their accursed folly,
let them be removed and driven far away from your city and its territory, as you have requested, so that, in keeping with your zeal in this matter,
which deserves praise, your city may be kept far from every defilement and wickedness, in accordance with the desire implanted in it,
and may devote itself to the practice of sacrifices, with the worship that is owed to the immortal gods. And so that you may know
how gladly we have received this petition of yours, even without a petition, without a request, entirely of my own free will and with rejoicing,
our benevolent soul has agreed to do this for your honor and to receive whatever great gift you wish to request in return for this disposition that loves God and [?].
For you will receive it without hindrance, so that, when it is given to your city, it may forever bear good witness for you to your worship of the immortal gods.
And that you received a gift from our benevolence, as your achievement deserves, in return for this disposition of your lives, will be made known to your children and your grandchildren.”
Chapter Eight. Concerning what happened afterward through famine, pestilence, and war.
These things, then, were being posted and proclaimed against us in every province, so that, as far as human beings were concerned,

they were driving us away from every good hope, in accordance with that word of God which says that, if possible, even the elect would stumble through these things. But when they had become elated with great expectation,
while those who were carrying out the provisions of this decree issued against us were still traveling along the road from place to place, suddenly
God, who is the helper of his church, not only brought to nothing the tyrant’s boasting against us, but also revealed his heavenly help.
The rain that usually fell in winter was withheld from the land. Famine took a fierce hold, and with it came a deadly disease.
Another disease was spreading: an ulcer that, because of its burning heat, was called a burning coal.
Although it put the whole bodies of those afflicted by it in danger of death, it developed especially in the eyes of many.
It blinded tens of thousands of men, women, and children. It blinded tens of thousands of men, women, and children.
Along with these things, a war arose against the tyrant—the war with the Armenians.
These people had been friends and allies of the Romans from the beginning, and they too were Christians.
They zealously carried out their worship of God. But this enemy [?] they zealously carried out toward God.
But this enemy of God wanted to force them to sacrifice to idols and to hostile demons.
Instead of having them as allies, he set them against himself in [?]. Suddenly all these things came rushing upon him at once.
They rebuked the tyrant’s insolence and his arrogance toward God. For he used to boast that, because of his devotion to the idols,
and because of his persecution of us, neither famine nor plague nor even war had occurred in his days. But these things became severe together, all at once,
and marked the beginning of his destruction. He himself, with his entire army, was being defeated in the war against the Armenians.
As for the rest of those under his rule who lived in all the cities, a deadly famine overwhelmed them, so that a single modius of wheat
was being sold for two thousand five hundred coins. Tens of thousands were dying in every city,
and those in the villages and countryside were even more numerous. Thus those who had formerly been registered for the poll tax,
who had been numerous, were almost entirely wiped out. For suddenly, through lack of nourishment and the deadly disease,
they had perished. Some people even sold their beloved children to the rich for a little food.
Others sold their possessions little by little until they reached the utmost deprivation of necessities. Others chewed hay,
and ate harmful wild grass, damaging and destroying their physical health.
Even well-known women, driven by desperate need, went out into the marketplaces without shame and begged,
while the gauntness of their faces and the modesty of their clothing showed evidence of how they had been fed in their former happiness.
Those who had wasted away from hunger wandered here and there like lifeless images.
Their lives struggled within them as they staggered, and, unable to stand, they collapsed and fell in the marketplaces.
As they lay there, they begged for someone to hand them a little morsel of bread, and their [?] was close to departing.
They cried out that they were hungry, and they had strength only for this bitter cry. But those who were rich—
They were astonished at the great number of those begging. After giving a great deal, they had come to have harsh, merciless attitudes.
For they were afraid that they too might suffer the same fate as those begging. And now, in the middle of the streets and in the open places, dead bodies
lay stripped, left unburied for many days. They presented a degrading sight to those who saw them.
For many even became food for dogs. For this reason, those still alive turned to killing the dogs,
out of fear that they might go wild and set about eating human beings. For the plague was also feeding on every household,
especially those whom famine had been unable to destroy because their supply of food was abundant. Thus the wealthy leaders and governors,
and the many prominent people who had been spared by the famine—they in particular, through the deadly disease, swiftly [?] famine.
They in particular were dying swiftly and easily from the deadly disease. Every place was full of wailing, in the streets and in the open places.
There was nothing to be seen except weeping together with singing and dancing. Thus, as we said before, death waged war with these two weapons,
namely famine and disease, and in a short time devoured whole families, so that two or three bodies together
could be seen being escorted in a single funeral procession. Such was the repayment for the arrogance of Emperor Maximinus
and for the schemes that the cities were devising against us, while the zeal and righteousness of the Christians in everything
became evident among all peoples. They alone, amid all this distress caused by calamities,
showed sympathy and practical compassion every day. Some escorted and buried those who died—
and there were tens of thousands who had no one to care for them. Others gathered those tormented by hunger throughout each city
into one place and gave out bread to them all. And this deed
was proclaimed and became known among everyone, and they praised the God of the Christians,
acknowledging that these alone were righteous and truly feared God, as their deeds themselves had shown them to be.
Chapter Nine. On the disastrous downfall of the tyrants’ lives. While these things were happening in this way, the great and heavenly God, the helper of the Christians,
having shown all humanity a fitting repayment through the things just described, in return for the harsh treatment they had shown us, then, in his care for us,
turned toward us again with love and joy, and made the light of peace shine anew upon us as though in the gloom of darkness.
He showed everyone that he is God and that he is always watching over us in every circumstance, who [?] in every affliction
and disciplines his people at all times, and again, after sufficient discipline, makes peace and is reconciled with those who hope in him.
Thus Constantine arose, whom we have described as an emperor and the son of an emperor, a righteous man and the son of a righteous man, and restrained in everything.
He had been raised up by God himself, the King of all, and by our Savior, against those tyrants and wicked men.
He fought against them according to the rules of war, with God helping him in a marvelous way. And at Rome the tyrant Maxentius fell at the hands of Constantine.
The tyrant in the East lived only a short time after him. He too died disgracefully at the hands of Licinius, who at that time had not yet gone mad.
Chapter ten. On the victory of the emperors who loved God. First, then, Constantine, who held first place in imperial honor and rank,
took pity on those who were being oppressed by the tyrant at Rome, and called in prayer upon the God of heaven
and upon his Word, who is the Savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, to be his helper. He went out to battle with his entire army,
for he was intent on restoring to the Romans the freedom of their ancestors. Maxentius, however, relied on the craft of sorcerers
more than on the affection of those who obeyed him. He did not dare to venture even a little way outside the city.
With countless armed men and tens of thousands of cavalry troops, every region and city around Rome and Italy
that was subject to their authority he had armed. But Emperor Constantine, who had been raised up through help from God,
attacked the tyrant’s first, second, and third armies and defeated them decisively. He continued advancing and entered Italy.
Chapter eleven. On the final destruction of the enemies of devotion to God. When he reached Rome,
so that he would not be forced to fight against the Romans on account of the tyrant, God himself, as though with chains,
dragged the tyrant out beyond the city gate. And the things that had long ago been said about the wicked,
which were written in the holy Scriptures and regarded by many as mere stories, and which were believed only by believers,
were then confirmed by the event itself, both for believers and for those who did not believe, when they experienced and saw the marvel with their own eyes.
For just as in the days of Moses and the first generation of the Hebrews, he cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea,
and his chosen warriors sank in the Red Sea, and the depths covered them, so too Maxentius and the armed men with him
sank into the depths like stones, when they turned their backs before the power of God that was with Constantine.
As he was crossing the river, where he himself had fastened boats together and built a bridge across it, he had constructed a device for his own destruction.
Of him we may say: “He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and fell into the hole he made. His wrongdoing will return upon his own head, and his injustice will descend upon his own crown.”
For this very structure that he had fastened across the river suddenly came apart when the crossing was filled with men.
The boats sank into the depths, full of men, along with this wicked man—he himself first—and all his friends with him.
And, as the words of Scripture say, “They sank like lead in mighty waters.” So now, even if not in words, yet through the deeds themselves,
like those who were with Moses, the servant of God, and received victory from God, these very words about that earlier wicked tyrant
let us also sing in praise and say here: “Praise the exalted Lord, for he has shown himself exalted. He threw horses and their riders into the sea. A helper and protector.”
The Lord became my savior. Who is like you, Lord? Who is like you among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness,
fearsome and glorious, working wonders? For with these words, others like them, and still greater ones, Constantine, amid these events,
was praising God, the ruler of all and giver of victory, as he entered Rome in a triumphal procession.
And everyone together, with women and children, the assembly of the Senate, and distinguished men, along with all the people of Rome,
with cheerful faces and rejoicing hearts, welcomed [?] him with praises and overflowing joy as their savior, their life-giver, and their benefactor.
But he, who possessed the fear of God as though it were firmly planted within him, was not swayed by their acclamations
or puffed up by their praises, because he was deeply conscious of God's help. Then he ordered
that the victory of our Savior's suffering should be depicted in his statue, with him holding in his right hand the sign of our salvation,
that is, the cross. He set it up in a prominent place in the public square in Rome, and above it they wrote the following in Latin:
“By this sign of salvation, which is the emblem of courage, I rescued your city from the tyrant's yoke and set it free.
I also restored the Senate and the Roman people to their former glory and splendor.” Along with these things, Constantine also,
and with him Licinius, who at that time had not yet fallen into the madness to which he later came when his mind changed,
both praised God, who had been the source of every blessing for them. With one purpose and one will, they enacted a comprehensive law on behalf of the Christians,
together with an account of what God had done through the wonderful victory they had won over the tyrant. This very law they sent to Maximinus,
who was still ruling over the nations in the East, for he was still deceitfully displaying friendship toward them.
But because he was a tyrant, he was distressed by what had happened. Yet he did not want to appear to have obeyed others,
nor could he disregard what had been commanded, because he feared those who had given the command. Then, as though acting on his own authority,
he wrote this first letter to the governor on behalf of the Christians, though under compulsion. And concerning something that had never happened,

he vainly lied to himself.
Copy of the translation of the letter of the tyrant Jovius Maximinus Augustus to Sabinus.
“We make it known both to Your Excellency and to everyone that our lords and fathers, Diocletian and Maximian,
when they saw that everyone had abandoned the worship of the gods and had joined the Christian people, rightly commanded
that all those who had departed from the worship of the immortal gods should, through specified tortures and punishments,
be brought back to the worship of the gods. But when I first came to the land of the East and learned that in various places there were
many people capable of contributing to the affairs of the empire who were being persecuted by the judges for the reason stated above,
I gave orders to each of the judges that from now on they should not deal harshly with any of these inhabitants of the provinces.
But they should turn them to the worship of the gods through persuasion and encouragement. Then, when the judges were observing what I had commanded,
and no one in the eastern regions was being persecuted or mistreated, but because nothing harsh was being done to them,
they were turning all the more to the worship of the gods. After this, when I entered Nicomedia the following year
and was staying there, the citizens came to me with images of their idols and earnestly petitioned me
that by every means such people should be denied permission to live in the territory under their jurisdiction. I answered them as follows:
I received their petition favorably, but I saw that this request had not come from everyone.
If, however, there are some who persist in this religion, each of them should have control over his own choice, according to his own judgment.
And if they wish, let them [?] become acquainted with the worship of the gods. Nevertheless, both to the citizens of Nicomedia
and to the other cities, which had likewise pressed such a petition upon me,
that none of the Christians should live in their city, it was necessary to give a favorable answer, because this practice
had been observed by all the former emperors. It also pleased the gods themselves, in whose hands are all human beings
and the administration of the affairs of the empire, that I should now approve such a petition, presented for the sake of worshiping their divinity.
Although, before this time, written instructions were also sent to Your Honor, and an order was issued with authorization that this practice should not be observed
toward the inhabitants of the provinces, care should be taken for them, so that they are approached not with harshness but with gentleness and moderation. Nevertheless,
they must suffer neither insult nor loss at the hands of the officials or anyone else. I therefore thought it right to remind Your Honor of this in this letter as well:

that you should act toward the inhabitants of our territories especially through persuasion and encouragement, so that they may become acquainted—through persuasion and encouragement you should act toward the inhabitants of our territories,
so that they may become acquainted with the worship of the gods. Therefore, if anyone willingly chooses the worship of the gods,
we ought to welcome him. But if there are people who wish to continue practicing their own religion,
leave them to exercise their freedom. Therefore, Your Honor is obliged to observe what has been commanded.
No one is to be given authority to subject the inhabitants of our dominion to insult and loss [?]. As I said before, through encouragement and persuasion
it is especially fitting to turn the inhabitants of our dominion to the worship of the gods. But so that this command of ours may become known to all the inhabitants of our dominion,
you must ensure, through an edict issued by you, that what has been commanded is upheld. But he was compelled by necessity to issue this command,
and not by his own choice. And no one believed or trusted him anymore, because of the earlier concession he had made, which was like this one,
after which he had changed again and deliberately acted falsely. So none of our people dared to hold an assembly or even to show himself openly.
Nor, indeed, had his letter ordered anything of the kind. He had merely given permission for them to be spared coercion.
He did not permit us to hold assemblies, or to build church buildings, or to do anything else that was customary among us.
Yet those emperors, the champions of peace and reverence for God, had also written to him and urged him to do likewise.
Through decrees and laws they had granted this freedom to everyone under their authority.
But this wicked man was unwilling to yield in this matter until he was pursued by God's just judgment. In the end, however, he came to this against his will.
For his situation was as follows. He could not bear the greatness of the government entrusted to him, of which he was unworthy.
Instead, because he was untrained in the sober judgment required of an emperor, he approached affairs without deliberation. And besides all this,
in arrogance and conceit he exalted himself even above those who shared imperial power with him and were superior to him in every respect:
in ancestry, upbringing, education, the dignity of their authority, understanding, self-restraint, and, above all, true reverence for God.
He dared to exalt himself and claim the highest rank of honor. He was carried away by the arrogance of his madness.
He broke the covenant he had made with Licinius and, in hostility, prepared for war against him.
In a short time he traveled everywhere, threw all the cities into turmoil, and gathered his entire army of countless tens of thousands.
He marched out and drew up his forces against him, trusting in those demons whom he regarded as gods. He was filled with pride because of his tens of thousands of armed men.
But when he engaged in battle, he was abandoned by God and left powerless. Victory was granted by the one God to the man who then held imperial power.
First he lost the army of armed men on which he had relied, and the clothes that had covered him left him naked.
He sought refuge with the man who held power. The coward was quickly stripped of the imperial splendor that had not suited him.
In fear, humiliation, and weakness, he hid among the crowd. He fled, hiding in villages and fields.
He barely escaped alive from the soldiers' hands. By what happened, he demonstrated that God's words are true and trustworthy, for God says:
“A king is not saved by a great army, nor does a warrior escape through his great strength. A horse is a false hope for deliverance;
with all its strength it cannot rescue its rider. The Lord's eyes are on those who fear him, who wait for his grace, to rescue their lives from death.”
Thus, filled with shame, the tyrant returned to the territories under his control. First, in his mad fury,
many priests and prophets of those gods whom he had formerly admired, whose prophecies had prompted him to launch the war,
he put to death as sorcerers and deceivers who had betrayed his life. Afterward, he gave praise to the God of the Christians.
He enacted a full and comprehensive law to secure their freedom. But he fell gravely ill with a fatal disease.
No further time to live was granted him, and he departed from this world. The law he issued was as follows: “Emperor Caesar,
Gaius Valerius Maximinus, Germanicus, Sarmaticus, Pius, Felix, Invictus, Augustus. In every matter we exercise particular care.”
for the benefit of our territories. We wish to carry out these measures, which can readily be accomplished in every respect.
We believe that everyone should know and acknowledge, through their implementation, the measures that promote the orderly administration of the empire and are welcome to everyone's mind.
Even before this, it had come clearly to our knowledge that, because our illustrious fathers had ordered
—Diocletian and Maximian—that the assemblies of Christians should be abolished, they had suffered great losses at the hands of officials.
This has continued to happen until now to the inhabitants of our territories, whose interests we are eager to care for as we ought.
Because their possessions were being despoiled, letters were sent to the governors in every province before this year,
in which we laid down a law that, if anyone wished to follow this custom or to maintain this kind of worship,
he should be free to exercise his own will without restriction, and should not be prevented or hindered by anyone, and that it should be easy, without fear or anxiety,
for each one of them to do what pleased him. Nevertheless, even now we could not remain unaware that some of the judges were uncertain about our orders,
so that people became confused about our orders, and they were making them continually take part in religious observances
that they wished to practice. But so that all anxiety and uncertainty about religion might be removed, we laid down a law
that this command should be added: those who wish to conduct their lives according to this belief and this religion shall have permission,
by this grant of ours, as each of them wishes and finds agreeable, to follow the practice he has chosen to observe according to his custom.
They are also permitted to build their church buildings. And to make this grant of ours more generous, we also wish to command this:
if there are houses or places that formerly belonged by right to the Christians,
and that, by the command of our fathers, were transferred to another ownership, or were taken over by one of the cities, or were sold,
or were given to anyone as an honor, we command that all these be restored to the Christians' original ownership,
so that through this too everyone may recognize our care and our mercy. These are the words of the tyrant,
when not even a full year had passed since he had set up his command against the Christians on pillars.
And from the very man who, a short time before, had considered us wicked and godless, and a cause to the world
of every disaster, and who had not permitted us to live in cities or villages or even in the wilderness,
laws and commands were now being issued in favor of the Christians. And those who, a short time before, had been thrown to fire and sword
and as food for wild beasts before his eyes, and who had departed this world in disgrace through every kind of torture and punishment,
and had endured these things as wicked and godless people—to these very people he himself now grants permission,
allowing them to practice [?] their religion and build churches, and to recover ownership of what had belonged to them. But when he had considered such things,
It was like a kind of help to him, because he suffered less than he deserved.
He suffered a sudden blow from God. On the second occasion of battle, he was overthrown. This was how he departed from the world.
For it was not like military commanders and men victorious in battle, who distinguish themselves in warfare through notable victories,
that he happened to meet a glorious end with courage, but rather as a wicked man and an enemy of God.
For while the army was in the plain—the wicked man and enemy of God [?]. For while the army was stationed in the plain, he was hiding inside a house.
He received the punishment he deserved through a sudden blow from God. His whole body was being scourged, and he was tormented by severe and violent pains.
He lay prostrate and helpless, wasting away from hunger. His whole body was being consumed by an invisible fire sent upon him by God. And when he had wasted away completely,
his former appearance had been destroyed, but only his marrow remained alive. He was left like an image that had wasted away over a long time.
Those who encountered him and saw him thought nothing else of him except that his body was a tomb for his soul,
which was buried like a dead person who had completely wasted away. A violent fever, as though from the depths of his brain,
was burning him. His eyes sprang out of their sockets and fell out, and he was left blind. Yet his soul still lingered within him.
He acknowledged our Lord and asked for death. Finally, while acknowledging that he was suffering these things by a just judgment because he had insulted Christ,
his soul left him. Thus Maximinus [?] from the world, he who alone of the enemies of the fear of God
had remained, and who was worse than all of them. But the churches, by the grace of God Almighty, were being rebuilt from their foundations.
The message of Christ was at peace, to the glory of God, and gained greater freedom than it had had at first.
Their wickedness received the freedom it had had at first. But the wickedness of the enemies of the fear of God was filled with shame and disgrace.
First, Maximinus, who had been the enemy of all humanity, by those who held imperial power
was publicly exposed in written proclamations and named as a wicked and disgraceful tyrant who hated God.
As for the images of him and his sons that had been set up in his honor in every city, some were thrown down from their heights to the ground and smashed,
while others had their faces blackened in appearance. And the statues that stood as though in his honor
were likewise thrown down and smashed. They were made objects of laughter and amusement for those who wished to insult and mock them.
Furthermore, the honors of those other enemies of the fear of God were also being wiped away.
All those whom he had especially honored with positions of authority were put to death, because, to flatter him, they had arrogantly mocked our teaching.
These included Peucetius, whom he honored above everyone and who was more celebrated and beloved than the others, who had been consul two or three times,
and, above all, had been appointed prefect by him; and also Culcianus, who had exercised the full authority of government.
He too used to boast of the great amount of Christian blood he had shed in Egypt. And there were not a few others besides these,
through whose hands the tyranny [?] of Maximinus had grown and become strong. But righteous judgment, which forgets nothing, was also approaching Theotecnus
for what he had done to the Christians. For through that idol he had set up in Antioch, he thought he had won—
and because of it he had even been honored with a governorship by Maximinus. But when Licinius entered the city of Antioch, he conducted an investigation into the sorcerers.
He subjected the prophets and priests of that newly erected idol to torture, questioning them about how they produced this deception.
When they could no longer conceal it, being hard pressed by the tortures, they disclosed and made known that the whole secret of the deception
lay in the contrivance Theotecnus had devised. After him, his accomplices in sorcery were also handed over to death after many tortures.
To all these were added the sons of Maximinus, who until then had shared in his imperial honor and in the portraits erected for them.
Moreover, those who had previously [?] boasted of their kinship with the tyrant, exalting themselves and oppressing everyone,
also suffered terrible disgrace, like those we mentioned earlier, because they had not accepted correction
and had not recognized and understood the command in the Holy Scriptures: “Do not trust in a ruler or in a human being, who has no power to save.
His spirit departs, and he returns to his earth, and on that day all his plans perish.” But thanks be to God for everything,
for he is the Almighty and King of all; and to our Savior and the Deliverer of our souls, Jesus Christ, God’s only Son and his Word,
through whom we pray that peace may always be preserved for us, firmly established and unshaken by disturbances from outside or within the mind.
The ninth book is finished.
The tenth book, again, of the History of the Church.
