Chapter One. The peace given to us by God.
But thanks be to God for everything, to the Father and King of all,
and to our Savior and the Deliverer of our souls, Jesus Christ, God’s only Son and his Word, through whom we pray that peace may always be preserved for us,
firmly established and unshaken by disturbances from outside or within the mind. Along with these things, let us pray that we may also add this tenth book to the other books
of the History of the Church that were written previously. We will place it under your name, holy [?], and name you as the seal of the whole history.
[?] For the discourse of the perfect number, let us set out here the renewal and completion of the church, obeying the Spirit of God, who commands as follows:
“Sing a new song to the Lord, for he has done a marvelous thing. His right hand and his holy arm have won him victory. The Lord has made known his salvation.”
And his righteousness is revealed before the eyes of the nations. And following the command that bids us sing a new song of praise, let us too respond and say:
After dark and hateful accounts and sights, we have been counted worthy to see such things and to celebrate festivals.
Many righteous people and martyrs of God who came before us longed to see these things on earth and did not see them, and to hear them and did not hear them.
But they hastened on swiftly and were counted worthy of things better than these. They eagerly pressed on to heaven and paradise, to delight in God.
We, however, acknowledge that even these things are beyond our worth, and we marvel at the gracious gift of the Giver. We are filled with wonder, as is fitting.
And with all our soul and strength we worship, and we bear witness to the truth of what was spoken prophetically in Scripture,
which says: “Come, see the works of God, who has done wonders on earth and puts an end to wars from the ends of the earth.
He breaks bows and shatters spears, and the chariots of the earth. He breaks bows and shatters spears,
and burns chariots with fire.” And as we rejoice in these things that have actually been fulfilled among us, let us now proceed with the account.
Chapter Two. On the renewal of the churches. The whole race of God's enemies had been swept away, as we said above.
And the very sight of those people suddenly vanished, so that once again the word of God might be fulfilled, which says:
“I saw the wicked boasting and rising high like the trees of the forest. But when I passed by, he was no more; I sought him and did not find him.”
And now the day is cheerful and bright, without even the shadow of clouds, for the rays of heavenly light have illuminated all creation through the church of Christ.
And there is no grudging that even those outside our faith should share with us in the good things God has given us.
For even if not equally, they share at least to some small extent. Indeed, all people were granted freedom from their subjection to the tyrants,
and found relief from their former troubles. One after another, people confessed that there is truly one God, who is the helper of those who fear him,
and especially of us who place our hope in God's Christ. With that inexpressible delight,
the joy of God was blossoming in everyone. And every place that a short time before had been desolate through the wickedness of the tyrants
was seen being restored, as though recovering from a bitter, deadly illness. Church buildings were being built from their foundations and brought to completion,
and those that had previously been ruined were receiving greater splendor [?]. Moreover, those exalted emperors,
through earnest laws on behalf of the Christians, were confirming God's gift to us with greatness and power.
Imperial letters addressed to the bishops were also arriving, along with honors, gifts, and material possessions. At the appropriate point in the account,
we will inscribe their words in this book as though on sacred tablets, so that they may be known as a memorial to those who come after us.
Chapter Three. On the festivals for the dedication of churches that took place everywhere. Along with these things came the sight that we all love and pray for.
For people were gathering for dedication festivals in every city, new houses of prayer were being built, and bishops were assembling together.
And the gathering of the people from distant regions; and one people became acquainted with another through the love of distant members.
And one people became acquainted with another through the love of the members of Christ’s body. They were drawn toward unity and peace and gathered together.
As was said in the prophecy, which symbolically made known what was going to happen: bone drew near to bone,
and joint to joint. And the other things that the word of God had foretold symbolically in prophecy were being fulfilled without falsehood.
And one power, through the Spirit of God, was at work in all the members; they all had one soul and one mind in faith.
And from them all one song of praise thundered out, along with the complete service of the leaders of the churches, worthy of God,
and the offerings of the priests and the ordinances of the church, worthy of God. In one place, psalms and words given to us by God could be heard.
And there was a place where the services of God’s mystery were being performed, which is the hidden [?] of the suffering of our Savior.
And together, every kind and rank of men and women, with all the strength of their minds, in prayers and thanksgivings, rejoicing in soul and understanding,
were praising God, the giver of good things. And all who wished were singing compositions for the festivals of dedication,
according to the ability each of them had, and they were honoring and delighting the festival gathering.
And one of them, among the least of them, stood in the middle and delivered an address to the assembly of the church, while many shepherds were gathered there.
They were ready to listen quietly and modestly. He addressed one bishop in particular, who excelled in everything and was worthy of God,
who was renowned for his zeal, especially in Tyre in Phoenicia, and had built a magnificent temple there. He delivered the following address.
The fourth. An address on the splendor of the affairs of the church. An address to the festival gathering concerning the building of the church,
addressed to Paulinus, bishop of the church of Tyre. O priests, friends of God,
you who are clothed in a holy garment and a heavenly crown of praise, with God’s anointing, the robe of priesthood, and the Holy Spirit;
and you, O glory of the holy temple of God, honored with wisdom from God,
you who are renowned for the excellent deeds and accomplishments of a new election and victory, whom God himself, who rules the whole world,
has honored with an excellent gift: that you should build on earth a house for Christ, his Word and his only Son, and for his holy church, glorious to God.
If someone wishes to call you a new Bezalel, the master craftsman of God’s tabernacle, or Solomon, king of a new and more excellent Jerusalem,
or a new Zerubbabel, who made the latter glory of the temple far greater than the former—but you too, O lambs of God’s flock,
a dwelling place for good words, a school of modesty, and a beloved audience devoted to the fear of God,
you who in former times received in your hearing, through the divine readings, praises of devotion to God and the wonders of our Lord,
and his help toward humankind, and offered up praises to God—it is permissible to say this even while we are being instructed.
O God, we have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us what you did in their days, in the days of old.
But now we receive the uplifted arm and heavenly hand of our good King and God, not merely through hearing or through a report in words.
Rather, in actual deeds we see with our own eyes that the things handed down long ago for our help are true, and we believe them.
Let us offer a second [?] hymn of victory, and on the strength of the event itself let us cry out and say: “As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the mighty Lord.”
“In the city of our God.” But in which city? In this one, newly built and accepted by God, which is the church of the living God,
the firmly established pillar of truth. For another word of God also proclaims this: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.”
God has gathered us into it through the grace of his only Son. Let each one of those who have been called give praise and cry out and say:
“I rejoiced when they said to me, ‘We are going to the house of the Lord.’” And, “Lord, I have loved the service of your house and the place where your glory dwells.”
And let us honor and praise Christ, not only each of us individually, on our own, but also all together, with one spirit and one soul.
He is the one who is greatly honored and praised in the city of God and on his holy and glorious mountain. For he is indeed great.
His temple is great, lofty, and glorious, and his appearance is more beautiful than that of human beings. Great is our Lord, who alone works wonders.
Great is he who performs wonders without end and mighty deeds beyond counting. Great is he who changes times and seasons,
who removes kings and establishes kings, who raises the poor from the dust and lifts the wretched from the dunghill.
He has brought the powerful down from their thrones and raised the humble from the earth. He has filled the hungry with good things and humbled the arm of the arrogant.
He has confirmed the record of the accounts of old, not only for believers but also for those who do not believe.
He is the one who performs great wonders, the Lord of all and Creator of the whole world, the ruler of all, who is good to all, who alone is the one God.
To him we offer a new song of praise, responding and saying: “He alone performs great wonders, for his mercy endures forever.”
“He alone struck down great kings, for his mercy endures forever. He struck down great kings and killed mighty kings, for his mercy endures forever.”
“He remembered us in our humiliation.” [?] Let those who are exalted on earth acknowledge him. He is not a king who is merely an ordinary human being.
Rather, let him rightly be worshiped as the beloved Son of God and as the Word of God himself.
For which king has ever possessed such glory that his name should fill the tongues and ears of all human beings on earth?
What king has thus laid down and established just and chaste laws,

so that they are continually read in the hearing of all people, from the ends of the earth to the limits of the inhabited world? Or who has pacified rebellious nations with their barbarous and cruel way of life
through his gentle laws, which are full of mercy? Who, while being torn apart among all the nations, has displayed such glory among all humanity,
so that every day his teaching increases and is renewed throughout the world? Who has established a people like this, whose like has never been heard of before?
For he is not hidden in a corner of the earth, but stands throughout the whole creation under heaven. Who has so powerfully equipped his soldiers with pure weapons?
So that [?] their souls may remain steadfast in the struggle against the enemy. What king like this one has triumphed and prevailed in battle even after his death,
and won victory over his enemies? Every region and city among Greeks and barbarians is full of the temples of his kingdom and shrines dedicated to his divinity,
like these beautiful features, ornaments, and offerings of this temple, which are truly glorious and magnificent and worthy of wonder.
Such are the practical demonstrations of our Savior’s kingdom. For even now, he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and established them.
For who was bribed to have this established at his signal—the signal of him who is the King of all and the Ruler of all, the Word of God’s teaching?
His words require demonstration, understanding, and explanation, and not merely according to the thinking of those who labor over them. For he is also with this one who [?] and is God.

He sees the temples within the souls of them all, and he is discerned in the house being built from the living stones that have been gathered together, the house firmly established on the foundation of the prophets and apostles.
Jesus Christ himself has become the cornerstone of the building. He was rejected not only by those former builders,
who no longer exist, but also by those who still exist today, the wicked builders of the structure of wicked human beings.
But he was chosen by the Father, both then and now, to be the cornerstone of the building of this universal church.
He has therefore established this living temple, built from you for the living God, great, worthy of God, and truly holy.
Its hidden interior cannot be seen or examined by everyone, for it is truly the Holy of Holies. Who dares to look upon it or speak of it?
Who can enter boldly into the sanctuary except him who alone is the great High Priest, who alone has authority
to examine the hidden things of the spiritual soul? Yet perhaps another, second after him, can enter within—one alone:
this leader who presides over this flock, whom the first and great High Priest has honored with the priesthood in this church, next after himself,
and has made shepherd of this flock of God that is yours, according to the purpose and judgment of his Father, who appointed him over your people to be his minister and prophet—this new Aaron,
or Melchizedek, who resembles the Son of God. Through the prayer of us all, may he remain and be preserved by him forever. Let this man alone, then, have authority,
after the great and first High Priest, to see and examine the meaning of the inward life of your souls, and through experience and the passing of years to examine each person carefully.
In his diligence and care, he loves them all with adornment and speech grounded in the fear of God. He is more capable than anyone else,
among those empowered by God, of also offering words that match his deeds. For that great and first High Priest of ours,
in everything that it pleased his Father to do, himself follows his example. And this foremost teacher also
contemplates him with the clear eye of the mind as the original model and pattern. As far as he was able, he imitated him, built, and gave help.
He fell short of Bezalel in nothing, the man whom God himself [?] with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of craftsmanship for constructing the tabernacle,
which was fashioned according to a heavenly pattern and with wonders. So too this man, looking to Christ, the Word of God, wisdom, and light.
He clothed himself in his image. It is impossible to describe how he was formed to resemble him in abundant wisdom and goodness of soul.
With lavish expenditure, he made this magnificent temple resemble God as an outstanding visible representation.
For he splendidly fashioned what is invisible in this visible form. And first we ought to speak about this site.
It had been buried under filthy things through the enemies’ malice. He did not neglect it or abandon it to the damage of many years.
He could have found many other sites in the cities and easily avoided the strain of the work.
But he first stirred himself to the undertaking and strengthened all the people with his wholehearted resolve. He gathered them all into one great working force.
And this was the victory of the first contest he undertook: that the church itself, which had been taken captive and afflicted by enemies,
and had suffered persecution before us, just as we did, and which, like a mother, had been deprived of her children—he considered that she too ought to receive joy with us,
through the great gift of God’s grace. For since the great shepherd had driven away the wild beasts and wolves, every fierce and savage kind,
and broken the lions’ teeth, as is said in the word of God, and gathered the church’s children, it was right that the sheepfold itself should also be restored,
so that the enemy seeking revenge might be put to shame. He raised it up as a rebuke to the insolence of the wicked enemies of God.
And now those enemies of God no longer exist, for they did not exist long ago either.

For a short time they caused turmoil and were themselves thrown into turmoil. They received the punishment they deserved by a just judgment: they, their friends, and their households perished together.
Thus we may know that the things foretold long ago in prophecy in the holy Scriptures have been confirmed by events, although the word of God is confirmed in other matters as well.
But it is confirmed also in these declarations concerning them, which say: “The wicked drew the sword and bent the bow to kill the poor and the wretched,
and those whose ways are upright. Their sword will enter their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.” And again: “Their memory has perished and is no more,
and their name has been erased forever and ever.” And when calamities overtook them, “They cried out, but there was no one to save them.
They [?] to the Lord, but he did not answer them.” But “They sank down and fell, while we rose and stood ready.”
And what was said about them—“Lord, in the city you will despise their image”—has truly become evident before everyone’s eyes.
But those who, like the giants, waged a hostile war against God met with such a deadly overthrow.
But the church, which had been laid waste and despised by human beings, has come to this visible outcome,
because of her endurance for God’s sake. Let Isaiah’s prophecy cry out to her and say these words:
“Let the thirsty wilderness rejoice, and let the plain exult. Let it exult like a lily, and let the wilderness blossom and exult. Be strengthened, you slack hands,
and be made firm, you trembling knees. Say to the fainthearted: ‘Be strong and do not be afraid. Look, your God is coming and will secure justice for you.
He is coming and will save you.’ For water [?] has burst forth in the wilderness, and rivers in the dry land, because the wilderness has been turned into pools.”
And the thirsty land into springs of water. These words were spoken long ago in prophecy and recorded in the Holy Scriptures.
But the deeds were fulfilled among us not merely as something heard about, but in actual events. And she who was like a wilderness and like thirsty land,
and was like a widow without a husband—she whose gates they split with axes, as though cutting the trees of a forest,
and whose carved work they broke and destroyed together with hatchets and hammers—they burned God's sanctuary with fire
and defiled the dwelling place of his name on the ground. She whom all who passed along the road plundered, whose hedges they demolished, whom the boar from the forest devoured,
and on whom the wild animals grazed—look, through the wonderful power of Christ, now [?] who comforted you among all the children you bore.
And there was no one to take you by the hands. Look, I have taken from your hands the cup of staggering and the cup of my wrath. You will never drink it again.
And I will put it into the hands of those who humiliate you. Awake, awake, and put on glorious strength. Shake yourself free of the dust; rise and sit down.
Remove the yoke from your neck. Lift your eyes all around you and see your children gathering and coming to you. As I live, says the Lord,
you will put them all on like ornaments and adorn yourself like a bride. For your ruins, your desolate places, and your devastated land will be crowded with inhabitants.
Those who devour you will flee, and the children of your bereavement will say in your hearing, 'The place is too cramped for us to live in. Make room for us to settle.'
And you will say in your heart, 'Who bore these children? I am bereaved and a widow. Who raised these? I was left alone; where were they?'
Isaiah arose and prophesied these things. These things were recorded for us long ago in the Holy Scriptures, and we were to receive their confirmation in actual deeds.
But the bridegroom, who is the Word of God, spoke these things to his bride, who is the holy Church. And this friend of the bridegroom, for this very one who had been desolate and overthrown
and was without hope in human eyes, stretched out your hands through the prayers of us all and raised her up, at the command of the will of God, the King of all.
And through the great manifestation of the grace of Jesus Christ, he raised her up and established her in this way, just as he had learned from the book of prophecy.
This is a great marvel and an immense wonder to those who contemplate it, even if their attention is confined to its outward appearance.
But a marvel surpassing this marvel is the renewal of the soul in the fear of God, which is a demonstration of the knowledge of God.
Of this these things are types and representations: the soul that the Son of God himself created in his image, granting to the image of God in every respect
a nature that is incorruptible and incorporeal, and [?] from every earthly defilement—a being endowed with the luminous understanding of the Word.
He who once, at the beginning, brought her into existence from nothing fashioned her and made her a bride and a holy temple for himself and his Father,
as he himself plainly declares and makes known when he says, 'I will dwell in them and be their God, and they will be my people.'
And such is the pure and perfect soul, which from the beginning [?], so that she might be clothed in the image of the heavenly Word.
But through the envy and jealousy of the demon who loves evil, by a deliberate choice of will, she became a lover of passions and a lover of hateful things,
and she was abandoned by God like a wilderness, so that it would be easy for those who envied her to devour her and take her captive.
And she was overthrown by the cunning schemes of hidden enemies, and her downfall was astonishing.
Until [?] there remained in her one stone upon another of the victories of righteousness. She was also thrown to the ground like a corpse.
She was completely stripped of all the upright thoughts of nature. And when this soul, created in the image of God, lay overthrown,
it devoured her—not that wild boar we can see, but the demon who works destruction, together with the invisible beasts of the wilderness.
In their wickedness they shot burning arrows into her. They cast down God's sanctuary and burned it with fire, and profaned the dwelling place of his name on the ground.
They battered and drove the wretched soul about with the affliction of their wickedness. They changed her and left her without hope of life.
But the Word, who is God, the light and Savior, cared for her and bore her burden, accepting the punishment her sins deserved.
He took her up again, according to the will of his merciful Father. First he chose for himself the souls of those exalted kings.
And through those who love God, he cleansed creation of all the defiled and ruined people,
and of the wicked tyrants who hate God. Then those men known to them, who had long served him as priests in secret,
and had sheltered beneath his wing, he revealed and brought into the light. He honored them with the Father's great gifts, as they deserved.
And again, through these men, the souls that had been stained a little earlier and had remained hidden in fear of the tyrants' decree,
he cleansed and purified with the reproof of his teaching. He illuminated and brightened the dwelling place of your minds, and then entrusted it to this wise leader, who is worthy of God.
Although he is discerning and intelligent in other matters as well, he knows especially well the souls entrusted to him.
He distinguishes and builds without ceasing, from the first day until now. At times he sets shining gold and precious, splendid stones within your souls,
so that the mystery of holy prophecy may once again be fulfilled in you in practice. In it, these words are spoken: “Look, I am making your stones beryls,
and I will establish your foundations with sapphires. I will build your walls with jasper and your gates with choice stones.
All your children will know me, and the peace of your children will increase. You will be established in righteousness.” Such is the great temple
that stands throughout all creation beneath heaven. The Word, who is God, the Creator of everything above heaven, also on earth
made its radiant likeness, so that his Father might be honored and worshiped by all creation and by all humanity.
But that place above heaven, which is here beneath it [?], is Jerusalem above and Zion, the heavenly mountain,
and the glorious city of the living God. In it are great hosts of angels and the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.
With surpassing, inexpressible praises they praise their Creator, the ruler of all. No mortal can praise him as he deserves.
For no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived these things that God has prepared for those who love him.
Having been deemed worthy of these things, a little out of much, men together with women, little children together with adults, all of us together, with one spirit and one soul.
But let us never cease giving thanks and praise to him who has been the source of all these good things for us, to him who forgives the wrongdoing of us all,
to him who heals the diseases of us all, to him who satisfies our desire with good things, who has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our wrongdoing.
For as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our wrongdoing from us. And as a father has compassion on his children,
the Lord has compassion on those who fear him. Then, both now and at all times, as these things are continually renewed in their respective places,
also on this joyful feast and this glad and radiant day, let us, by day and by night, keep him who is the source and origin of this feast
before our eyes at every moment and with every breath, loving and worshiping him with all our strength and soul.
Now too, let us rise and plead with him in a voice of love, that he may shelter us under his protection and preserve us until the end, and send us the everlasting peace that comes from him,
which cannot be shaken or broken, through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom glory belongs to him forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter Five. The emperors' legislation concerning the rights of Christians, and an account of Licinius. Such were the things that God's heavenly grace granted through the appearing of our Savior.
And such abundant blessings were given to all humanity through our peace. Here, meanwhile, we were celebrating joyful feasts.
But the envious hater of good, the demon who loves evil, could not bear the sight of these things. Thus, not even Licinius's intentions were sufficiently checked
by what had happened to the tyrants whom we mentioned earlier. He was prospering in his rule, holding second place in honor, and was a kinsman by marriage of the great Emperor Constantine.
Yet he was very far from imitating Constantine's noble qualities. Instead, he emulated the wicked conduct of the ungodly tyrants.
He wished to follow the intentions of those whose ruinous end he had seen with his own eyes,
rather than remain in friendship and love with the emperor who was his superior. He envied the very man who had been his benefactor,
and prepared a hateful and bitter war against him. He had no regard for the law of nature, or for his oaths, or for their ties of blood.
Nor did he remember the covenant between them. For Constantine himself had given him a sign of genuine love,
as a good emperor, and had not begrudged making him his kinsman, but had given him his sister in marriage.
He had also considered him worthy to share in his ancestral lineage and his ancient royal family.
He had given him authority to rule over all as his brother-in-law and partner in the empire, empowering him, like himself, to govern and administer the nations under Roman rule.
But this man acted in the opposite way. Every day he plotted against his superior and devised every kind of deceitful scheme,
to repay his benefactor with evil. At first he concealed his treacherous schemes and presented himself to him as a friend.
But he repeatedly attacked him deceitfully and in secret, thinking that he would easily achieve what he wanted.
God, however, was Constantine's friend, his caretaker and guardian. The plot being forged against him in secret and darkness
he brought to light and exposed. Thus Constantine possessed the great weapon of reverence for God with which to repay his enemies.
And the power that guarded his life, through which our king, beloved of God, remained strong and [?] from the schemes of this abominable man.
But when he saw that his hidden deceit was not succeeding as he wished, because God had revealed all his deceit and evil intentions to the king who was pleasing to God,
he no longer acted in secret, but openly launched a war against both Constantius and God.
For he knew that it was God whom he worshiped. Then he began to destroy those who feared God, who [?] had never harmed [?].
At first, however, [?]. He did these things cunningly [?], claiming that he was compelled [?] the evil planted [?] in him, without [?].
His eyes [?] the memory of those before him [?] the Christians. Also [?] that he had destroyed [?] them. But when he turned away from sober thought and his mind became deranged,
he waged war against God, who was Constantine’s helper, instead of against the man who received help from him. First he persecuted the Christians who were in his household.
The wicked man deprived himself of the prayer they offered to God on his behalf, as they had received this teaching from their fathers:
that they should pray for everyone. Afterward, he also ordered that the soldiers in every city be dismissed and stripped of the honor of their rank
if they were unwilling to sacrifice to demons. Yet these things were small when compared with others greater than them.
But why should we recount one by one the deeds of this hater of God, and how [?] himself from the law [?]?
And did he not violate the law in this? For concerning those who [?] were in prison [?], there was a law that no one [?] with a piece of bread [?]
[?] to them, and no one [?] those who were perishing [?] from hunger. Nor was anyone to be kind or to do anything good,
though nature itself draws people to have compassion on their neighbors. It was an utterly shameless violation of the law,
harsh and alien to every peaceable instinct, for he imposed a punishment on those who showed compassion:
they were to suffer the same fate as those on whom they had compassion, and were to be bound and confined in prison.
Those who showed mercy were to receive the same punishment. Such were the commands of Licinius.
But why must we enumerate the new laws he enacted concerning marriage and those departing this world?
Through these he dared to alter the ancient laws of the Romans, which had been established well and wisely.
In their place he enacted barbarous and harsh laws, and devised enormous financial losses
and imposed them on those under his authority through levies of every kind, in gold and silver, and through measurements of land.
He collected poll taxes for people who had died in the villages long before. Along with these things, whenever this hater of humanity found people,
though they had committed no offense, he expelled them from their homes. He cast out honored men of distinguished ancestry,
separated their wives from them, and handed the women over to filthy slaves for abominable acts.
And how many married women and young virgins this filthy old man himself violated, satisfying his own lustful desire!
But why should we prolong the account of these things? For the enormity of his later deeds
made his earlier ones seem like nothing. At the height of his madness, he even dared to attack the bishops.
He regarded them as servants of God and as opponents of what he was doing. Yet, because he still feared the man who was superior to him,
he plotted evil against them not openly but in secret. He had the most distinguished among them killed through the governor's treachery.
Even the manner of their death was extraordinary: nothing like it had ever been heard of.
But what happened around Amasea [?] and in the other cities of Pontus surpassed all cruelty. There, God's churches
were in some cases razed to the ground, while others were shut so that no one could gather in them or conduct worship in them,
or offer God the service that was due to him. For he thought that the prayers conducted in them were not on his behalf. Rather, he was convinced
that they did everything to please God on behalf of Constantine, the emperor beloved by God. For this reason he attacked us in his fury.
The flattering governors understood what the impure man wanted them to do. Some of them, against the bishops,
imposed punishment as though they were trying criminals. The bishops were taken away and tortured without cause.
In other ways they endured a strange and terrible end: their bodies were cut into small pieces with a sword
and thrown away. Once again, God-fearing people were persecuted and fled, and once again the countryside and the wilderness,
the mountains and the hills were filled with servants of Christ our Lord. And because that wicked man was succeeding in these things,

he now planned to stir up persecution against everyone throughout the whole country. This would have happened if God, the swift helper of our souls, had not, as though out of darkness and the gloom of night,
suddenly caused a great light and a savior for all to shine forth—Constantine, his servant. With an uplifted arm he led him and brought him forward,
and from heaven gave him victory over the wicked man as the fruit of righteousness that he deserved. As for that impure man,
together with his advisers and all his friends, God overthrew him and cast him down at Constantine's feet.
For when he advanced against him in the extremity of his madness, this friend of God formed a sober plan and combined firm justice with mercy.
Thus he resolved to secure justice for those who were being oppressed by the tyrant, and determined to save a great multitude of human beings
through the destruction of a few evil men. For before this time he had shown nothing but mercy toward a man who did not deserve it,
but who would not turn away from his evil deeds. Instead, his madness grew still greater against the peoples under his authority.
Those who were suffering had neither hope nor life left, because the tyranny of that evil serpent had overpowered them.
For this reason, the man who was the helper of the good combined hatred of evil with love of goodness, and went out to extend a life-saving right hand
to all who were perishing. Then he called upon God, the King of all, and upon his Son, the Savior of all.
to be his helper and guide. He divided the army into units against God's enemies and easily won the victory.
Everything was suddenly and swiftly brought low before him in battle by God. Those who only yesterday were breathing threats of death
did not even leave their name [?] in remembrance. Their images, together with their portraits, received the disgrace they deserved.
The very things that Licinius had seen with his own eyes happen to those earlier wicked tyrants happened to him, because he too refused to learn.
He was not put to shame by the blows suffered by his companions. Because he followed the path of their wickedness, he was condemned to a judgment like theirs.
But while this man lay overthrown in this way, the victorious Constantine, who was distinguished by every excellence of devotion to God,
together with his sons who loved God and resembled their father in everything, took possession of their eastern territory. And as before,
they established a single Roman government. From the rising of the sun, spreading throughout every corner of the inhabited world,
their peace prevailed. All the fear that had previously gripped people was taken away from them.
They celebrated splendid festival days, and light shone joyfully everywhere. With joyful faces and cheerful eyes, those who previously had been [?]
all looked at one another. With hymns and psalms, too, in every city and marketplace,
they praised God, the King of all, before everything else, as they had been taught; and after him, the emperor who feared God.
All who loved God acclaimed him. The former evils and acts of wickedness were forgotten.
They enjoyed the good things that were present and looked forward to those yet to come. The victorious emperor's decrees were published everywhere,
full of mercy, along with great laws. They contained generosity and demonstrations of true devotion to God.
Thus, when all tyranny had been cleared away, the empire that rightfully belonged to them was preserved for them alone, firmly established without opposition:
for Constantine and his sons, who purged the world of the hatred toward God shown by all their predecessors.
We experienced the good things God had granted them, just as they themselves, through their love of virtue and love of God,
openly displayed thanksgiving and worship toward God before all people. The writing of the ten books of the Ecclesiastical History is finished.
Composed by Eusebius of Caesarea. Book One: thirteen accounts of the church. Book Two: twenty-six accounts of the church.
Book Three: thirty-nine accounts of the church. Book Four: twenty-six accounts of the church. Book Five:
twenty-eight accounts of the church. Book Six: forty-five accounts of the church. Book Seven: thirty accounts of the church.
Book Eight: seventeen accounts of the church. Book Nine: eleven accounts of the church. Book Ten: five accounts of the church.
The accounts written by Mar Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, number two hundred and forty in all.
Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen and amen.

Blessed be God and his Messiah, who strengthened his lowly, sinful servant Isaac, who wrote this book for the honored, excellent, and chosen servant of God, Mar [?]. Therefore, everyone who reads and learns,
let him remember the owner and the scribe, and pray that the Lord God himself will bring them through that dreadful place, the abode of terror, and bring them to the kingdom of his beloved Son,
our Lord Jesus Christ, and seat them at the table of his majesty with his holy chosen ones, when they are served by the blessed angels. [?] Amen and amen.
It was written and completed in the month of Nisan in the year seven hundred and seventy-three, [?] city. May all who fear Christ be remembered forever. Amen.
May there always be a good remembrance before God for Mar the priest [?], the village of [?], the sister of Mar [?]. [?] And amen.
Through the prayers of all the upright and chosen, may mercy rest upon the scribe who wrote with care, as he hoped. Yes and amen.
Another notice: concerning the different versions of the divine Scriptures. From the work of Eusebius of Caesarea.
From chapter sixteen of the sixth book of the Ecclesiastical History: how Origen devoted himself to the holy Scriptures.
Origen investigated the holy Scriptures so carefully that he even learned the Hebrew language.
He also acquired the books that the Jews possess in Hebrew writing.
He also investigated the versions of the sacred translations made by others besides those seventy.
He found other translations of the holy Scriptures that differed from those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.
Although they had been concealed and hidden away for a long time, he searched them out and brought them to light. And because it was not known who had translated them,
he reported only this about them: that he had found one of them in Nicopolis, and the others in another place.
In the translation of the Psalms that he prepared, after those four known translators, he showed that there was also another translation—a fifth, a sixth, and a seventh.
He reports concerning one of them that it was found at Jericho in a jar, in the time of Emperor Antoninus, the son of Severus.
He gathered all these translations together, went through them, and arranged them opposite one another, along with the Hebrew characters. He left a copy of what are called the Hexapla.
And from these [?] he also arranged those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion together with that of the seventy-two.
From chapter seventeen: Symmachus, who translated the Scriptures. We ought to know that Symmachus, one of those who translated the Scriptures,
was an Ebionite. This is the heresy called that of the Ebionites, who say that Christ was born of Joseph and Mary,
and consider him to have been an ordinary human being. They say that the Law must be observed in the Jewish manner, as we have already explained in this history.
There are writings by Symmachus that survive to this day, in which he argues against the Gospel of Matthew
in order to establish this heresy. Origen reports concerning these writings, together with other translations of the Scriptures made by Symmachus,
that he received them from a woman named Juliana. He said of her that she had received these books from Symmachus.
From chapter twenty-five: how Origen mentions the books accepted in the church. Now, when he was commenting on the first Psalm,
He set out a numbered list of the sacred books of the Old Testament. He spoke as follows:
“We should make known that the accepted books, as the Hebrews have taught [?] us, are twenty-two, corresponding to the number of their letters.”
Afterward he added: “These are the twenty-two books among the Hebrews: the one called Genesis among us
is called ‘The beginning of the book’ among the Hebrews, that is, ‘Bereshith.’ Exodus is called ‘Wezelmaoth’ in Hebrew, which means ‘And these are the names.’
Leviticus is ‘Weniqra,’ that is, ‘And he called.’ Numbers is called ‘Aspequdim’; Deuteronomy, ‘Ellehdebarim,’
that is, ‘These are the words.’ Joshua son of Nun is ‘Joshua ben Nun.’ Judges and Ruth are called ‘Ahushpatim.’
The two books of Kings are called ‘Ana.’ Dabrimin is one book, that is, ‘Words of the Days’; and Ezra is two books,
which they call ‘Ihiezra,’ meaning ‘Helper.’ The book of Psalms is called ‘Seph Tellim.’
The Proverbs of Solomon are called ‘Maloth.’ Ecclesiastes is called ‘Qoheleth.’ The Song of Songs they call ‘Shir Shirim.’
Isaiah, ‘Iaisia’; Jeremiah with his Lamentations, ‘Ahermia’; Daniel, ‘Daniel’; Ezekiel, ‘Hezeqiel’;
Job, ‘Job’; Esther, ‘Esther.’ [?] Besides these there are also the books of Maccabees, which bear the title ‘Sabna Eli.’”
He set these things down in the discourse we have mentioned. In the first discourse that he wrote on the Gospel of Matthew,
he upheld the rules of the church and testified that he recognized only four Gospels. He wrote as follows:
“From tradition I have learned about the four Gospels, which alone are undisputed throughout the whole church of God under heaven.
First Matthew wrote, who had formerly been a tax collector and afterward became an apostle of Jesus Christ.
He wrote it in Hebrew letters for those who had come to faith from Judaism. Second was Mark,
who wrote as Peter related things to him. Peter called him ‘my son’ in his general letter, writing, ‘The church in Babylon, chosen just as you are, sends you greetings,
and so does Mark, my son.’ Third was the Gospel of Luke, whom Paul commends, who composed it for those who had come to faith from the nations.
Last of all was John’s.” In the fifth commentary that he composed on the Gospel of John, he spoke as follows about the letters of the apostles:
“Paul, who was found worthy to become a minister of the new covenant—not of the letter, but of the Spirit—
who had fulfilled the preaching of the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, also wrote letters to all the churches [?].
But even the letters he wrote contain few words. Peter, on whom Christ’s church was built, against which the gates of Sheol cannot prevail,
left only one letter acknowledged by the church. Perhaps there is a second as well, since there is disagreement about it.
What shall we say about John, who [?] would produce so many things that the world could not contain them? He also wrote Revelation,
and was commanded to remain silent and not to write down the voices of those thunders. He also left one letter.
whose words are few. But let there also be a second and a third [?], since not everyone acknowledges that they are his.
Yet the two together do not contain even a hundred words. He also spoke again about the letter to the Hebrews while explaining it:
That the character of the language of that letter to the Hebrews, while he explains it, that the character of the language of that letter to the Hebrews:
Its expression is not unpolished, as the apostle himself acknowledges about himself in his own words, that he was unpolished in speech.
For this letter is more accomplished in its composition in the Greek language than the apostle’s other letters.
Everyone competent to judge differences in expression acknowledges this. Furthermore, the thoughts it contains
are remarkable and are not inferior to those the apostle wrote. Everyone who knows how to examine the apostle’s writings agrees that this is true.
After this he adds, saying, “I judge and say that the thoughts contained in this letter—
someone who remembered what the apostle used to say and, like a disciple, wrote down what his teacher used to say.
Therefore, whatever church possesses this letter, let them hold to it as belonging to the apostle.
But who actually wrote this letter, God alone knows. An account concerning it has reached [?],
that some say Clement wrote it, the one said to have been bishop of the church of Rome. Others, however, said
that Luke wrote it, the one who wrote the Gospel and Acts.” These things, then, have been said up to this point. …
